generated_text: Honestly, Maisie, you wouldn't believe the day I’ve had. Proofreading a whole brochure for a dog grooming salon. Dog grooming! Who knew that was a thing? And their fonts…oh, the fonts. It was a visual assault. A dog grooming salon brochure? You’re right, that  is  pretty niche. Sounds… stressful. How's little Leo behaving? He looks like he’s about to launch into a full-blown eruption any minute. He's a little bundle of chaos, isn’t he? On the verge. Just trying to distract him with a rattle. He'll be one next month, can you believe it? It's flying by. We need to start thinking about a party, don't we? Though, realistically, it'll probably just be a few close friends and family. Absolutely. A big one would just be too much with him. I was thinking maybe at our place? We’ve got the garden, and it's easier than coordinating with Grandma and Uncle Derek. So, what did you have in mind? Cake and chaos is always a winning combination. Cake and chaos is  definitely  the theme. I’ll handle the catering, you could sort out the decorations? Something low-key, Leo won't notice the streamers anyway. Speaking of which, have you heard from Mum about visiting next weekend? She was talking about coming up to see Leo. She texted earlier. Says she's booked the train. Sounds like she's really looking forward to it. Though she did mutter something about needing to find a present for his first birthday. She’s always so flustered with presents, isn’t she? She is. Last time she bought Finn a giant inflatable dinosaur for his third birthday. He was terrified of it! Right, I need to change Leo. Did you manage to get anything done today, or was it just a day of watching daytime TV? A bit of both, to be honest. I’ve been trying to sort through some old photos for the family album. It's a monumental task, you know? So many memories! I found some absolute gems of us as kids. Remember that ridiculous perm I had? Oh my god, yes! It was like a poodle had exploded on your head! You looked so mortified. Your dad thought it was hilarious, though. He kept calling you “Fifi.” Don't remind me! I wanted to be like Madonna, and ended up looking like a poorly groomed sheepdog.

Right then. So, tell me  everything  about your trip to Portugal. Honestly, the pictures you sent were gorgeous, but I need the full gritty details. Did you actually manage to escape academia for a bit? Escape is a strong word, Maisie. I took a very extended study break, let's say. And yes, it was...amazing. Lisbon was mental, in the best possible way. Such a vibe. Completely different to Birmingham, even. Did you know they have these little trams that clamber up these ridiculously steep hills? Nearly gave me a heart attack trying to keep up with one. Oh, sounds like  you  gave it a heart attack! Were you actually looking at anything historical, or just soaking in the sun? Because realistically, you, a PhD student, doing a "study break" in Portugal... I’m suspicious. Okay, you got me. There  was  some historical sightseeing. Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower… the usual. Tidied up my literature review notes while I was there. But most of the time, I was wandering around Alfama, getting deliberately lost in the alleyways, eating pastel de nata way too often… and generally trying to switch off. They call it  saudade , that feeling of longing... Honestly, it's a mood. I felt it acutely.  Saudade ? Sounds intense. See, that's the kind of thing I need. I’ve been buried in reports for months, it feels like. I'm craving  saudade . Though I’m not sure Portugal is the answer for me. I was thinking more Iceland, actually. Completely different vibe, right? Stark, desolate beauty instead of… well, Lisbon’s vibrant chaos. Iceland! That's spectacular, but brutally cold, right? You’d need a serious packing list. Portugal was mild, even in October. We did a day trip to Sintra, the Pena Palace is insane. Like a Disney castle dropped into the mountains. Tourist trap, obviously, but worth it for the photos alone. I nearly tripped over a pug wearing a tiny crown. You're winding me up! A pug wearing a crown? I swear! It was the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever seen. Honestly, it perfectly summarised the trip - a combination of profound beauty and utter absurdity. Have you considered the Schengen area at all for your trip? I've been thinking about going on a cycling tour through the Netherlands and Belgium next year, but with all the Brexit bother, the travel insurance looked a nightmare to figure out.

Right, Monopoly is officially banned for at least a month. I’m feeling emotionally drained. But Mummy, it was  so  close! I was about to buy Park Place! I had the boot! A really good boot! Darling, a boot doesn’t win you Monopoly. It just lets you… well, boot people around. And you two were absolutely ruthless. Honestly, I felt like I was being financially assaulted. We were being strategic! It’s a game of strategy! Yeah! Strategy! Absolutely. Brilliant strategy. But my strategy is to never play Monopoly with you two again. At least, not until I've recovered. So, moving on... dessert. What are we thinking? I was thinking crumble. Apple or rhubarb? Apple! Definitely apple. With lots of custard! Thick, gloopy custard! Custard  and  ice cream! Please, Mummy! Ice cream  and  custard? That's a serious sugar rush you’re aiming for. Alright, apple crumble with lots of custard, and a little scoop of vanilla ice cream for the special requests. Yay! Can we watch a cartoon while we eat it? Of course. Which one? We can't watch Paw Patrol  again . Your dad would stage a coup. Bluey! Bluey is good. Bluey is boring! Peppa Pig! Peppa Pig? Really? You’re nearly ten! It’s funny! George is silly! You’re something else, you are. Alright, Peppa Pig it is. Now, about the Monopoly money… I’m seriously considering declaring bankruptcy for  all  of us. It’s causing too much tension in the house. But Mummy! I need money for… for buying things! Like dinosaurs! You have a whole room full of dinosaurs, darling. You don’t  need  Monopoly money to buy dinosaurs. It’s just… pretend money. It’s not  just  pretend money! You can buy houses and hotels and be rich! And then you can bankrupt your poor, unsuspecting mother. See? That’s why it’s stressful! Look, maybe we can agree something. No more Monopoly for a month. And instead of trying to amass a fake fortune, we can actually save some real money. We could all put a pound in a jar each week. A jar? For what? For something fun! Maybe we can go on a little day trip somewhere. Somewhere with... ice cream. Ice cream! Yeah! And maybe dinosaurs? We’ll see. Saving money is the first step. Now, who wants to help me peel the apples? And try not to squabble over who gets the best ones.

Honestly, this drizzle is brutal. I thought moving south meant sunshine, not perpetually damp grey. Dramatic much, Liv? It's a bit of rain. It'll pass. Besides, you said you wanted to experience a different part of the country. This  is  England. Expectation management, darling. Expectation management coming from the lad who claims to be able to build a bridge with a paperclip and some sticky tape. You set the bar pretty high, remember? That was a theoretical exercise! And quite brilliant, if I do say so myself. More importantly, are you settled in alright? The flat? Work? The flat’s…small. Very small. But it's mine, and it’s in London, which is buzzing. Work's…interesting. Proper, proper different from what I’m used to. It's just, everyone talks proper posh. Like, I feel like I’m constantly tripping over me words, trying to sound…refined. Refined? You? Liv, you’re Liv! You've got a vocabulary that would make a dictionary blush, even if you  do  occasionally throw in a rogue "gan" for good measure. They’ll get used to you. Honestly, people are mostly just…pretentious. Ignore it. Easy for you to say, Mr. Postgraduate, Consultant Engineer, practically groomed for polite society. I’m used to having a proper geordie banter, like, a bit of back and forth. Here, it's all…subtle hints and meaningful glances. I practically got blanked at lunch for saying someone’s shirt was a "bonny bit of kit”. Right? A "bonny bit of kit"! Oh, Liv. You're a delight. See, that’s what I love about you, you just say what you think. London isn't ready for that level of honesty and charm. Charm? I nearly caused an international incident involving a cashmere cardigan! Seriously, I think I saw a monocle pop out. Well, you’re shaking things up. Good! Staying true to yourself is what matters. And speaking of shaking things up, how's the Corpus Administration going? They’re not expecting you to re-write the entire English language, are they? Don't even. It's a  lot  of metadata and categorization. And ancient texts. Lots and lots of dusty, ancient texts. Honestly, the sheer volume of baffling grammar from the 17th century is enough to drive a girl mad. I spent half a morning arguing with a scribe about the correct usage of ‘thou’. And who won that argument?

Right then. Didn’t expect young Amelia to be quite so… enthusiastic about this restoration project, did you, Arthur? Seems she’s got a bee in 'er bonnet about authenticity. Authenticity, eh? That’s a fancy word for youngsters. Back in my day, we just called it using what you 'ad. You’re talkin' about the Old Mill, aren’t you? Saw her goin' on about reclaimed timber and whatnot. Bound to be a bit pricey. Pricey is right, Arthur! Honestly, the things they want to do. Amelia was explaining it all, the principles of sympathetic restoration – and I’m trying to follow, I really am! But it's all so technical. Biscuits anyone? Ginger snaps. Ginger snaps, just what I needed. And yes, the Old Mill. It's a landmark, you know. Should be respected. But spending a fortune to make it look like it did in 1887? Seems a bit much, doesn’t it? Especially when the council’s got so many other things needing attention. Council’ll be stickin' their noses in, mark my words. They always do. Remember when they tried to put those modern streetlights along the river path? Looked like somethin’ out of a spaceship. Had to fight tooth and nail to get ‘em taken down. They did, didn't they? And it was a right palaver. Amelia’s determined to keep the council happy, though. She’s saying she’s involved them from the start, got preliminary approvals. She mentioned something about grant applications too. Grant applications... therein lies the rub. Always a mountain of paperwork, and you’re at the mercy of some committee in London who’ve probably never even  been  to Norfolk. What do they know about a proper Norfolk mill? Bureaucracy. It’ll swallow you whole, it will. Reminds me of me trying to get a bus pass when I first turned seventy. Forms, forms, and more forms! Ended up with Mrs. Higgins down the road helping me fill 'em out. Bless her heart. Poor Arthur! Well, Amelia’s quite resourceful, you know. She's got that sharp mind, always has. She's talking about using local craftsmen, too. Which is good. Keeps the money in the community. Good point, that. Local hands are important. You know a mill, a proper one, is more than just timbers and stone. It's the  feeling  of the place. The history. You can’t buy that with grant money.

Honestly, Anon, your place is lovely. So much brighter than I remember! Birmingham’s really changed, hasn’t it? And these cushions – where did you get them? They're perfect. Cheers, Chloe! Glad you like it. Found the cushions at a little vintage shop down the Jewellery Quarter, actually. Bargain! Right, so, Honest Skincare – where do we even begin? I’ve been pulling my hair out this week. Well, you said on the group chat you were struggling with marketing? What specifically’s not working? We talked about that Instagram strategy. Yeah, Instagram’s a black hole! I'm posting regularly, decent photos… but the engagement is  tiny . Like, single digits on most things. I've even tried stories, Reels… it’s just not grabbing anyone. I feel like I'm shouting into the void, you know? And the website traffic is mirroring it. Right, okay. Firstly, are you using relevant hashtags? Really  relevant  ones, not just the generic #skincare stuff? And what about competitor analysis? Are you seeing what others are doing successfully? Hashtags… I’m trying, but it’s such a minefield. And I’ve glanced at a few, but honestly, it’s a bit overwhelming. There are so many brands, all bigger and flashier than me. I was thinking maybe paid ads? But the thought of throwing money at it… Paid ads  can  work, but you need a really targeted campaign. Let's not jump to that just yet. Have you considered influencer marketing, even micro-influencers? Someone with 5-10k followers who genuinely cares about ethical and sustainable skincare? It can be far more effective than a massive ad spend. I’ve thought about it! But finding someone reliable, authentic, and within budget... it feels a bit tricky. And how do you even negotiate those things? Like, do you pay them per post, per product featured… what’s the going rate? It varies  wildly . I've helped a few small businesses with this before. Generally, starting with gifting products and offering affiliate links is a good way to test the waters. If they genuinely love your stuff, they're more likely to promote it authentically. Affiliate links mean they earn a commission on sales generated through their link – so it's performance-based, which reduces your risk. That's smart. Affiliate links... okay, I'll look into that. Speaking of products, the feedback on the Lavender & Chamomile Soothing Balm has been amazing.

Dreadful weather, isn’t it, Arthur? Just relentless. Reminds me of that November we had in Inverness back in… oh, must be ’67. Couldn't see your hand in front of your face. You and your memories of Scotland, Margaret. Brighton’s not  quite  as dramatic as the Highlands, thankfully. Though this grey is a bit oppressive, I’ll grant you that. Did you manage to get the garden tidied up a bit before the downpour started? Tried my best. Crocuses are peering through, at least. They’re quite determined little things. Speaking of determination… did you see that article in the Telegraph about the proposed expansion of the airport? Oh, here we go. The airport again. Yes, I did. Honestly, Margaret, the noise pollution alone… it’s already bad enough. And the traffic! Think of the increased congestion on the A27. Well, they’re arguing it’ll bring jobs, Arthur. Economic growth. You know, modernise the town. Bit of a cliché, really, but… Jobs at what cost? Losing the character of Brighton? And who benefits most, I wonder? Not the residents, certainly. They just shove these plans through without any real consultation. Remember old Mrs. Higgins down the road? The constant flights kept her awake at night. She was a wreck. Poor Elsie. Yes, I remember. It’s dreadful, isn’t it, when progress comes at the expense of people’s well-being. It's the same story everywhere, I suppose. They promise the world, and often, all you get is a bit more hassle. It’s not unlike… well, thinking about my own situation, it’s a bit the same feeling. Promised stability, then… nothing. Now, Margaret, don’t go down that road again. We’ve talked about this. The benefits… the delays… they're frustrating, I know. But you've got me, haven’t you? That’s something. I do, don’t I? It’s just… sometimes, you know? It’s hard not to feel a bit… adrift. Like a little boat without a sail. I should be contributing, doing something useful. Teaching young minds… You  did  contribute, Margaret. You dedicated your life to it. Thirty years teaching history. You shaped so many lives. Don’t you diminish that. And frankly, the current state of education… I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy. You're just saying that to cheer me up. It’s all Ofsted reports and test scores these days.

Honestly, this mulled wine is divine, Chloe. You've really outdone yourself! It's the perfect antidote to this ridiculous weather. I swear, it's colder than December should be. Thanks, Elodie! I’m glad you like it. I’ve been tweaking the recipe for years. And you’re absolutely right, it's bizarre. The heating’s been on full blast since lunchtime. My energy bill is going to be terrifying. Tell me about it! My workshop is freezing. Trying to get the wood to cooperate when it's that cold is a nightmare. Though, I’m getting some beautiful grain patterns from the cold, ironically. Keeps things interesting. Are you lot getting a lot of frost where you are? Frost, Rhys? Mate, we’re practically living in an ice rink! Newcastle's proper draughty this time of year. I’m constantly fiddling with the thermostat at the factory. The older machinery doesn't exactly appreciate the cold, let me tell you. We had a whole line down this morning because of a frozen sensor. Frozen sensors! That sounds… stressful. I’m heading back to Swindon next week, thankfully. Need a bit of sunshine. Speaking of stressful, I've been doing a lot of fieldwork lately for my PhD. Glacier research in Greenland – you can imagine the cold there! It makes this feel a bit… pleasant. Greenland! Wow, Elodie, that sounds incredible. Though rather chilly, as you pointed out. I’m buried in research papers myself. My project's going well, but I’m already starting to think about what comes next. Retirement seems a million miles away, but I suppose it'll creep up on us. Any thoughts on what you'll do, Mark? When you finally hang up your technical support hat? Retirement? Don't even go there! I'm barely halfway through! But… I’ve been tinkering with the idea of starting my own small fabrication business. Less… corporate. Something hands-on. Maybe build custom storage solutions, or restoration work. Something like that. You know, using my actual practical skills for once, instead of just solving other people's problems. That’s brilliant, Mark! Building things is so satisfying. It's why I do what I do. This little carving is for my niece. She's obsessed with badgers. It started as a bit of scrap wood, turned into something she'll hopefully treasure. Do you still have your old toolbox, Rhys?

Honestly, Mum, this cutlery situation is ridiculous. We’ve got three forks for every spoon, and a mountain of knives. It's like you’ve been stockpiling since the war. Don't be dramatic, Liv. It's just a bit messy. Dad’s probably been rearranging things again. You know how he gets. I was not rearranging! I was trying to organize it. There's a difference, you know! And three forks are perfectly sensible. You need forks for salad. Salad? We haven’t had salad in weeks, Maureen. Just roast dinners and… well, more roast dinners. Used to have a lovely salad. With radishes. Remember? See? He’s asserting dominance over the cutlery again. Dad, seriously, we're not expecting the Queen for dinner. Dad’s just being Dad, Liv. Relax. He likes feeling useful. He probably thinks he’s preventing a cutlery catastrophe. I am preventing a cutlery catastrophe, thank you very much. It’s important to have order! Remember Auntie Agnes? She couldn’t find a teaspoon to save her life! Chaos reigned! Agnes was a character, that one. Always losing things. Remember the time she put her dentures in the sugar bowl? Aye, that was a sight. Thought she was having a right good laugh, she did. Okay, okay, Auntie Agnes's denture debacle aside, can we maybe thin out the knife collection a bit? It’s genuinely taking up half the drawer. Maybe we could donate some to the church jumble sale? Donate good cutlery?! Absolutely not! Those knives are perfectly serviceable. It’s the younger generation that doesn’t appreciate good quality these days. Everything’s disposable. Mum, they're not antiques. And look, remember Hannah from university? The one who's doing that amazing charity work in Nepal? We could send her some. Building a school or something, she needed kitchen equipment. Nepal? Well, alright then. As long as they appreciate it. It’s a shame, really. I spent years collecting these. Speaking of appreciating things... did you ever finish that crossword, Margaret? I was looking at it earlier, seemed a bit tricky. Not yet, John. It’s got some devilish clues. “A nocturnal bird with a thirst for knowledge.” What on earth could that be? An owl? Because owls are wise... it's a bit of a cliché, though. Used to have an owl. In a picture. Beautiful thing. Actually, about Hannah, I was thinking… maybe we could have her over for dinner next weekend?

This shepherd's pie is lovely, isn't it? You’ve really outdone yourself tonight, love. Mmm-hmm! Best ever! Can I have more peas, please? Of course, sweetheart. More peas coming right up. Right, so, about work. It was a bit… chaotic today. You won't believe what happened with the Henderson account. Henderson? Is that the grumpy one? You've met him, haven’t you? Yes, the grumpy one. Apparently, he’s decided he doesn't like the new brochure design. After we've been working on it for six weeks! The feedback was ridiculously vague, too – just, “It doesn't  feel  right.” Honestly, I nearly pulled my hair out. That's not fair! You work so hard. Did you tell him how you felt? I tried to be diplomatic, darling. Explained the design choices, the research… but he just kept saying it wasn't capturing his brand essence. Marketing meetings can be so draining sometimes. I’m just glad it’s Friday. Skiing tomorrow! Skiing! Yippee! Are we going to see snow? I really, really hope so! The forecast looks promising, lots of fluffy white stuff predicted. And you’ve got your new snow boots, haven’t you? We need to make sure those are zipped up tight! Last time you fell over trying to build a snowman. I did! But that was  because  it was icy. And Daddy helped me up! He did, didn’t he? He's always got your back. Right, so, I was thinking, maybe we should book a ski lesson for you? Just a short one, to get you comfortable with the basics. A lesson? With a teacher? I can ski! I slid down the little hill at the park! That's lovely, darling. But the slopes in the Alps are a  little  different. It's just to make sure you're safe and having fun. And I can have a proper go on the black runs while you’re having your lesson. Can I have hot chocolate with marshmallows after? Absolutely. The biggest, most marshmallow-filled hot chocolate you've ever seen. So, are you excited about the holiday now? Yes! Are we going to see mountains? Big mountains? You are! Huge, snowy mountains. And we’ll build a snowman with a carrot nose, and maybe even have a snowball fight. What do you think? Snowball fight! But be careful not to hit Daddy!

Honestly, Chloe, this Maths homework is  criminal . Like, who decided quadratic equations were a good idea at fifteen? It’s just… meaningless. Tell me about it. Mr. Davies seems to think we're all about to become rocket scientists. I swear, I spent the entire lesson drawing little doodles of pineapples instead of focusing. Are you even  starting  on it? Started? I  glanced  at it. One equation. One. It spat back a cryptic error message. I’m giving up. We should be learning about music production instead. Much more useful. You’re obsessed with that GarageBand thing, aren't you? It's pretty cool though. You've got a real knack for it. Did you lay down any new beats today? I tried! I was going for this chilled-out, lo-fi vibe, but it just ended up sounding like a strangled cat. Still, I learned something. What about English? That essay on ‘The Great Gatsby’ due Friday feels like a mountain too. Ugh, Gatsby. All that dramatic longing and expensive parties. I’m just not feeling it. Mrs. Thompson wants us to analyze symbolism, but I’m drawing a blank. What do you think the green light  really  means, anyway? Is it just… green? You’re terrible. It’s obviously hope and the American Dream, yeah? But like, a corrupted, unattainable version of the American Dream. It's rather sad, when you think about it. I actually got a bit into it. My mum's been reading it again, so I've been listening to her talk about it. It’s surprisingly compelling. See, you're actually thinking about it! I just see millionaire problems. Anyway, less school stresses, more important things. Did you hear about the Food Tech competition? The one where we have to create a dish representing our heritage? Yeah, a bit daunting, isn’t it? My mum suggested a full-on Sunday roast… it’s ambitious. Ambitious is good! My gran’s got this amazing recipe for chicken and chorizo paella. I was thinking I could do that. It feels… Spanish, you know? It’s probably easier than a roast though. Less chance of setting the kitchen on fire. True. Speaking of Spanish, are you sticking with your Duolingo? I’m thinking of dropping out. It’s so boring. No way! I'm actually getting quite a bit better, honestly. I can order a coffee and ask for directions now.

Oh, that film was a bit much, wasn't it? All that shouting! Gave me a right headache, it did. A little intense, yeah, but I thought the cinematography was stunning, honestly. The way they used the light… Did you notice the long takes in the desert scenes? Really pulled you in. Long takes? Love a bit of a quick cut, I do. Too much staring at one thing for me, love. Makes me fidgety. What  was  it about, anyway? Seemed a bit… complicated. All that talk of legacy and redemption. It's a generational story, really. About a father passing down his business to his son, but the son wants to do something different. There's a lot of conflict, obviously. And a bit of corruption thrown in. It's based on a true story, actually. Corruption, is it? Don't need that sort of thing, thank you very much. Used to like a good Western, you know. Something with a clear good guy and a clear bad guy. John Wayne, now he was a proper hero. "Rio Bravo," that’s a film. Grandma, you and John Wayne! I'm glad you enjoy those old classics, but the world's a bit more grey now, isn't it? Things aren't always black and white. Grey’s dreary. Give me a bit of sunshine and a bit of a sing-song any day. Speaking of which, did you ever see "Singin' in the Rain?" Now  that's  a film. Gene Kelly, splashing about in puddles... delightful! Of course! Everyone's seen "Singin’ in the Rain." It’s iconic. But it’s a very different kind of film than the one we just watched. That felt a lot more… real, wouldn’t you say? Grittier. Real and gritty usually means depressing, dear. Though, I do enjoy a good drama now and then. Remember that one with Meryl Streep… the one about the iron lady? "The Iron Lady"? Yeah, that was powerful. You know, talking about powerful women… I saw "Little Women" last year. Saoirse Ronan was just brilliant. It totally modernised the story, in a way, without losing the heart of it. Ah, "Little Women." Read those books as a girl, I did. Jo was my favourite. Always wanted to be a writer, like her. Never turned out that way, of course. Ended up working at a grocer’s, I did.

Honestly, Mum, this rain is relentless. It's been grey for days! I'm starting to feel like a mushroom. Aye, it’s a proper soaker, innit? Birmingham weather, always a bit unpredictable. Though, I remember winters as a girl, snow up to your knees! This is just… damp. Not unpleasant, mind you. At least the garden’s getting a good watering. I suppose. I was thinking about taking Leo for a walk in Cannon Hill Park tomorrow, but if it's like this… He’ll hate it. He’s such a drama queen when he gets his paws wet. He is a bit of a pampered prince, that Leo. But you’ve done a good job with him. He's a lovely dog. You should take him even if it's a bit drizzly, fresh air’s good for him. Or we could go to the botanical gardens? They've got that lovely glasshouse. That’s a good shout, Mum! The glasshouse is always a winner. Right, I'll check the forecast properly tonight. Speaking of plans, have you had a think about Aunt Carol’s birthday next month? It’s her 70th, after all. I have, love. I was thinking about booking a table at that Italian place she likes, La Dolce Vita, down on Broad Street. But it needs to be a Saturday, she’s got her bridge club on Tuesdays and Thursdays, you know how she is about that. Perfect! I can look into availability. I was thinking we could get a cake from that bakery near the Jewellery Quarter - the one with the amazing salted caramel brownies? Oh, you know how to butter me up! Yes, please do. Anything for Aunt Carol. She's been a bit down lately, hasn't she? Something to do with Mr. Henderson retiring from the court. Apparently, they were quite close. Really? I hadn’t realised. That's a shame. It must be unsettling for her after working so closely with him for so long. It’s the same at the school, you know. Mr. Davies retired last year and it's completely changed the atmosphere. It's odd, isn't it, how much one person can impact a place. It is, love. Keeps you grounded, though, doesn't it? Reminds you nothing stays the same. Being a court usher, you see it all the time. People’s lives on the line, families ripped apart…

Honestly, this air is just  amazing  after a day cooped up in that stuffy lecture hall. It’s so clean, isn’t it? I almost forgot what it felt like to breathe properly. You're romanticising a bit, love. It’s still air. And I think my sinuses are having a field day with the pollen. Did you manage to find those silk scarves you were after today? The ones with the little embroidered details? I did! Well,  almost . I found a gorgeous selection in that little shop near the university – the one we passed earlier. They had the colour scheme I wanted perfectly, a lovely dusty rose and jade green, but the embroidery wasn't quite right. Too…busy, somehow. I was envisioning something more delicate, you see. Delicate is your middle name when it comes to scarves. You’ll be searching for ages then. Should we check that market tomorrow? I remember seeing a few stalls with hand-embroidered things. Maybe we’ll get lucky. That’s a brilliant idea. Want to make a proper morning of it? We could grab some of those steamed buns from that little place near the entrance - you know, the ones filled with pork and vegetables? They’re divine. Steamed buns it is! A very persuasive argument. Although, I’m still slightly traumatized by that last batch. Remember that one with the… unexpected burst of chilli? Oh, don’t remind me! I practically set my mouth on fire! It was worth it though, wasn't it? At least it was memorable. Speaking of memorable… how did that presentation to the department go this afternoon? You seemed a bit stressed this morning. It was…okay. Prof. Li was being particularly difficult. Kept harping on about the need to “modernize” my teaching methods, as if I’m still teaching Chaucer with a blackboard and chalk. He clearly doesn't appreciate the value of a good, solid lecture. Oh, that old chestnut. He just wants to implement another one of those online, interactive simulations no one actually uses. He’s obsessed. Did you manage to steer him away from that particular path of doom? Mostly. I managed to convince him that a small focus group would be a better starting point, rather than a full-scale departmental overhaul. Basically, kicked the can down the road. It bought me some time. Smart move. Procrastination is a valuable skill in academia.

Right, okay, so let’s solidify this. Saturday’s the photoshoot, isn't it? And I’m still a little hazy on who’s doing what. Saturday! Pirates! Can I have a cookie, Mummy? Lovely bit o’ sunshine we’re havin’ today, innit? Reminds me of that trip we took to Norfolk when I were a lad. Remember the horses on the common? Proper shying things, they were. Oh, I do, Arthur. Bit of a fortune these tickets cost these days, let me tell you. Makes you wonder if it's worth it. Speaking of fortunes…have you heard anything more about Margaret's house sale? Yes, actually. I told her she should really look into getting one of those stairlifts. Makes life a lot easier. Stairlifts! Fancy that. Not long ago, they were a thing of the future. Now everybody's got one. Honestly, this week with Leo has been  intense . He’s decided sleep is optional. Like, actively avoids it. I’m running on fumes and instant coffee. Oh, I remember that phase. She said Elsie wasn’t "thriving" because she hadn't put on enough weight in a week. Can you believe it? We had a  full  lecture on the benefits of powdered milk. Classic Grandma. Cor, this rain’s a proper misery, innit? Reminds me of a right gloomy November back in '72. Though, truth be told, most Novembers feel a bit gloomy to me these days. I need to get them checked, I suppose. Just been so busy with Reginald. What about you? You always did squint a bit. It’s a preventative measure, Penelope. As we get older, one must be vigilant. And I booked mine for next Tuesday. Now, Arthur, you've been awfully quiet. Are you feeling alright? Just pondering on things, Richard. Been thinking about how much the buses have changed. Remember when you could hop on a number 28 to Wymondham for tuppence?! Now it's nearly £3 to go to the shops. Daylight robbery, I tell you. Used to be able to get a full day's wages for a few shillings. Oh, don’t start on the buses, Arthur. You’ll have us all depressed. Remember that time you fell asleep on the number 11 and ended up in Attleborough? You were furious! That I was!

Right, so, I’ve looked at the map again. Think we should head over to St. Mark’s Square first, then? It's just… iconic, isn’t it? I mean, the pictures don't  really  do it justice. Now it's overrun with tourists and pigeons, bless 'em. You're telling me! I saw a video online of a guy practically wrestling a pigeon for a crust of bread. It was madness. Still, you can’t say you've been to Venice without seeing it, can you? Though, I was readin' about Rialto Bridge too. That looked pretty stunning. Oh, Rialto's lovely, that it is. But it gets just as packed, I reckon. Before the tourists really boomed, there used to be a lovely fish market there, full of fresh catch. The smell used to be somethin' special, a proper seaside scent. Not that awful smell you get now with all the street food. Street food's alright though, isn't it? I’ve been lookin' at some reviews and the cicchetti—those Venetian tapas—sound amazing. We  have  to try some of those. Especially the crostini with baccalà mantecato. Have you ever had it? Baccalà mantecato? Child, I’ve been eatin’ baccalà since before you were born! My grandad used to make it, a proper recipe passed down through generations. Nowt like a bit of creamy, coddy goodness on a bit of toasted bread. Better than any fancy restaurant food, that. Brings back a lot of memories, it does. See, that's what I mean! It's like, the history's  in  the food. It’s not just about tourist traps and Instagram photos. Do you think we should try to find a less crowded spot for lunch then? Somewhere a bit more…local? Absolutely. Let's get away from St. Mark's. There's a little trattoria down near the Cannaregio canal – ‘Trattoria Al Gatto Nero’ I think it’s called. Serves some of the best seafood in the area. Not flash, mind you, just good honest food. And the owner, Marco, is a lovely lad. He’ll keep us right with the specials. Cannaregio, noted! Do you remember what it was like around here when you were a kid, Mam?

Honestly, this is  exactly  what I needed after that meeting. Absolute chaos. Mr. Davies decided to completely change the scope of the project, like, two hours before the deadline. Oh, no way! Are you actually getting into the nitty-gritty of health advice, or is it more like lifestyle stuff? Mostly lifestyle. Think healthy recipes, stress-busting tips, that sort of thing. It's interesting, but sometimes I feel a bit… detached. Like, I'm selling them an idea of wellness, rather than genuinely helping anyone. What about the gym? You were saying last week you’d finally started that HIIT class? Ugh, don't even. I almost threw up on Tuesday. Seriously. I thought I was going to die. But, strangely, I liked it? The trainer, Mark, is terrifying, but effective. I'm actually feeling… stronger. Did you manage to finally book that yoga retreat? I did! Thailand, October. I'm so excited! It feels like a proper escape, you know? I’ve been needing one. Work has been crazy, and I've just been feeling a bit… blah. What about you? Any holiday plans brewing? After all this project nonsense, you deserve something amazing. I wish! Mum's hinting at a family trip to Bournemouth, which, while lovely, isn't exactly exotic. I’d kill for a week in Greece. Or Italy. Anywhere with sunshine and pasta. Remember that disastrous weekend in Brighton with Liam? Oh my god, please don’t remind me! "The inherent futility of seaside amusements.” I'm paraphrasing, obviously, but that was the vibe. I'm so glad that ended. You saw him recently, didn’t you? At Chloe’s birthday? Briefly. He has your eyes, Arthur. Absolutely your eyes. Little Leo. It’s quite extraordinary. He does, doesn't he? A proper pair of eyes they are. Full of mischief, I imagine. Living abroad, though… France. Though she does miss proper crumpets. And our garden, of course. The property market there, apparently, is quite something. You could find a lovely little farmhouse for a song, if you were willing to do up. Or, as she says, sink your life savings into a crumbling chateau! Property... yes. Lovely people, but agonizingly polite. They were utterly baffled by our… directness. Directness! . That’s a polite way of putting it. Speaking of baffling… did you hear about Chichester Cathedral? That spire, partially collapsed! Dreadful. Porden, the architect who designed it - a genius, apparently. Though perhaps a little overconfident? I did see something about that on the news. Terribly sad. Apparently, they’re having an open day and photo exhibition soon, documenting the restoration efforts and the history of the spire. They're even running an art competition inspired by the cathedral. An art competition… now that’s interesting. I've been sketching the local bollards, you see. A rather overlooked form of civic art, wouldn't you agree? I'm trying to make a case for their aesthetic merit. The bollards, Arthur? You’re serious? Absolutely. They're everywhere, shaping our lives. And most of them are utterly hideous! Though, I must confess, the new ones they put up on Kennington Road are particularly offensive. A blot on the landscape, I tell you! You're a force to be reckoned with, you know that? Speaking of local concerns… this new housing management company, Apex Properties... honestly.

Honestly, I’m starting to think Mrs. Davies actually  enjoys  seeing us fail her history essays. It's brutal this year. Like, seriously, who expects us to memorize every single date of the Tudors? The one with Robert Pattinson? Yeah, it looks intense. Very different from the previous ones. Actually, reminds me of a storyline my Nan was telling me about… some ancient Chinese warrior... Wait, are we going to derail this conversation into a discussion about ancient Chinese warriors now? We were talking about superheroes! Let him finish. My Nan's stories are usually pretty wild.

But you’d need a good camera, wouldn’t you? Yeah, that's the hurdle. Mum keeps saying I should focus on my schoolwork. “Perfect duty,” she calls it. Like I’m some sort of robot! Your mum is…  interesting . Mine says the same thing, but then she’s watching reality TV all evening. Hypocrite! She is! Anyway, speaking of school, PE is a disaster this term. Mrs. Davies is making us do cross-country. Cross-country! I’m going to die. Oh no! I'm dreading that too. I’m not exactly built for running. I'm better at volleyball, but apparently, no one likes volleyball. They just want a good show of suffering over muddy fields. It’s ridiculous. Totally. Do you think we’ll be able to get out of it?

"It's lovely to see you all again. Anon really has done a wonderful job with this place. So much brighter than I remember his flat being." “Aye, it is that. Bit too bright, if you ask me. Give me a bit of gloom any day. Easier on these old eyes, it is.” "Gloom used to be all we had, Arthur! Remember those grey days down Costessey? Couldn't see the end of the garden, you know." "Oh, don't remind me, George. I used to complain to my mother constantly. 'Mother, it's raining  again !' She'd just say, 'Well, dear, Norfolk weather!'" "Sounds familiar! But today's a beautiful day. I was driving over and saw a kestrel hovering over the fields. It was magnificent. Any of you seen any interesting wildlife lately?” "Kestrel, you say? Now  that’s  a proper bird. Haven’t seen one myself in a while. Used to work on a project down near Hockham – saw dozens then. Bold as you like, they were, pinching sandwiches right out of the workers' lorries." "Sandwiches! Now you’re talking. Though I mostly remember the skylarks, back then. Used to hear them singin' proper loud in the mornings. You don't hear 'em as much these days, do you?" “No, you don't. Progress, they call it. Less fields, more houses. Sad, really.” "It is. Though there's a lovely nature reserve not far from here, near Witton. I was thinking of taking my niece there next week. She's fascinated by hedgehogs." "Hedgehogs… used to have one that got into my shed once. Near broke my heart, thought it was trapped. Turned out it was just after my socks – kept nicking 'em to line its nest! Soft little beggars, they are.” “You and your socks, Arthur! Always losing ‘em! Remember that Morris Minor you had? The one with the dent in the bonnet? Always needed a new pair of socks to prop up the wheels when it was parked on a slope!” "Oh, George, you're incorrigible! Speaking of old cars, I was reading about the new electric models. They're supposed to be incredible, but I confess, the technology still a bit bewildering to me. It’s all… software these days, isn't it?" "Software! Don’t even get me started. I tried to download a picture for my granddaughter the other day. Three hours I wasted!

Cor, Anon, that’s a right state your wardrobe’s in, isn’t it? Brenda here was just sayin’ about how she’s sorted out hers. Must be lovely having the space. My wife, she keeps threatening to get rid of half of it, claims it's "clutter." It is, Martin. I did a proper clear-out last month. Got rid of so many things I hadn’t worn in years. Felt terribly guilty at first, throwing things away, you know? But then I thought, “What’s the point of hoarding?” Though, I did keep that awful sequined top from the seventies. Just because. Sequin tops, eh? I remember those. My Elsie, bless her soul, she had a collection. Said they were “glamorous.” Didn't seem very glamorous when she wore 'em down the shops. You know, it's funny, these young lads today, they’re all about Twitter, innit? Postin' and tweetin’… doesn't seem like a proper way to spend your time. Twitter, eh? My daughter keeps telling me I need to be on it. Says I could share my classroom observations and things. I told her, “I’ve got enough observations to contend with already, thank you very much!” Hard enough keeping thirty fifteen-year-olds quiet, let alone explaining the nuances of social media. I’ve tried, Martin. Honestly, I have. Got a profile, sent a couple of tweets… felt ridiculous. Apparently, you’re supposed to ‘engage’ and that. Engage with what? Cat pictures? Cat pictures! That’s about the level of it, isn’t it? Just a load of silly pictures. Used to be, you’d have a proper chat, meet someone down the pub. Now it’s all… digitalised. Speaking of pubs, remember old Bert down at the King’s Head? He could knock back a pint or two faster than you could blink. Proper binge drinker, that one. Bert! Now  there’s  a legend. Used to get him to help me move furniture when I was startin’ out. Strong as an ox, and fuelled by ale. We need characters like that, don't we? Though probably not in today's climate. Health and Safety and all that. Poor Bert. I hope he's alright. It’s sad, really, when people rely on that kind of thing to get them through. It's the same with the health service, isn't it? You hear so many stories.

"Bleedin' 'eck, it's cold in 'ere! I thought Cambridge would be all…posh and temperate. This is proper Arctic, isn't it? Proper snowed under, like." "It's definitely a bit brisk, yeah. Not quite Sunderland weather, I imagine, though. Glad you made it over alright. Traffic was a nightmare coming in from the station. And you brave enough to cycle all the way from the train station?" "Aye, well, what else was I gonna do? Catch a taxi? Don't be daft! It's a bit of a workout, mind. The snow slowed me right down. Though, I have to say, it looked bonny, all sparkly and white. Makes you want to build a snowman, doesn't it?" "It does. Though I suspect my attempts at snowman construction would be rather…lopsided. I'm more of a gardener, as you know. Speaking of which, I was hoping you could lend a hand this weekend. Some of the roses need pruning before the worst of the weather hits. Want to brave the cold?" “Roses, eh? Right then. I’m happy to give it a go. Though I’ll need gloves, proper warm ones. My fingers went numb cycling, I tell you. Right, what's cookin' then? Smells amazing." "Just a hearty stew. Needed something to warm us both up. Been watching loads of  Come Dine With Me  lately; inspires me to try and make something a bit fancy, even if it's just a proper stew." "You and  Come Dine With Me ! You’d be a nightmare to compete against. All precise presentation and obscure ingredients. Though, I’d be laughing even harder if I got to judge your disastrous attempt at a soufflé." “Hey! My soufflé skills are perfectly adequate! Okay, maybe not. Speaking of things that are slightly chaotic…have you heard anything more about Liam and Sophie’s stag and hen do? It sounds like they're pulling out all the stops." "Aye, I 'eard. Liam’s got some full-on paintballing planned – apparently, he's roping in all his uni mates. Sophie’s is a spa weekend in Brighton, all fluffy robes and cocktails. Sounds like polar opposites, doesn't it? I'm glad I'm not coordinating either of 'em!" “Absolutely. I wouldn’t wish that on my worst enemy. We need to make sure we’re free to go to both, though, even if it’s just for an hour or two.

Honestly, this is glorious, Mum. You’ve really outdone yourself. These roast potatoes are perfectly crispy. Oh, stop it, love! Just a bit of rosemary and a good bit of heat, that's all. Your dad did all the peeling, you know. He's been grumbling about his back all afternoon, bless him. Grumbling’s what I do best. Knees ache too, now. Not like you youngsters… bouncing about. Dad, you’re fine. Don’t exaggerate. It's lovely to be back in Norfolk, though. Feels like stepping back in time. Definitely. Especially with Mum’s cooking. It's a comfort. I’ve been trying to recreate her bread sauce at uni, but it just doesn't  taste  the same. What's the secret, Mum? Don’t tell me it’s just butter and milk! Darling, there's a bit more to it than that! You’ve got to infuse the milk with the onion and cloves, simmer it  just  right, and don’t skimp on the nutmeg. And a proper knob of butter, of course! You can’t have bread sauce without a good knob of butter. It's that simple, really. It's the simmering slowly that makes all the difference. You have to be patient with it, like everything good. That’s fascinating. I’ve never really thought about the science of cooking like that. It’s just assumed knowledge, isn’t it? Learned at our parents' knees. Exactly! It’s all implicit knowledge. My students are used to everything being formalised, put into bullet points and assessed. They wouldn't know a parsnip from a potato if it hit them! Though, they  are  surprisingly keen to learn about traditional cooking. I did a demonstration last month on Victorian puddings – it was a huge hit. Puddings? Back in my day, puddings were proper puddings. Not these sickly things you get now. Treacle pudding, spotted dick… that was a pudding! He’s right, dear. Nothing quite like a warm treacle pudding with custard. Remember when we used to make those, love? Every Sunday, without fail. So, Dad, you’re saying you yearn for a culinary flashback? Don’t be daft. Just saying things were simpler. And tastier. Less complicated. You’re just saying you want someone else to make it for you! Seriously though, Mum, I’ll try again with your tips. Rest assured, it won't be on the same level as yours, but I'll give it a shot.

Honestly, Mum’s roast potatoes are just… legendary. I don’t think I’ll ever manage to replicate them, no matter how many YouTube tutorials I watch. There’s just a certain  je ne sais quoi . Absolutely, Elara. They're the highlight of the meal, every time. You tried using goose fat today, didn't you? I did! Figured it was the secret weapon. Didn't quite work the same magic. Maybe it's the specific oven? Or the sheer amount of rosemary she uses… Now, now, lass! There's no secret ingredient but a good dollop of love, that there is. And a bit of patience. Them spuds need a good parboil, you know, before they even  think  about going into the oven. Everyone rushes it these days. Patience is a rare commodity these days, Maureen. Used to be, Sundays were for slowly simmering stews and letting things cook right. Proper cooking. Aye, stew. My Elsie used to make a champion stew. With dumplings. Big, fluffy dumplings. Could feed a whole army, that stew could. That sounds amazing, Grandad. What kind of meat did she use? Lamb, mostly. Sometimes beef, if we were lucky. And carrots, and parsnips… all fresh from the garden, o' course. Not like this supermarket stuff. You still make stews, Maureen? Now and then, love. Though these days, it's mostly for me and George. The kids are all about their ready meals, aren't they? Brings a tear to me eye, it does. Remember when you all used to try and ‘help’ in the kitchen and covered everything in flour? Oh god, the flour explosions! Dad used to be so exasperated. I think I permanently coated the kitchen in a fine white dust for about a year. I do remember. You little scamps. Always getting into mischief. Though, to be fair, your mother did let you. Most mothers wouldn’t have. Don't you start, Derek. I let them learn! It’s important to know how to cook a decent meal. So they don’t end up eating chips every night. Speaking of chips, did you guys ever go to that chippy in Bishop Auckland, Maureen? The one down by the river? Oh, The Neptune! That was a proper chippy. Best fish and chips I’ve ever had. Used to go there every Friday after school with me best friend, Brenda. We’d sit down by the river and watch the ducks.

Honestly, this view is doing wonders for my brain. After wrestling with that marketing presentation for 'Bloom,' a good dose of blue sky is exactly what I needed. Bloom's sounding promising, you know. The feedback from the pilot program seems genuinely positive. But you looked like you were about to spontaneously combust earlier. What was the crisis this time? Just the usual. Trying to convince investors that a subscription box for mindful productivity isn’t  just  a millennial indulgence. Apparently, “adulting tools” aren't as universally appealing as I’d hoped. Well, the world needs mindful adults. Though, I suspect a gentler, more nuanced pitch than “adulting tools” might be necessary. It sounds a bit…patronizing. Absolutely. You're right. I'm getting too close to it. Right, so, university education. Let's dive back in. I was thinking - we talked about personalized learning paths, right? What if we incorporated some of the same principles as Bloom? Not the box itself, obviously, but the idea of micro-challenges and rewards for consistent effort. Gamification, but not in a cheesy, points-and-badges way. I like that. True gamification should feel organic to the learning process, shouldn’t it? I've been doing some reading on intrinsic motivation, and it’s fascinating how much that plays into long-term engagement. It wouldn't be about forcing engagement, but creating an environment where students  want  to learn. Exactly! Imagine having modules structured like mini-startups, where students work in teams, define a problem related to their field, brainstorm solutions, and present a ‘pitch’ at the end. It's project-based, naturally collaborative, and simulates real-world skills. That’s brilliant, actually. It taps into a kind of entrepreneurial spirit, doesn’t it? But what about assessment? How do you fairly assess that kind of project? It’s difficult to compare a team pitching a sustainable energy solution to another team working on a new marketing campaign. That’s the tricky bit. We could incorporate peer evaluations – structured and anonymous, of course – and focus on process as much as the final product. Track their brainstorming sessions, their problem-solving approaches, their communication within the team. We’d need a pretty robust rubric, though. What's your experience assessing group work been like? A mixed bag, I confess. It’s always a challenge to ensure everyone contributes equally and to fairly judge the collective output.

Honestly, this week has been  mad . The Henderson project is threatening to swallow me whole. Three different stakeholders, all wanting slightly different things. It’s like herding cats, I swear. Sounds intense. You need a serious chill-out session this weekend, then. What are you thinking? Are you coming to Liam's Halloween party? Liam’s? Ugh, probably. It’s kind of obligatory, isn’t it? Though I’m not feeling very festive. I keep picturing spreadsheets instead of pumpkins. What are you dresssing as, by the way? Don’t tell me you're going as a Florence Nightingale again? No, no Nightingale this year! I'm doing something a bit more...spooky. A Victorian ghost bride. Found this amazing antique veil at a jumble sale. It's seriously proper creepy. What about you? Still saving the world in a business suit? Tempting, actually. So effortlessly me. But maybe something a bit ridiculous this time. Like…a giant strawberry? Think about the Instagram opportunities! Okay, I'm genuinely picturing it. A giant strawberry. You'd rock it. Seriously though, are you eating properly at work? You look knackered. Not really, no. Vending machine sandwiches and lukewarm coffee. The glamorous life of a project coordinator. I need to start batch cooking again like you do. This smells incredible, what is it? It’s a lentil shepherd’s pie. Proper comfort food. I made a huge batch; there's loads for you. You absolutely  have  to eat something decent. Look, you've been working crazy hours. Let's make Saturday a full recovery day. No spreadsheets, no meetings, just walks in the park and junk TV. That actually sounds...amazing. I'm in. Where should we go for a walk? I’ve been meaning to check out that new nature reserve near Sevenoaks. Apparently the autumn colours are stunning. Sevenoaks? Nice! I’ve only driven through. It's pretty countryside, isn't it? We could even pop into a pub afterwards, warm up with a cider. It's been ages since we’ve just chilled out. Cider sounds perfect. Right, you've sold me. So, Saturday – nature reserve, cider, pure relaxation. What about beyond the weekend? Five years from now, where do you see yourself, Nurse Amy? Still battling demons, I presume? Five years... That's a big one. Hopefully, I'll be a senior mental health nurse, maybe specialising in adolescent trauma.

Honestly, love, this Cambridge air is a bit… crisp, innit? Not quite like back home, is it? Essex is much milder, even in November. It is a bit chilly, yeah, but it's worth it for the architecture. Look at this gargoyle on the building across the street – pretty impressive, right? Much more exciting than Lewisham, I suppose. Though, I do miss the bustle sometimes. Gargoyles? Fancy. I never paid much mind to gargoyles growing up. More bothered about getting the washing on the line before it rained. You know, the practical things. Lewisham… I haven't been back to Lewisham in ages, have you? Not recently. Mum says it’s changed a lot. Gentrified, apparently. Loads of craft breweries and, like, organic bakeries. Not exactly the Lewisham I grew up in, you know? Still got the high street though, I hear. Gentrified. That's a lovely word for pricing everyone out of their own neighbourhood, ain’t it? Always the same, isn’t it? Progress. Supposedly. So, how’s work going, darling? Still wrestling those production schedules into submission? You know it. It's pretty intense at the moment. We're ramping up for Christmas, so absolutely frantic trying to get everything ordered and shipped on time. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m herding cats. Cats! Cor, you’re having a right time then. Remember your Uncle Barry used to say, "A watched pot never boils, but a production line needs constant attention!” He was a card, that one. Never could understand modern technology, though. Still using a dial-up modem until 2005! He sounds brilliant. Grandad was the same, though. Refused to get a smartphone until last year. Said he didn't  need  to know what everyone was doing all the time. Bit of a Luddite, really. See? There’s wisdom in that, I reckon. All this constant connection… it can’t be healthy. Though, I do love a good Facebook peek now and then. Just to see what the grandkids are up to. Are they behaving themselves, those little hooligans? Mostly. Lily's being a drama queen about her school play costume, and Tom's convinced he can build a rocket out of cardboard boxes. Standard. I'm thinking of bringing them over for a weekend in December, if you’re up for it? It’s been ages since they’ve been up. Oh, that would be lovely, darling, absolutely lovely.

Honestly, this café is alright, but it’s not a decent cuppa like you get back home, is it? Proper Yorkshire tea, that's what I need. I'm getting a right headache trying to decipher this menu. You and your tea! You’d think you were stranded without it. It's France, love! They have amazing coffee. Are you even trying to look at the pastries? They look incredible. And honestly, the French have a  way  with croissants. Croissants are alright, I suppose. But they're not a bacon butty, are they? And trying to read all this fancy French… it's a nightmare. I’m attempting to order a pain au chocolat, but I'm terrified I'll end up with a plate of snails. Don't worry, you won't get snails. 'Pain au chocolat' is pretty straightforward. See? You  can  do French. Remember that linguistics lecture last week? We finally understood the root of so many words. It's not all lost on you, you know. Aye, well, lectures are different to trying to actually translate things in a real-life situation. Speaking of lectures, I’m having a proper nightmare with Professor Davies’ scientific methods class. He expects us to understand everything immediately! It’s like he’s speaking a different language - worse than French, even. Oh, Davies! I know, right? He's intense. But honestly, think back to what he said about hypothesis testing. Remember the example with the… what was it? The impact of fertiliser on wheat yield? Vaguely... something about statistical significance. It all blurred into a massive equations-filled mess. I just keep thinking, “Why do I need to know this? I’m studying history!” It’s about critical thinking, isn’t it? About analysing data and drawing conclusions. Useful skills, no matter what you’re studying. Besides, you're brilliant at piecing together historical narratives. That’s a form of analysis too, just with different materials. True, I suppose. Speaking of analysis, did you catch the football last night? Man United looked proper awful. Absolutely no bite in the midfield. Tell me about it! That was painful to watch. Honestly, their tactics were all over the place. They really need to bring in a central defensive midfielder. Someone with a bit of grit. I was thinking someone like... well, never mind. They won't listen to me. You’re probably right.

Honestly, I’m starting to feel like I live in a nature documentary. It's been…a week. A week, you say? What’s been lurking, then? Don’t tell me it's started with the spiders again. I swear, this time of year, they're everywhere. Worse, actually. Much worse. I found a mouse in the kitchen this morning. Bold as brass, nibbling on a biscuit tin! I nearly jumped out of my skin. A mouse! Oh, I know how that feels. Had a family of 'em in the shed a few years back. Cheeky little blighters, they were. Eating through the birdseed bags like they were nothing. Did you manage to… deal with it? Well, I tried the humane trap, you know, the one with the peanut butter. But it ignored it completely! It just sat there, twitching its nose, and then scampered off. I’m starting to think they're mocking me. I ended up calling a professional. Bit embarrassing, really. With my… background, you wouldn’t think I’d be losing a battle with a rodent. There’s no shame in it, love. Honestly. Even the grandest houses get pests. It’s nature, innit? And them traps… they’re useless sometimes. My grandson tried one for a field mouse once. The mouse just dragged the whole thing around like a toy. Exactly! It's mortifying. But it’s not just the mouse. The spiders are back with a vengeance, too. Huge ones, all hairy legs and beady eyes. I swear, one was the size of my hand! Oh, those cellar spiders! Nasty things. But mostly harmless, they are. Just jumpy. Give 'em a wide berth, and they’ll leave you be. I've learned to live with them. They eat the flies, you know. A bit of a trade-off. A trade-off I’m not sure I’m willing to make! I feel like I'm constantly scanning the ceilings and walls. And the birds...they're relentless! Always pecking at the windows, making an awful racket. Keeps me up at night, it does. The birds can be a trial. Sparrows, mostly, 'round here. They gather in flocks and squabble something fierce. I put up a few feeders, trying to keep 'em occupied, but they mostly just use it as a launching pad to harass the cat. See? It’s a whole ecosystem in my house, and I’m just trying to survive.

Do, please, sit down, Bronwen. It’s lovely to finally meet you. Anon has told me so much - mostly about how you’re a whiz with family history research. It's a bit of a rabbit warren for me, I’m afraid. Oh, it is, dear, it certainly is. Though some rabbits are easier to chase than others! Lovely to meet you too, Eleanor. Anon speaks highly of you as well, a teacher, you say? A good profession, a good profession. Keeps you on your toes. It does! I’ve been at the primary school in town for, goodness, nearly twenty years now. Can’t believe it. It’s… well, it's demanding, but rewarding. You were a teacher as well, weren’t you, Bronwen? Anon mentioned that. I was. Secondary, mostly. English Literature. A passionate bunch, teenagers, you know? Thankfully long retired now. My knees aren't thanking me for all those years spent chasing skirts and collecting dropped pens! So, you've been teaching little ones? Must be different entirely. It is. Very different. Less Shakespeare, more building towers with blocks and learning to tie shoes. Though, I do try and sneak in a bit of poetry whenever I can. It's precious, isn’t it? Family history, too. It feels like pieces of a puzzle, connecting us to… everything. Anon’s been helping me delve into my side, the Tringtons. Turns out we're connected to some rather unremarkable farmers, mostly! Farmers are important! Don’t underestimate the farmers, Eleanor. They fed the nation, didn't they? My own family tree is a right tangle. Mostly Welsh, naturally, from the valleys. My grandmother, Morfudd, she came over to Bristol during the war, looking for work. That’s where I was born, in Bristol. Funny, isn’t it? Born in England, but with the valleys coursing through my veins. That's fascinating. Anon was telling me about your research into the Griffiths family. Apparently, you uncovered some rather surprising connections to… well, it's a bit complex! Let me tell you! It was a distant cousin, married to a sailor. He ended up getting involved in… smuggling! Not grand, organized crime, mind you. Just a bit of whisky and tobacco, getting it past the customs. Scandalous for the time, I can tell you. Nearly ruined the family reputation. Oh, wonderful! It’s so much more interesting than the farmers.

Honestly, look at that. A perfect morning for a hot air balloon. You’d be able to see for miles from up there, wouldn't you? Remember that trip we almost booked in Tuscany? I do. And remember how Buster absolutely  hated  the idea, even just watching the promotional video? He was practically vibrating with anxiety. Wouldn't have left your side for a single second. He probably thought we were going to be snatched up into the clouds by some giant bird. Honestly, that dog’s imagination is wild. Speaking of Buster, where  is  he? He usually has a better nose for rabbits than this. He’s got his nose buried in something over there by those power lines. Probably some unfortunate vole. You know, I was reading an article the other day about how the electromagnetic fields from power lines can disorient wildlife. Really? I hadn’t heard that. Disorient them how? Apparently, it interferes with their magnetic sense, the one they use for navigation. Birds, insects, even larger mammals. So, they get lost, can’t find their way home, struggle to find food… a bit grim, really. Goodness. That’s dreadful. I always thought those lines were just an eyesore. Another example of human infrastructure messing with nature, I suppose. It makes you wonder about the cumulative effect over years. It does. Makes me wish we'd opted for solar panels on the house, but Mrs. Henderson next door would have had a fit about the aesthetics, wouldn't she? Oh, don't remind me. "It would ruin the village vista," she declared, as if a few shiny panels were going to single-handedly destroy Norfolk’s charm. Speaking of money... did you manage to sort out that paperwork for the research grant? Nearly there. Just a couple of pages to sign and return. It’s surprisingly stressful, even though it’s basically guaranteed. You know, the university's being ridiculously bureaucratic about it this year. They’ve added a whole new section about ‘impact assessment’. Apparently, we have to demonstrate how our work on medieval agricultural practices will "benefit society." Benefit society? How exactly are we supposed to quantify that? Will people suddenly start growing turnips more enthusiastically? Precisely! They want statistics, apparently. Projected impacts on… I don’t know… local food security? It’s ridiculous. Feels like we're justifying our existence to a committee of accountants.

Honestly, that was a scorcher! I thought Solihull in September would be a bit more…gentle. Feels more like July, doesn't it? Aye, lass, you're tellin' me! Brings back memories o' summers back home in Leeds. Used to be proper heatwaves, you couldn't move for the sweat. Though, mind, we always had a bit more rain to follow it. This just feels relentlessly sunny. It is. Makes teaching French even more difficult – everyone’s wanting to be outside, not conjugating verbs! I had a student the other day ask if ‘soleil’ was the only verb they needed to know this term. They've got a point, haven't they? What sort of classes do you teach, then? I can barely manage a decent sentence in Spanish, let alone French. Tried a few lessons years ago, but my brain just wouldn't stick with it. I mostly teach adults, conversational French and some business French. Lots of people wanting to brush up for holidays, or whose jobs require it. It’s rewarding, seeing people gain confidence. And surprisingly, a lot of them are trying to learn to connect with their heritage. I had a lovely lady last year who was rediscovering her Algerian roots. That’s nice. Being connected to yer roots. I suppose it’s important. My job doesn’t really involve that sort of thing, mostly just making sure the gyms are running smoothly and the staff are motivated. It's a bit like coaching, really. Got to keep everyone on track, positive. Coaching, you say? Is that something you use deliberately? I’ve been looking at coaching techniques for my teaching – things like active listening and setting goals - it's apparently quite helpful in getting students to push themselves a bit further. Definitely. We use it all the time. Positive reinforcement, targeted feedback, helping people see their potential… it's not just about shouting and telling folk what to do. Though, you do need a bit of that sometimes! Year’s experience in this business teaches you that quickly! What's your take on goal setting with your students? Do you find it works? It does, surprisingly well. It’s easy to get bogged down in grammar and worry about making mistakes, but when someone has a tangible goal – like ordering a coffee in Paris without any prompting – they're much more engaged. I’m trying to encourage them to focus on communication, not perfection.

Right then, tha knows, this is lovely having tha' both here, it really is. But honestly, George, yer sat starin' at the telly like a statue. Doesn’t tha want a biscuit? Or a proper Yorkshire brew? Just watchin' the badgers, love. Calm fellows, badgers are. A bit like me, quiet as a mouse most o’ the time. Badgers are alright, Grandad. But they ain’t got TikTok. TikTok, is it? Always somethin' new. Daniel, put that thing away for five minutes, will tha? Your grandma and grandad have travelled all the way from Hull. Show a bit o’ respect. Don't be harsh wi’ him, Maureen. He’s a teenager. They’re all glued to them things. Reminds me o’ yer dad wi’ his transistor radio. Wouldn't leave the house without it. It’s not  just  TikTok, Grandma. I was looking at student accommodation in York. Got to start thinking about next year, right? Aye, sensible lad. See, George? He’s doing somethin’ useful. Unlike watchin’ badgers. Watchin’ a bit o’ nature, Maureen. Educational in its own way. Less disruptive than those TikToks. Speaking of disruptive, I’ve got that neighbour, Mrs. Higgins, drivin’ me mad again. She keeps leaving her bins out for days, right against the wall. Looks a right mess. Oh, I know Mrs. Higgins! Always a drama with her birds feeders, weren’t they? Attracting every pigeon in Hull. Seriously? Pigeons cause that much hassle? Tha wouldn’t believe it, love. The noise! And she complained when I tried to dust the window sill lookin' out at 'em. Said it was disturbin' the wildlife! Women… always somethin’. Now, now, George. Don't go there. Though, I did complain to the council about them bins. Told 'em it was an eyesore. Got a letter back saying they'd look into it. Never 'eard nothin' since. Councils! What can ya expect? Listen, I need to pop out to the shops later, just for a few bits and bobs. Daniel, could you give me a hand bringing the shopping in? Your grandad’s legs aren’t what they used to be. Sure, no problem. What do you need? Anything exciting? Just the usual, love. Milk, bread, tea bags… and a few biscuits for your grandma and grandad. They need treatin’ after their journey. Don’t need nothin’. Got me badgers to keep me company. Good, quiet life, this.

Right then, are you  absolutely  sure this is the way, love? This road’s narrower than a sheep track! And it says "Unsuitable for HGVs" – I’m starting to think it’s unsuitable for  anything ! Relax, Maggie. It's the quickest route, according to the magic box. Besides, a bit of adventure never hurt anyone. Remember that time we got completely lost in the Lake District trying to find that obscure wool shop? Don't you remind me! Ended up in someone’s cow field, didn't we? Nearly got trampled! And all for a skein of heather-coloured Shetland. Still, the tea and scones at that farmer’s wife's kitchen were decent. Did you pack the oatcakes? I’m peckish. Of course. Oatcakes and cheese. And your favourite lemon drizzle cake. Thought you might need the sugar rush for cheering on the band. This gig's a big one for them, isn’t it? Aye, it is. First time they’ve played outside the county. Nervous as a kitten, poor lads. Especially young Ethan – he’s convinced he’ll forget the lyrics to "The Northern Lights." He’s practically glued to his setlist. He'll be fine. He's got a good voice. And those jigs are top-notch. Heard they've been working on a new one, something inspired by Wordsworth, wasn’t it? That's right. A rather ambitious piece about Grasmere. I’m not entirely convinced it’ll work, to be honest. A bit...highbrow for a ceilidh band, maybe? Though, I suppose Wordsworth  is  our lad, born nearby. Speaking of which, should we have stopped at that little stone circle back near Penrith? I kept meaning to. We’re already running a bit behind schedule, Maggie. Eliza's getting married next week. Need to get to Carlisle, drop off those last few knitted napkins and ensure the floral arrangements are sorted. Auntie Flo is having a full-blown meltdown about the table settings. Said the napkins are ‘slightly off-white’. Slightly off-white! Flo’s a terror. Though, I do sympathise. Wedding planning is enough to send anyone round the bend. At least you’re getting to write about it all, aren't you? That academic paper on traditional wedding rituals? It’s proving fascinating, actually. Researching old ballads and folk customs. Quite different from my usual historical fiction stuff. Do you know, they used to throw ash at the wedding party to wish the couple well?

Honestly, I’m still reeling from that cladding decision. The client just… seemed determined to ignore everything we presented about thermal efficiency. It’s like they saw 'shiny' and stopped listening. Shiny does win people over, doesn't it? Especially when budgets are vaguely defined. I had a similar battle with Mrs. Featherstone about the window detailing on her extension. Wanted wrought iron. Wrought iron! In 2024. Said it was "classic." Classic and freezing! Did you manage to convince her otherwise? Eventually. Highlighted the thermal breaks, showed her simulations… pointed out the potential for condensation. Played the energy bill card. It's a delicate art, swaying wealthy clients. Anyway, what did you get for breakfast? I went for the usual, couldn't resist the croissant. Just a granola and yogurt. Trying to be vaguely healthy. You know, after spending the morning staring at a mock-up of gaudy aluminium. Speaking of gaudy, did you hear about Chloe? Chloe? Oh dear. No, what’s happened? She seemed so on top of things at the last drinks. Apparently, she’s struggling with the Lambert project. Big client, incredibly demanding, and they’re constantly changing their brief. She was practically in tears on the phone last night. Said she’s losing sleep and barely eating. That's awful. It's a terrible pressure cooker, architecture. Lambert are notoriously difficult. Remember Mr. Davies telling us those horror stories when we were at Uni about their insistence on "grand gestures" regardless of practicality? Exactly! And they’ve decided they want a complete redesign of the atrium, just three weeks before handover. She’s dreading presenting it to them. I told her to remind them of the original brief – repeatedly – and to document  everything  in writing. Solid advice. Grey documentation is your friend in these situations. Did she remember that memo we wrote about dealing with difficult clients, back in our studio days? The one with the contingency plans? I think so. I sent it to her this morning. Honestly, it's heartbreaking to see her like this. She's always been so driven. I remember when we were working on that university project, the ‘Communal Living’ brief, she was the one with the innovative ideas about shared spaces and vertical gardening. Ah, yes! That was brilliant. Remember the entire concept revolved around maximizing natural light and incorporating biophilic design principles? We got such a good mark for that, partially thanks to Chloe’s presentation skills, which were a bit sharper than ours back then.

Honestly, the A1 was utter chaos this evening. Absolute gridlock. I think someone decided it was a good idea to have a tractor convention on the eastbound carriageway. A tractor convention? Seriously? Mum, you're pulling my leg. I wish I was, love. A whole fleet of them. Bright red, shiny green…you name it. Held everyone up for at least forty minutes. I swear, I aged ten years just sitting there. How was your day? Anything more exciting than spreadsheets? Not really, no. Usual paperwork mountain. Sarah from HR had a massive meltdown about the new filing system, though. Said it was going to lose them all their jobs. Dramatic as ever. Oh, Sarah. She always was a bit prone to the dramatics. Reminds me a bit of Auntie Brenda when she couldn’t find her reading glasses. Remember that? She accused the cat of stealing them. Oh God, I do! The cat looked completely bewildered. Anyway, about the traffic…was it all just tractors, or was it the usual aggressive driving we get around here? That too, naturally. A fellow in a black Audi was tailgating me, practically breathing down my neck. Honestly, some people have no spatial awareness. I had to keep merging into the slow lane just to let him pass. It’s infuriating! And then they speed off like they’ve won the Grand Prix. It's mad, isn't it? People just seem to think the rules don’t apply to them. Like on the way home, this bloke was hogging the middle lane on the bypass for ages. Wouldn't let anyone past. You could hear horns blaring from everywhere. Exactly! It’s like they’re actively trying to provoke a fight. Drives me mad. You’d think people would be a bit more considerate, especially after the last year. Everyone’s stressed enough. True. So, are you and Dad still going to Liam’s birthday next Saturday? We are! I've already got his cards and I’m thinking about getting him that new gadget he wanted. You're coming, aren't you? Definitely! I've got a gift sorted. Plus, Chloe said she's going to be there, so it should be a good night. Actually, speaking of socialising... there's a new pub opened up in town, "The Heron's Rest." Have you heard about it? Apparently, they do really good cocktails.

Right, so I’ve had another look at this job description for the Media Coordinator role at Midlands Voices. It's… quite dense, isn't it? They really want someone with their finger on the pulse. Aye, they do. Radio's a changing beast, innit? It’s not just what's on the airwaves anymore. It's about podcasts, social media, all that online carry-on. Shows they’re looking for someone well-rounded. So, tell me where you’re stuck? Is it the skills section causing bother? A bit of everything, to be honest. They mention "experience in community engagement" which… I mean, I’ve done lots of outreach with my language students, but is that the same thing? It feels different somehow. Like, radio needs a wider engagement, doesn't it? Hmm, that's a good point. Outreach is good, but community engagement, for a radio station, implies building relationships, actively seeking out stories  from  the community, collaborating with local groups. Think about when you organized that French film club – you weren’t just teaching French, you were creating a space for people to connect, to share experiences. That’s community building, love. Reframe it. You’re right. Okay, that helps. I was getting tangled up in literal translation. What about this bit about “data analysis and audience insights”? I can barely tell the difference between a bar chart and a pie chart. Don't panic! They don't expect you to be a data scientist. They mean you can look at basic analytics – website traffic, social media engagement - and use it to understand what people are listening to and talking about. Have you been looking at Midlands Voices’ own website and social media? Yeah, I spent ages on it yesterday. They're really pushing their local news and arts coverage.
