I spent the rest of the night staring at faces, convinced everyone was going to smile at me menacingly. Tell me about it! I watched it with Liam last weekend and I couldn't sleep for two nights. He kept joking about smiling at me. Not funny, Liam! I thought it was alright. A bit predictable, maybe. But the tension was well-built. And the score was brilliant. Predictable or not, it genuinely unnerved me. I prefer something lighthearted. Like, remember "Paddington 2"? Now  that’s  a good movie. Pure joy. Oh, Paddington 2 is always a winner. Comfort viewing, definitely. Speaking of comfort, this shepherd's pie is amazing, Mum really outdid herself tonight. Totally! I’m going to ask her for the recipe. I've been attempting shepherd's pie for ages, and it always ends up a soggy mess. My attempts are disasters too. I’m sticking to pasta. Much safer option. Anyone tried that new food app, "Tastebud"? It suggests recipes based on what you already have in your fridge. No, but that sounds genius! I waste so much food because I don’t know what to do with random odds and ends. Is it any good? Apparently, yeah. It's got pretty good reviews. It’s even got a section for finding local farmers markets – which could be helpful for Mum, right? To get fresh ingredients? That  would  be amazing! Always looking for new suppliers. But finding reliable ones near Peterborough is a challenge. Everything feels a bit…corporate these days. What about that craft fair they had at the community centre last week? There was a lovely lady selling homemade jams and stuff. Good point! I’ll look into that. Right, moving on from food… any updates on the friend situation? Liam’s still being a bit…Liam-y. Don't even get me started. He keeps sending me these ridiculous memes. It's cute initially, but it’s starting to feel like his entire personality consists of sending memes. Classic. My Ben’s not much better, honestly. He’s obsessed with finding me the "perfect" plant for my flat. He’s currently researching the light requirements of several different ferns.

Blimey, look at that! Proper downpour this is, isn't it? Makes you wish you were tucked up indoors with a nice cuppa. Aye, fierce it is. Remember '68, Arthur? We had a flood right down The Street in Costessey. Water up to your knees, it was! Nasty business. Oh, you two and your reminiscing! It’s just rain, Bertram. Though I have to admit, it does make the drive home a bit treacherous. John's expecting me back in an hour, you know. An hour? That’s pushing it, Doreen. You'll be battling that weather all the way to Harrow. Are you thinking of taking the bus? The bus? Don't be daft, Arthur! It’ll take me twice as long. Plus, the hills! My poor old knees wouldn’t thank me. I’m hoping it’ll ease up a bit. John's not thrilled when I'm late for supper, you know he isn't. He gets all grumpy. Grumpy old thing, your John. Always has been. Remember that time he complained about your rhubarb crumble being ‘too tart’? Absurd! Don't remind me, Bertram! He’s a strange one, that John. But a good soul, under all that grumbling. So, Arthur, what are  you  doing for the evening? Still stuck in here, are you? Well, yes, Doreen. Can’t exactly pop down the pub in  this . And my car's still having bother, you know. That blooming exhaust. Keeps rattling something awful. Took it to that chap down on Aylsham Road, said he couldn't fix it without a fortune. Youngsters these days, can't fix anything properly. Back in my day, a bit of string and a bit of elbow grease and you could bring anything back to life! Remember old Mr. Higgins, Doreen? He could mend a tractor with a paperclip and a smile. Oh, I do remember him! He was a marvel. Arthur, are you thinking of getting another car? It can’t be pleasant being stuck in. I've been considering it, Doreen, I have. But the prices these days! It’s ridiculous. And young people driving – a menace, truly. All glued to their phones. You’re tellin’ me! Saw a lad yesterday almost plough into a lamppost. Blasted mobile phone! Should revoke their licences all of ‘em. Now, now, Bertram, don’t be like that. Not  all  young drivers are reckless. Though I do agree, it’s worrying sometimes.

Honestly, this traffic is dreadful. I thought leaving London a bit earlier would help, but no such luck. Are you two alright back there? No biscuit-crumb emergencies? All good here, love. Just contemplating the sheer volume of vehicles all heading… somewhere. Makes you think, doesn't it? About journeys and destinations. Speaking of destinations, how are you feeling about the move, Moira? Really feeling it? It’s… it’s a strange feeling, David. Exhilarating, certainly. A new chapter, as they say. But leaving behind… well, the familiarity of everything, the school, my garden… it’s a bit of a wrench. Forty years I spent there. I understand completely. Selling my flat felt the same way. Even though it was a tiny, slightly damp flat, it was  mine . Moving into a house with Liam…different, exciting, but definitely a leap. You’ll get used to the new place, Moira. It's got that big garden you were talking about, right? It does, a proper rambling thing! But it needs work. David keeps talking about decking and patios and… well, it all sounds rather overwhelming. I’m more of a ‘plant a few roses and leave it at that’ kind of gardener. We’ll tackle it together, love. Rome wasn’t built in a day. And I’m surprisingly good with a trowel, you know. Remember that prize-winning marrow I grew back in… well, never mind  when  it was. The point is, I have skills. I’m sure you do, David. Although, I'm slightly apprehensive about a prize-winning marrow dominating your new garden. What about the car though? Are you happy with the Volvo? I mean, it’s a sensible choice, but… Sensible is exactly what I need at my age, darling! I’m not planning on doing any Formula One racing. It’s comfortable, reliable, and it has a HUGE boot. Perfect for transporting gardening implements and… well, whatever else a retired maths teacher needs. It's a bit…beige, though, isn't it? We need something a bit more…spirited. Something with a bit of  oomph . I was thinking a vintage Jaguar. A vintage Jaguar, David? Seriously? On a fixed income? It's an investment! They hold their value! Plus, imagine cruising down the M6 in a classic Jag! People would  respect  us. I think the respect comes from knowing your numbers, David. Something I specialized in for decades.

Right, darling, you won't believe this. You absolutely won’t! What? Did you finally find that recipe for lemon drizzle cake you were struggling with? Better than lemon drizzle, love. Much, much better. Remember how gutted you were about your bike being stolen? The blue one, your Raleigh? Yeah… like, still massively upset. I can’t believe someone would just… take it. Especially because I was saving up for new cycling shoes! Where were you when I told you? I remember. You were practically incandescent! Anyway… they found it! They did?! Seriously? How? Where was it?! Apparently, someone saw a group of lads trying to sell it down by the marina. A couple of fishermen recognised it – they said they’d seen you cycling past the harbour loads of times. No way! That’s brilliant! Those lads… I bet they thought they could get away with it. So, the police got involved? Not exactly. The fishermen called the shop that sold you the bike, 'Wheel Wizards'. They’d kept a record of the sale and serial number, thankfully. They went down and the lads legged it, but thankfully, the bike was undamaged. They towed it back to Wheel Wizards, and they called me. Wow. That's a ridiculously happy ending! I feel so relieved. I was planning on doing the Coastal Path this weekend. I can’t believe it’s back. Do you want a cup of tea? I’ll make one. Yes, please, darling. And a biscuit. It’s been a bit of a stressful afternoon sorting it all out – paperwork and stuff. Though, it was worth it to see your face light up. You know, this whole thing makes me think about how much people share on social media these days. What do you mean? Well, if you hadn’t posted pictures of your bike on Instagram, maybe they wouldn’t have recognised it! It's a strange one, isn't it? Sharing everything… it can be helpful, but also risky. Do you think you should be more careful about what you post? Maybe. I guess I was showing it off a bit. It's got those clips on the handlebars. I'm trying to get a new profile pic for my cycling group. But you're right, I probably shouldn't be broadcasting where my bike is parked all the time. Do you think I should post about it being found?

Right then, Cardiff to Newport. Standard fare, eh? Nothing fancy this time. Reminds me of the trips I used to take back when I worked for Save the Children. Could spend hours on those trains. Standard seems to be the theme of this game, doesn’t it? Everyone just plonking down lines wherever they fancy. I’m trying to build a proper network here, Gareth, you’re just scattering routes like confetti. Scattershot is a good strategy, Rhys. Sometimes you need to disrupt the established order. You’re obviously trying to play the long game, the safe game. Requires a lot more patience, doesn't it? Patience is something I’ve learned over the years. Especially dealing with the clients I do. Though, watching you lot play this game, I reckon I've just as much patience as anyone. Rhys, you're awfully competitive! What's for lunch? I was thinking a big pot of cawl. Cawl is essential. A proper holiday needs cawl. And bread, naturally. Don't forget the bread, Mum. Naturally, Alun! Bread is the foundation of any decent meal. And speaking of foundation, Anya, you’re hoarding all the teal trains. What’s the plan there? A teal monopoly? Teal is strategically advantageous, Rhys! And besides, I need them for the route from Hereford to Bristol. It’s crucial for connecting the South West! You wouldn't understand, you're too busy flitting about. When I was working in Singapore, for three years, we used to have train journeys that would last days! Not like these short hops. Everything felt so… momentous. You’d meet all sorts of characters. One woman spent the entire trip knitting a cardigan for her grandson. She knitted the sleeves  backwards ! Oh, you could write a book about the people you meet, Dai. Bless him. It's good to hear those stories. Makes this little game feel a bit… trivial, doesn't it? Still, it’s lovely to be all together. Trivial? This is strategic warfare, Mum! Gareth is clearly about to cut me off in Birmingham. I need to deploy reinforcements. You think I'm cutting you off, Alun? I was merely considering expanding my network to strategically avoid  you . There's a difference. Honestly, you two! You're like a pair of arguing teenagers. Gareth, are you going to actually play this thing, or just commentate? Actually, this reminds me of a train journey I took back from Cardiff once...

Right, that’s it. I’m officially declaring war on this Monopoly board. It’s rigged, I tell you! Absolutely rigged! War, darling? Seriously? It's just Monopoly. And I’m winning, might I add. Park Lane and Mayfair, both mine. A strategic masterpiece, really. Strategic masterpiece? You've just landed on every single one of my properties and charged me extortionate rent! It’s more like ruthless exploitation. Reminds me a little of London property prices, actually. A little bit of a parallel, perhaps. Though I’m not trying to bankrupt you permanently, just… establishing a dominant position in this miniature capitalist society. It’s all part of the fun. Did you remember to grab the crisps from the kitchen? This strategic domination requires sustenance. Yes, they’re on the coffee table. Salt and vinegar, your favourite. It's just, I hate how this game encourages that cutthroat behaviour, doesn't it? Always building hotels, snapping up everything… It feels a bit aggressively consumerist even for a board game. I think you’re reading a bit too much into it, love. It's a game, a bit of lighthearted competition. But you're right, there  is  something rather… fascinating about the way it reflects our culture, isn't there? The rush to accumulate, the scramble for resources... It mirrors the real world in a strangely simplified way. Do you think our parents ever played this as kids and saw it the same way? I doubt it. It was probably just a way to pass the time. I imagine their version was far less strategic and a lot more about accidentally landing on Free Parking and hoping for a windfall. It’s funny, isn’t it? How something so simple – rolling dice, moving around a board – can suddenly reveal something about our values, or at least, the values we project onto a game. Absolutely. And the drinking culture surrounding it! Remember university? Monopoly nights fueled by cheap cider and increasingly hostile negotiations? It was a… memorable experience. Oh god, yes. The rule bending was legendary. "That's not  really  a mortgage, I'm just temporarily... restructuring.” The arguments! And the inevitable accusation of cheating. Good times, though. Less stressful than marking essays, that's for sure. Definitely. Though, there's a certain charm to the chaos. It’s a peculiar tradition, isn't it? Having these kind of board game fueled gatherings.

Honestly, Kerrie, you’ve outdone yourself this time. It looks like a craft fair exploded in here! Are those felt hedgehogs? They are! Kerrie’s been on a hedgehog-making spree. Apparently, they’re going to be Christmas tree decorations. Quite charming, actually. And the pasta’s brilliant, by the way. What is it, pesto? It  is  pesto, love. And don’t be rude to my daughter and her crafts. They're wonderfully quirky. You know, reminds me of when I used to dress my grandkids in handmade outfits. They looked like little walking rainbows. Right, well, I hope the recipients of these hedgehogs appreciate the effort! Speaking of effort, how's the unpacking going, Mum? Last I heard, you were wrestling with a flatpack wardrobe. Don’t even  mention  it! It's a nightmare. I think I’ve used every curse word I know. Honestly, they should come with a diagram that’s actually readable. And the screws! Half of them are the wrong size. It’s giving me a headache. I'd have been better off calling a handyman. Though, that would have cost a fortune, wouldn't it? Yeah, handymen are expensive. Did you look at those online tutorials, Kerrie? There's a really good one on YouTube for IKEA wardrobes. Saves a lot of hassle, sometimes. I tried! It was… not helpful. It assumed a level of spatial reasoning I clearly don't possess. It just ended with me staring at a pile of wood and questioning all my life choices. Exactly! It's all well and good for those who are naturally gifted at building things. I’m an accountant, for goodness sake! Numbers, spreadsheets, balance sheets. Not… carpentry. Do you remember when I got that flatpack bed frame years ago? Took me a whole weekend and a very patient neighbour. Oh yeah! I remember that. You were threatening to throw the instruction manual out the window. Right, changing the subject before we all descend into a flatpack-induced rage. So, Dad's complaining about the bins again. Apparently, the new schedule is completely illogical. Don't even start. They collect the recycling on Tuesdays now, but the general waste is on Thursdays. It makes absolutely no sense! It’s like they’re actively trying to make our lives difficult. He’s emailed the council, of course. He's relentless. Dad always was. Remember when he campaigned for a better bus route?

Honestly, Mum, this traffic is mental. I swear it gets worse every time we come this way. Feels like we're barely moving. Well, darling, it  is  rush hour. And you know North London gets clogged up something fierce. Just breathe, love. No point getting worked up about it. Did you remember to grab that box from Amy's flat? Yeah, got it in the back. It’s got the TLS stuff in it. You were saying it’s really important? Absolutely. The TLS submission deadline is looming, and that final batch of proofs is crucial. It's a landmark edition dealing with modern poetry – all those young voices, you know? Requires a hawk-eye, and sadly, mine isn't quite as sharp as it used to be. Hence needing your fresh eyes. Right, the modern poetry one. Sounds intense. So, like, actual paper still? In this day and age, you’d think everything would be digital. You'd think, wouldn’t you? But The Times Literary Supplement is steeped in tradition. There’s a certain… gravitas to the printed word, especially with something like this. It feels more substantial, more worthy of the writers featured. Plus, the layout artists are brilliant – they need the physical proofs to really finesse things. It’s a beautiful, painstaking process. Though it does drive me up the wall sometimes, let me tell you. This new intern keeps inserting rogue semicolons. Semicolons everywhere! Rogue semicolons? Seriously? That's your biggest nightmare? I thought it would be dealing with difficult authors. Oh,  those  are a different story entirely. But a misplaced semicolon can halt production! It’s the little things, darling. Anyway, how's your research going? Still wrestling with that thesis? It’s…progressing. Slowly. I think I’m getting somewhere with the Baudelaire comparison, but my supervisor keeps pushing me to look at the influence of TikTok on contemporary poetry. TikTok! Can you even imagine Baudelaire scrolling through TikTok? Oh, I can. He’d be utterly scandalized, probably writing scathing verse about it. Though, I suppose even he understood the allure of fleeting moments and visual imagery. It’s all about adaptation, isn't it? Now, did you end up getting that scarf for Sophie's birthday? She mentioned she liked the blue cashmere. Sorted. Got one from that place in Shoreditch, the one with the really chunky knit. She'll love it. I also saw a vintage Citroën DS – seriously gorgeous!

…and then the seagull just  snatched  the whole baguette right out of Gran’s hand! Honestly, she screamed like a banshee. It was pure chaos on Scarborough beach. Aye, Scarborough, eh? My auntie went there last year, said it were filled with seagulls lookin' for a free dinner. Sounded right lively! So, Yorkshire holidays, eh? Always a bit... dramatic. Dramatic’s putting it mildly, Sarah! Your gran sounds like a force of nature. Mine just complained about the sand getting in her shoes for the entire week we spent in Blackpool. Blackpool! Tell us more, Liam! I’ve never been. Is it as rubbish as everyone says? Don't listen to her, Blackpool's a  classic . Sore thumbs from the arcades, greasy chips, horrifyingly bright lights... it’s a rite of passage, innit? I spent most of my pocket money there one summer trying to win a giant teddy bear. Never did. Blackpool’s a right mess, let’s be honest. Remember that time we tried to go on the Big One, Emily? Don’t remind me! I felt like I was going to chuck up before we even got to the top. And then that drop… I nearly lost it completely. I think I spent the next hour clinging to your mum, Chloe. You were a right state, love. Honestly, clinging like a limpet. But the Big One is brilliant! You just gotta embrace the terror. Right, let’s move on before Emily has flashbacks. What about you, Chloe? Got any holiday disasters to share? Was your Blackpool experience any better than Liam's? Come on, spill the beans! Yeah, Chloe, give us a good one! Something to make us laugh. Ideally something involving a lost passport or a rogue donkey. That’s the holiday gold standard, you know. Or a disastrous attempt at making paella. Remember Uncle Dave's paella attempt in Spain? That was a culinary catastrophe. Oh god, don't even start on Uncle Dave's paella. It was like concrete. And suspiciously green. He genuinely thought you could use chicken stock  and  chorizo. It was a flavour clash of epic proportions. It was… an experience. That’s why we love him, isn’t it? He tries. Right then, Chloe, your turn! Don't tell us it was all beaches and sunshine. Everyone needs a good holiday story involving something going horribly, wonderfully wrong. We're braced for it!

Right then. So, Alistair’s been going on about this ‘wild winter camping’ business for weeks. Sounds positively barbaric, doesn't it? Freezing to death in a tent while the rest of us are huddled by a roaring fire. Oh, don't let him fool you, David. It's not barbaric, it’s… invigorating! Though I admit, the first time I went with Hamish, I nearly turned right back around. The wind! The sheer ferocity of it! Aye, it’s definitely not for the faint of heart, Dad. But that’s part of the appeal, isn’t it? It strips everything back. You're completely reliant on your wits and your equipment. And the silence… the silence is incredible. You hear things you never hear in the city. Silence? I imagine you hear the wind whistling through your ears and your teeth chattering. I mean, you're practically begging for frostbite. What’s the point, Alistair? Honestly. The point, Dad, is connection. With nature, primarily. But also, with yourself. It’s a massive mental challenge. You're pushing yourself, battling the elements, problem-solving constantly. It's incredibly grounding. And, there's a profound beauty to a winter landscape - the snow, the crisp air, the way the sunlight hits the trees… it’s quite magical, actually. He's right, David. It changes your perspective, honestly. And it’s not just about battling the elements. There’s a real skill to it. Knowing how to layer your clothing properly, choosing the right location for shelter from the wind, building a proper fire - it’s all quite fascinating. Hamish even showed me how to detect frost pockets in the snow. Apparently, they can be a real hazard. Frost pockets? Good heavens. You're telling me you’re out there, traipsing through snow, worrying about frost pockets? It’s all a bit… intense for my liking. I prefer a nice bit of birdwatching, myself. Far less perilous. It’s not  always  intense, Dad! There are quieter days. Days where the sun shines and you can just sit and watch the deer move through the snow. It's about finding those moments of stillness, even in the wild. I have this one memory, sitting by a frozen loch, the only sound the cracking of the ice… it was utterly breathtaking. Aye, and the stars! You see stars like you've never seen them before, away from all the city lights.

Right, so, “Dune.” Honestly, Liam, I still don’t  get  it. All that sand and whispering and giant worms… it was…a lot. A lot of what, El? A lot engaging? A lot visually stunning? Because, I thought it was phenomenal. Villeneuve really nailed the scope and the atmosphere, don't you think? Engaging, maybe a bit. Stunning, yeah, undeniably. But  get  it? The politics were swirling around my head like a dust devil, and I'm not even talking about the spice. It felt like everyone was plotting against everyone else, and the motivations were all… vague. I mean, all that talk of “the Kwisatz Haderach” and the Bene Gesserit… it just flew over my head. It needed a flipping glossary! That's kind of the point, isn't it? It's deliberately dense, reflecting the complexity of the universe Herbert created. It’s not supposed to be spoon-fed to you. The Kwisatz Haderach, for example, is about the convergence of male and female voices, the potential for a being with prescience that transcends limitations… it’s profound stuff. Profoundly confusing, more like. I mean, I read the blurb on the back, about a young man destined to save everyone, right? But he mostly just looked worried and ran a lot. It felt like a very long, serious advert for desert tourism. You're being rather harsh! And you're focusing on Paul’s journey solely as a ‘saviour.’ It’s also about the dangers of messianic figures, the cyclical nature of power, and the clash of cultures - the Fremen and the Imperium. Think of it like  Lord of the Rings , but with more Machiavellian politics and a significant environmental message. Right,  Lord of the Rings . Now  that  I got. Good versus evil, clear objectives, hobbits. Much more straightforward. I read  The Silmarillion  once, though… now  that  was dense. Took me a month and a spreadsheet. Speaking of reading, did you ever finish  Circe ? I did! Madeline Miller is incredible. Her prose is just so lyrical and evocative. I loved the way she explored Circe’s isolation and her gradual embrace of her own power. The mythological context was fascinating, but it was the character development that really captivated me. Aye, it was brilliant. Gave me right hunger, though. All that honey and figs and goat's cheese... remind me, are we stopping for that Greek place in Watford?

Right, who’s feeling sleepy? Or who’s got a favourite story they want to tell? It feels like ages since we had a proper story time. Tell one! Tell one about a princess who rides a dinosaur! No! A pirate! A pirate who finds a treasure chest full of Lego! Alright, alright. We can have both, can’t we? Maybe the princess  rides  a dinosaur… to find the pirate’s treasure! See? A bit of both. But before we do that, I was thinking about something silly today at school. We were reading this very old book, and it kept using phrases like "forsooth" and "hark!" Honestly, the kids looked at me like I was speaking Martian. "Forsooth?" What's 'forsooth'? Does it mean something fancy? Well, it used to mean ‘truly’ or ‘indeed’… like, "Forsooth, this cake is delicious!" It’s all a bit old-fashioned now, isn’t it? I remember my grandma using it sometimes. She was proper old school. Can the pirate say "Forsooth?" Then it's extra pirate-y! He absolutely can! “Forsooth, me hearties, I’ve found the buried treasure!” How’s that? It sounds a bit silly, doesn’t it? Speaking of silly, remember when Dad tried to learn Excel? It was a disaster. Daddy got cross with the computer! It kept saying ‘Error!’ It did! He was trying to make a spreadsheet of all our Lego bricks. He thought it would be neat – categorized by colour and type. It was…ambitious. He ended up just closing the laptop and saying, “This thing is witchcraft!” Witchcraft! Like a wizard hiding the treasure! Exactly! Actually, speaking of computers… Remember that old typewriter I found at a car boot sale? The clicky one? Can we play with it again? We can! It's quite fun, isn’t it? It’s so different from typing on a computer. No backspace, you know? If you make a mistake, you have to take the whole paper out and start again. It really makes you think before you write. It's like ancient technology! Is it older than the PlayStation? Oh,  much  older! Decades older. The PlayStation is modern magic. You can play games with people all over the world! I want to play Minecraft again! Can we play Minecraft tomorrow? We absolutely can. Maybe we can build a castle  with  the treasure from the pirate. A dinosaur-proof castle, just in case!

Honestly, David, you look like you've been wrestling a badger. Is that… is that paint on your trousers? It might be. Bit of a morning, actually. Roadworks on the A650. Absolute chaos. Took me nearly an hour to get here from Ilkley. And yes, it’s paint. Retaining wall at the allotment. Needs pointing. An allotment! Fancy you taking on something like that. I’m still battling the slugs in my little herb garden. Basil’s looking particularly sorry for itself. Slugs are the bane of any gardener’s life, aren’t they? Though, I’ve found beer traps are surprisingly effective. You should try it. More coffee? Please. And you know, I was reading about fruit farms down in Kent the other day. Massive ones. All automated, apparently. Not a pick-your-own punnet in sight. Pity, isn’t it? Used to be such a lovely family thing. Progress, they call it. Though I do miss those days. Remember that farm we went to near Windsor when the children were little? All those brambles and slightly bruised apples. Oh, yes! And you ended up with blackberries in your hair for days. Speaking of Windsor, how’s your sister doing? Still railing against the junk mail? Still the same. Piles of it. She’s convinced the postman’s deliberately trying to wind her up. Apparently, she got four different takeaway menus this morning, none of which she’s ever ordered from. Honestly, at her age – nearly eighty, you know – you’d think they’d realize she’s not exactly impulse buying a vindaloo. It's dreadful, isn’t it? All that waste. It’s the same with these marketing calls. I swear my phone rings at least five times a day with some automated voice trying to flog me something I don’t need. Absolutely infuriating. Tell me about it! And they never listen when you say you're not interested. Just keep rattling on. I sometimes wonder if they're even people on the other end of the line. It’s probably just algorithms, isn’t it? No actual person. Now, did you hear about old Mrs. Higgins down the road? She's sold her house. The one with the prize-winning roses. No! Goodness me. To whom? I hope it's someone who appreciates those roses. She put so much effort into them. Apparently, some young couple from London.

Right then, that was a lovely Christmas dinner, wasn’t it? Honestly, I’m still full. Though, I do wish Dad hadn’t insisted on having that fruitcake. Never been a fan, you know. Bit of a classic, though, isn't it, love? Can’t have Christmas without a fruitcake, can we? Even if you do wrinkle your nose at it. And it wasn't  that  bad this year. I think I actually managed to sneak a decent chunk of brandy in it. You’re both hopeless! Dad, owning up to spiking the cake now? Brilliant. Mum, you’re secretly wondering if you should have another slice, aren't you? I did not! I’m being sensible. My knees are a bit dodgy today, you know, after all that standing around at work. This damp weather isn't helping them at all. I’ve been meaning to try that new cream Sarah recommended, arnica-based. Have you seen it anywhere, John? Arnica? Yeah, I think I saw it in Boots the other day. Near the bandages, probably. Why don’t I pop out tomorrow and grab you some? Need anything else while I’m there? Some of that fancy ginger beer you like? While you’re out, Dad, could you pick up some of that lactose-free milk? I'm out. And honestly, having everything online is a nightmare. Delivery charges, the wait… it's so much easier just having you run out. She's got a point, John. Honestly, these online shops – a right faff they are. Remember when you could just pop to the corner shop for everything? Everything’s gone all complicated now. Complicated is an understatement. And speaking of complicated, have you two been on Facebook much over Christmas? Seeing all those perfect family pictures… drives me mad! People just showing off. It's curated, Dad! Nobody posts the photos of the screaming kids and burnt brussel sprouts. It's all strategically chosen to look idyllic. I did post a picture of the dog attempting to steal the turkey, though. That was authentically chaotic. Oh, bless him, that little rascal! Speaking of chaotic, Tilly's still haven't texted to say when they're heading back down from Scotland. I'm starting to worry. Give them time, love. They’ll be having a post-Christmas sherry and relaxing. Tilly usually sends a message when they’re about to hit the M1.

Honestly, this copywriting gig is driving me mad sometimes. They want “aspirational yet relatable” for dog food.  Dog food , Elara! How do you even  do  that? Aspirational dog food? That's… a challenge. Right, well, sounds stressful. You mentioned last time you were looking for a change, is this still the feeling? It is. It’s not that the work itself is awful, it’s just… soul-crushing at times. Last week I spent three hours crafting a paragraph about the "wholesome goodness" of dry kibble. Three hours! I could have written a short story in that time. And the clients... dear God, the clients. This one wants his online dating profile to sound "like James Bond, but approachable." Oh, bless him. Everyone wants to be James Bond. Though, “approachable” and “James Bond” feel like opposing forces. What about that coding course you were looking at? Did you ever look into it? I did! And it’s even more expensive than I thought. Student loan repayments are scary enough as it is. I was looking at the courses offered at City Lit, you know, nearer to where I’m living. It was a good option, relatively speaking. But the upfront cost... Honestly, I'm terrified of getting into more debt. Plus, I'm thinking about Mum again. What’s she doing? Is everything alright? Last I heard, she was still struggling with the house repairs. Yeah, it's the roof. It’s got worse, hasn’t it? The quotes are astronomical. She’s trying to do some of it herself, bless her, but she’s got to be careful. I'm trying to help where I can, but obviously, my salary isn’t exactly overflowing. And she’s being stubborn, refusing to ask Dad for anything. That's classic Dad. Foot-stamping refusal to acknowledge any financial responsibility. Though, honestly, I’m not surprised Mum's wary. He'd probably just use it as ammunition later. Speaking of family, how are your cousins? Did you see Amelia and Tom at Christmas? I did! Amelia's stressing about her dissertation - unsurprisingly, if you know her. Tom’s just… Tom, you know? Still trying to be a ‘content creator’, still largely failing to pay rent. They're living in that ridiculous tiny flat in Hackney. I feel for them, really I do, but it’s a bit sad. So much potential, just… floundering.

Honestly, Eleanor, this place is lovely. You’ve really made it your own. Much more… you, than that sterile box you had in the city. Oh, thank you, darling. It needed a lot of work, mind you. The garden was a jungle when I moved in. But it’s so much more peaceful here, don't you think? And the neighbours are actually… well, they’re neighbours! Absolutely. I can't say I miss the constant sirens and the questionable smells wafting from the kebab shop downstairs. Though, I do miss Pad Thai readily available at 3 am. Not that I ever actually  needed  it, of course. Just… convenient. Of course not. You were just stocking up for emergencies. So, tell me, how is the transcribing going? Still drowning in legal jargon, I imagine? Drowning is putting it mildly! It’s a new case this week - corporate espionage. Dry, dry, and even drier. I'm starting to dream in footnotes. I did manage to squeeze in a Pilates class yesterday, though. Felt utterly ridiculous, frankly. All those toned bodies bouncing around. I felt like a particularly uncoordinated walrus. You always were wonderfully self-deprecating. Pilates is good for you, though, isn't it? Keeps the back strong. Essential for a transcriber, that. I’ve been trying to get a bit more active myself. Thinking about joining that walking group down the road, the "Wanderers." Sound frightfully earnest, but fresh air is fresh air, isn’t it? The Wanderers? That does sound a bit… intense. But you’re right, fresh air is vital. Better than hunching over a laptop all day. Speaking of intensity, have you seen the house prices around here? They're mental! I was looking at properties online just for fun, you know, and… good grief. Don't even start me! It's outrageous. I’m so glad I bought when I did, even if this place  was  a bit of a fixer-upper. You wouldn’t stand a chance now, not with that sensible London salary. Though, that sensible London salary allows you to order Pad Thai at 3am, remember? A fair point. Still, it’s scary. How are things with David? Still putting up with your eccentric writerly lifestyle? He is. Surprisingly well, actually. He's been experimenting with sourdough again, which means a lot of flour explosions in the kitchen, but he seems very pleased with his latest loaf.

Blimey, look at the size of that thing! Proper Victorian, innit? Never realised the Botanic Gardens were this big. It is impressive, isn’t it? I’ve spent a few afternoons wandering around here when I was studying, it's a proper escape from the bustle of the city. So, how's the corpus work going? Are you still wrestling with intransitive verbs? Aye, still. It’s a constant battle, really. Loads of archaic stuff popping up, clashing with modern slang. You wouldn’t believe the volume of tweets using “lit” in seemingly random contexts. Trying to categorise all that is… well, it’s a test of patience, that's what it is. But it's fascinating, too, seeing language evolve like that. Much more interesting than spreadsheets, anyway. Definitely. Sounds a bit like my structural analysis work, actually – trying to find patterns and connections, just with bridges and buildings instead of words. Though I doubt there's much archaic structural engineering involved! Doubtful! What are you working on at the moment then? Still that viaduct project south of London? Yeah, it's been keeping me busy. Lots of calculations, site visits… the usual. It’s got a really tricky foundation problem, the ground’s a bit unstable. Actually, speaking of busy, did you see anything about the budget announcement? It hit me hard, the changes to student loan interest rates. Aye, I saw. It’s a proper kick in the teeth, isn’t it? I mean, I managed to get through without a huge amount of debt, thankfully, but for anyone just finishing uni… it’s rough. Feels like they’re penalising us for trying to get an education. Exactly! And all this talk about cutting public spending… it’s worrying. I'm worried about future infrastructure projects. You know, the ones that actually keep things running smoothly? Tell me about it. Although, I'm more worried about me Nan. She’s on a fixed income, and these increases… it’ll make a difference. Makes you want to scream! Totally. Right, need to try and stay positive. Speaking of which, have you seen anything good lately? I was thinking of going to a show next month. Ooh, you know me, always on the lookout for a good musical. There’s a touring production of ‘Wicked’ coming to Newcastle soon. I’ve been wanting to see it for years! 'Wicked'? I've heard good things.

Blimey, this is a right awkward angle, innit? Feels like I'm wrestling with a stubborn badger. You wouldn’t believe the sheer amount of dust that’s come loose from this wall. Good thing you’ve got that tarpaulin spread out, Anon. Aye, it's a beast of a job. You're doing brilliant though, Karl. This’ll look proper smashing when it's finished. Bet it’ll really liven the place up. Bit of colour, eh? Needed it. You know, I drove past that new development down by the docks yesterday. They've knocked down the old Majestic cinema. Oh, the Majestic! That’s a tragedy. Such a beautiful art deco building. They're building flats, aren’t they? More overpriced shoeboxes no one can actually afford. That's right. Luxury apartments. Said it’ll ‘revitalize the area.’ Revitalize it into a playground for the rich, more like. Remember seeing some right good plays there back in the day. Local lads, proper up-and-coming actors. I do, vaguely. Though my theatre going days are mostly back in Germany. We had a phenomenal student theatre group, you know. Truly experimental stuff - Brecht, Ionesco... Gave you something to chew on. Rather different from a Saturday night panto. Speaking of acting, did you ever see that film – "Get Carter"? Michael Caine at his absolute best. "Get Carter!" Classic! Knew a fella once, looked  exactly  like Michael Caine. Proper hard bloke, too. Used to do a bit of painting himself, actually. Not like this, mind – graffiti, mostly. Bit more... rebellious. He could blend a colour like nobody's business. Makes you think, doesn't it? Proper talent wasted. Indeed. Such a waste. It’s funny, isn’t it? How often talent is squandered. I’ve got a nephew, actually, in Berlin. He's trying to make it as a painter. Struggles terribly. Keeps telling me he needs a 'significant artistic statement.' I don’t even know what that  means ! Typical artist, innit? Always needing to be profound. Tell him to paint what he sees, what he feels. Don't try to  be  profound, just  do . Speaking of doing, you wouldn’t happen to have a stepladder kicking about, would you, Karl? My gutters are overflowing again. It's been raining cats and dogs. Ah, the gutters! A perennial problem. I might. Let me have a look in the garage. I think I've got one lurking back there under a pile of… well,  stuff .

Right, so that sign said Tarnów’s about another hour and a half? Honestly, this Polish countryside is… well, it’s  something . Not quite the Black Forest, is it? Though the fields are lovely. All that gold. No, not quite the Black Forest. But it has its own charm, doesn't it? So much quieter than Białka. Much more… settled. Relaxing, actually. I’m almost glad we left the mountains. All that hustle and bustle with the skiers. Hustle and bustle is putting it mildly! It was chaos getting out of that car park. I think I aged a year dealing with those minibuses all trying to squeeze out at once. Speaking of finances, have you worked out roughly what we’ve spent on petrol so far? I’m trying to keep track. I haven't, no. I just... tend to avoid thinking about it. Petrol is always a surprise, isn’t it? Reminds me of when I used to drive my little Mini back home to Cambridge. Remember that, Tilly? Before… well, before everything. Before you decided to sell everything and become a nomadic TEFL tutor, you mean? Trying to clear out the clutter, right? Honestly, I admire you for it. It takes guts. I’m perpetually surrounded by stuff. My flat's a disaster. Guts or slightly mad, I’m not sure which. It was tempting to get rid of everything I owned rather than face having to deal with it. It’s rather freeing to own so little, actually. Except food, of course! I'm starving. Are we stopping soon? I’m thinking a layby in about half an hour? There's a little shop marked on the map. We could grab some bread and cheese, maybe some fruit. Polish pastries, definitely. You have to try a pączek! It’s like a donut, but… better. You and your food. Always thinking about the next meal! That’s good, though. It’s comforting. Reminds me of Bridget, actually. You remember Bridget? From university? Always organising picnics. Vaguely. Lots of people at uni, you know? Was she one of your English Lit lot? I was over in Philosophy. Actually, I bumped into Mark from Philosophy the other day. He's doing surprisingly well – Head of Acquisitions at a publishing house in Manchester. Said he missed our ridiculous debates. Mark! Good for him. I lost touch with most of them, to be honest.

Right then, are you sure this is the best way, love? Feels like we're going round in circles a bit. St Anne’s was straight up the A56, weren't it? Dad, the satnav says this is faster, alright? It avoids the roadworks near Freckleton. Remember last time? We were stuck for ages then. And honestly, you need to let the technology do its thing. Let it go, Mark. Google Maps knows best. Besides, a few extra twists and turns are good for the scenery. Look, there’s a nice field of cows! Cows! At this hour? I’m hungry, that’s what I am. We’re going to Preston for the supermarket, right? Need to stock up. Bethany's got that dreadful cold, hasn't she? Yep. Still coughing something awful. I’ve got some throat lozenges in my bag, I can give her one when we get there. School's been a nightmare this week, too. Exam stress is really hitting everyone. Oh, darling, how are your exams going? Are you feeling confident about the history one? I’ve got some notes if you want to have a look later. Thanks, but I’m alright for history. It’s biology I’m dreading. It's just…so much to remember. Thinking about a trip to the Hay Festival might be a good distraction after, though. Remember reading about it? The Hay Festival? Fancy that! A load of bookish types talking about themselves. Not really my cup of tea, that. I’d rather be watching football. Though, your mum used to drag me to a book fair in Bolton once. Dreadful day, it was. Rain lashed down, and I ended up buying her a ridiculously oversized poetry book she never read. Oh, Mark! That's a classic. You've always been a bit wary of anything intellectual. I bet you didn't even understand a word of it. I understood 'expensive'! And cold. Speaking of which, I'm frozen. These car seats aren't what they used to be. Dad, you’re wearing a fleece! A thin fleece! I used to be able to walk miles in the snow without a coat. Now, I shiver if the temperature drops below fifteen. Remember that time we went sledging down Winter Hill? Blisters the size of footballs, I tell you. Oh, I do remember that! You fell headfirst into a snowdrift.

Well, I'll be! Agnes, what a surprise! You're looking… bright. Really bright! Did you get a new dye job? Oh, love, don't be daft. It's just the sunlight. And a bit of a flutter, if I’m honest. That train journey from Kendal… absolutely dreadful. They're worse than ever, these trains. Doesn’t used to be like that, you know. Gran! You made it! I thought you were going to bail. There’s this  amazing  new filter on TikTok – you have to try it. It puts rabbit ears on you. Rabbit ears? Good heavens, no. I haven't the slightest interest in these… Tick-tocks. What even  is  a Tick-tock? Is that some sort of clockwork thing? It's an app, love. A social media thing. Honestly, David, put the phone down for five minutes, your grandmother’s just arrived! Agnes, he’s obsessed. It’s a constant battle. Says it’s how he stays connected. It  is  how I stay connected, Auntie Sarah! Everyone's on it. And it’s not just silly filters; there are proper comedians on there. Did you know there’s this comedian from Leeds… Dear boy, comedians are best enjoyed in a proper theatre, with a pint of ginger beer. Not staring at a small, glowing rectangle. Though, I  did  see a rather amusing sketch on the television the other day... about a man trying to assemble flat-pack furniture. Dreadful, truly, but brilliant in its misery. You and flat-pack furniture, Agnes. Don’t get me started. Remember that bookcase you bought for me? Took us three days and a whole tube of plasters. It was a terrible design, that bookcase. Practically engineered to induce despair. I felt… rather cross with it, I must admit. Things like that can get to you, you know. All the relentless consumerism. What do you mean, Gran? She means… sometimes things can feel a bit overwhelming, love. Life can get a bit much. She's been thinking a lot about clearing out the attic lately. Yes, the attic. It's a right state. Generations of… well, accumulated things. I’m thinking of having a big clear-out. Getting rid of it all. It’s quite liberating, actually. Letting go of the past. Though, finding the energy is… another matter entirely. We can help with that, Agnes. David and I can pop over next weekend.

Right then, looks pretty swanky, doesn't it? Loads thinner than your old one, Liam. Did you get the one with the – whatchamacallit – the fingerprint scanner? Yeah, the fingerprint thing’s good. Bit of a faff at first, trying to get it to read, but once it’s locked on, it's dead easy. And the screen’s brilliant, honestly. The colours are just popping. It really is a nice bit of kit. Good choice, Liam. So, how’s the speed? You mentioned it was struggling a bit with some of those rendering programs you use for your artwork? That's what I was hoping would be sorted. It was a bit sluggish with Photoshop last night. I ran a diagnostics thing, and it said the RAM was being maxed, which is a bit odd 'cause I bumped it up to 16GB, remember? You helped me with that, didn’t you, Jake? Absolutely. Tidied up your cable management too while we were at it, didn’t we? Let me have a quick look. Okay, it’s definitely reading the 16GB. Weird. Is it getting hot, though? Hot? Like, radiator-hot? Because if it is, you’re gonna need to get those fans sorted. Luton’s been scorching these past few days. Nah, not that hot. Just…warm. Like, a normal laptop warm, not a ‘melt your face off’ warm. It's just, when I'm doing stuff with layers in Photoshop, it freezes for a second, then catches up. Drives you mad. Could be a driver issue? Have you updated the graphics drivers? Those things can be seriously buggy sometimes. I had a nightmare with my old graphics card a few years back – spent a week troubleshooting. Ended up having to uninstall and reinstall the whole thing. You and your tech wizardry, Jake. Some of us just like to dig holes and watch things grow. Much simpler. Anyone fancy a cucumber sandwich? I've got some decent ones I picked up from the market. Cucumber sandwich sounds lush, honestly. Distraction tactics are appreciated. Just need to figure out this laptop thing before I can really get back to work. This commission's got a deadline, you know. Right, okay. Let's try a different approach. Right, see what's munching on your resources while you're running Photoshop. Could be some background processes hogging the CPU. Have you got a load of Chrome tabs open, Liam?

Honestly, this place is a revelation, isn’t it? Tarnow needed a decent bistro, desperately. Everything else has been pierogi and kielbasa until now. This latte is actually… good. Proper good. It is rather pleasant, yes. A nice change. Though, I confess, the pierogi are a comfort. Familiar. Are you enjoying your time here, Elara? Teaching is going well? It's brilliant, actually! The kids are fantastic, really eager to learn. I’m teaching a group of university students mostly, improving their conversational English. And the whole experience… living in Poland, meeting people, experiencing a different culture… it's exactly what I needed after uni. A bit of a kick up the backside, really. What about you, Penelope? How’s the occasional TEFL work going? Sporadic. Very sporadic. A few online lessons here and there, mostly with students in Asia. It’s… a distraction. A way to fill the hours, I suppose. I miss the classroom, though. The energy. The sense of purpose. It’s hard to replicate in a virtual world. I can imagine. It must be tough. Listen, I was thinking… we should try that little shop down the street tomorrow. The one with the handmade soaps and those funny, knitted animal hats. Remember I said I wanted to get my mum something? Yes, I remember. Animal hats. She'll adore that, the eccentric old dear. I suppose I could manage a little browse. Though I’m not feeling particularly energetic today. My knees are protesting again. Don't talk yourself out of it! A bit of fresh air will do you good. We could even walk along the river afterwards. I was thinking of joining a gym when I get back to Bury, actually. Getting fit, you know? It’s all part of the… well, part of feeling like I’m in control of things. Control. That’s a slippery thing, isn’t it? I used to… I used to feel very much in control. Everything in its place. Now… Penelope, are you alright? You seem a bit… distant. Is everything okay with you? Honestly, you can tell me anything. It’s just… I've been thinking a lot, lately. About who I am, really. Without a job, without a… a defined role. It's unsettling. I feel like I'm adrift. All my identity was wrapped up in my career. English Literature, you know? All those clever analyses and insightful discussions… And now… It’s a big shift,

Right, so Dorset Steam Fair this weekend, eh? It  is  a bit of a trek, isn’t it? Are you sure, Dad, you're up for it? Trek? Bournemouth's not exactly the Arctic, love. And I haven't missed it in fifteen years. Besides, your mum's been badgering me non-stop. Need to get the tickets sorted though. Did you manage to book online? I did, actually. Got us three standard tickets. I thought we could grab a picnic lunch there, save some money. It’s always a bit pricey on-site. Brilliant, thanks, Mum. You’re a lifesaver. Dad, remember last year when you nearly tripped over that wonky paving stone and spilled your tea  everywhere ? That was a rogue paving stone! And besides, the tea was lukewarm anyway. Are they still doing that decent hog roast? That's the main reason I go. Apparently so. But, and this is important, I checked their website regarding accessibility. They do have designated parking closer to the entrance, and there are ramps on most paths, but some of the ground can still be a bit uneven, especially around the field. Good point, Mum. We should probably bring Dad’s walking stick just in case. He doesn't always like using it, but it might be a good idea. Don't you start nagging me, Elsie! I'm perfectly capable of walking without a stick. Though… these knees aren't what they used to be. It's not nagging, George, it’s being sensible. Speaking of sensible - did you see those property prices in Poole? Absolutely ridiculous! I was looking at a little flat near the harbour, just out of curiosity, and it’s nearly half a million! I know! It's insane. I was online yesterday, browsing estate agents, and everything is just… sky-high. I might have to seriously reconsider moving anywhere after I graduate. Bournemouth itself isn’t much cheaper, is it? Bournemouth’s always been pricey. It’s a nice place, though. Pleasant enough. Remember when I was thinking about buying a little bungalow out in Southbourne? Never happened, of course. Couldn’t have afforded it then, and certainly can't now. It's a shame. Still, at least we’ve got this lovely place. Oh, speaking of lovely, Jasper is being particularly clingy today. He’s decided my lap is  the  place to be. That’s classic Jasper.

Honestly, this weather's typical Yorkshire, isn’t it? Just when you think you've had enough grey, it delivers more. Aye, lad. It's a northen blessing, that. Keeps the tourists away. Grandma, you’re looking particularly contemplative today. Everything alright? You’ve hardly touched your scone. Just thinking, dear. Thinking about the move. Kendal's been my home for so long… it feels a bit… unsettling, doesn’t it? Leaving behind familiar faces, the way the light falls on the fells in the morning... It’ll be an adventure, Grandma! Thirsk’s got loads of cool shops. I saw this one online, a proper artisan candle maker. Apparently, they do amazing scents. He’s right, lad. Thirsk market’s brilliant. We'll have to take you. And the Hambleton Playhouse is just a short drive away. They're putting on a production of "A Midsummer Night's Dream" next month. Fancy seeing it? Shakespeare, you say? I used to take my children...though I do dislike the modern interpretations sometimes. They take liberties, don't they? Miss the grandeur completely. All those flashing lights and thumping music... Aye, that’s my pet peeve too. Give me the Globe Theatre any day. Though, I did see a rather inventive production with puppets once...it was surprisingly moving. Speaking of moving, is everything boxed up, love? Dad’s been on about it relentlessly. Nearly. Just a few odds and ends still to sort through. I was thinking of donating some of Grandma's old books to the church. They could use them for their little lending library. Oh, that would be lovely, dear. Though… ...those first editions of Tennyson…are you sure? They were my father's. Tennyson? Is that one of those old-timey poets? My school do loads on poetry. I hate it. It’s all so…serious. Honestly, lad! Tennyson’s fantastic. Full of imagery and emotion. You'll appreciate it when you're older. Maybe. What are you looking at on that phone, anyway? Just…Twitter. There’s a petition going around about the school's decision to ban phones during lessons. It’s ridiculous! Everyone has one! Twitter. Honestly. A breeding ground for opinions and outrage. You’re better off reading a decent book. Though I do use it for my writing sometimes, linking to articles and that. Gets the word out. I've heard tales of it, dear, this "Twitter".

Right, so, Anya, darling, are you feeling alright? You seemed a bit quiet during dinner. And Leo, you’ve been fiddling with that Lego for ages – are you thinking about building a Monet landscape? Monet! He painted water lilies! I saw them in a book. Can we go to a museum and see them, Mummy? Can we go  now ? Please? Not  now , sweetie. Museums are a bit of a day out. Maybe during the Easter holidays. We'll have to look at the dates. Speaking of which…Have you two remembered about your cousin Chloe's birthday next week? Chloe's a year older! Yay! Does that mean she gets more Easter chocolate?! Possibly. But you both get plenty of chocolate too, don’t worry. And remember, Chloe and Tommy share a birthday, don't they? It's always a bit mad trying to remember everyone's birthdays. Tommy’s older! By one whole year! Yes, you’re right. It’s quite a coincidence, isn’t it? Two siblings born on the same day. Remember when I was telling Mrs. Davies about it at school? She said it was quite rare. She even mentioned that she had to get her hearing tested recently. Apparently, it runs in families. Will  we  have to get our ears tested? Does it hurt? No, darling, it doesn’t hurt at all! It’s just a little check-up. To make sure everything's working properly. Like a dentist, but for your ears. We might get you both booked in for one after Easter, just to be safe. Better safe than sorry, eh? What about Ashaad? Does Ashaad have a birthday coming up? He said he's going on a school trip. He does! Actually, it's just after Chloe and Tommy. I think it’s in May. He's going to the science museum, isn't he? He's been absolutely obsessed with rockets lately. It's wonderful to see them so engaged, actually. It makes all the Maths homework a little more manageable, knowing they’re applying it to something they love. Maths is hard! Radishes are easier. I like radishes. Radishes are good, aren't they? Snappy and crunchy. You know, my Dad used to grow radishes in his garden when I was little. He’d always have us tasting them straight from the earth. They tasted so much better then. And this reminds me, we need to remember to get some for dinner tomorrow.

Oh my god, this place is  exactly  as I remember it! Still perpetually chaotic, isn't it? Mum hasn't changed a thing. Nope. Chaos is a family birthright, apparently. Welcome back, Rach! It’s so good to see you. Didn't expect you to arrive with a suitcase the size of a small car. What's all that? Just… well, London life. You accumulate stuff. And I really needed to purge. Plus, I thought I'd bring a few treats from Borough Market - proper fudge, not that supermarket rubbish. You still haven't moved on from that, have you? Rude! I appreciate a bargain. Fudge is fudge. Especially when you’re dealing with shift work. Speaking of which, how was the journey? Did the trains behave themselves, or did you experience the usual Southern Rail horrors? You know. Delays, cancellations, a brief existential crisis wondering if I'd be stuck in Lewisham forever. Nothing new, really. But it’s good to be home. It’s… relaxing. I miss this. Even the chaos. Good. Because I've been in full-on Mum mode all week. Dad booked that new ‘experience’ for her – a pottery class. You know how she gets when she tries new things. It’s… an event. And Jasper’s been chewing the sofa legs again. Jasper! Still a fluffy menace, then? I remember when he was a tiny terror, trying to eat my shoelaces. How’s Mum handling the pottery? I’m picturing a lot of lopsided, wonky mugs. Precisely. She insists they're "rustic and individual." The problem is, they’re also unusable. She gave Dad one that looks like a melted snail. He’s put it on display. Bless him. But honestly, after a day with stroke patients, dealing with her pottery is a welcome distraction. Sounds… intense. How’s work, genuinely? I’ve been meaning to ask. Adult acute, that must be… emotionally draining. It is. It's incredibly rewarding too, though. You see people regain their independence, rebuild their lives... It’s just…heavy sometimes. This week's been particularly challenging, a few difficult cases. That's why I'm so relieved you're here. It’s nice not to be 'on' for a bit. I can only imagine. Copywriting can be soul-crushing in its own way, but it’s a slightly different flavour of despair. Have you thought any more about that masters course in neurological rehabilitation?

You know, thinking back… being a young dentist, joining the NHS… it really was quite a different landscape. The perks weren't about money, of course, but the opportunities… Extraordinary. They offered us sailing lessons! Can you imagine? An oral surgeon, bobbing about in a dinghy. That's delightful! Sailing? I can just picture you, Stanley. You’d have been a sight. Did you actually get very good? Oh, no, not particularly. More the unfortunate spectacle, I suspect. We had lectures all at sea, actually. Lectures on… well, dentistry, naturally. They’d bring in the professor and we’d be trying to concentrate with the waves rocking the boat. Ridiculous, but wonderful. And the trips they offered… incredible value. Remember when you could go to Prague for next to nothing? Prague! I went a few years ago. Magnificent city. The architecture… utterly breathtaking. Did you go to the Charles Bridge? Of course! Several times. And the astronomical clock. You could spend a week just wandering around. It's unbelievable what you can find these days for a pittance, isn’t it? Though, trying to get into a theatre or exhibition that’s already fully booked... that’s a different story. I’ve learned to be incredibly persistent. Persistence is key, Stanley. You need to know the right people, or at least be prepared to charm them. I've found a little bit of persuasive arguing can get you quite far. Speaking of events, I’ve been busy trying to organize this jive evening. Remember I mentioned it? The jive! Yes, of course. How’s that coming along? Where are you holding it? We’ve booked the old barn just outside of town. You know, the one they’ve been converting? Apparently, they’re going to turn it into a microbrewery and a wedding venue after the jive. Quite the transformation. It's got wonderful character, though. Plenty of space to swing a partner, so to speak. A converted barn! Sounds lovely. A bit… rustic. I hope they’ve sorted out the heating. November evenings can be nippy. It’s good to see the area being revitalized, though, isn't it? This town… it’s seen better days. Remember how vibrant it used to be? All the independent shops and the beautiful Victorian architecture? Oh, absolutely. It was a flourishing place. Now it’s all chain stores and boarded-up windows. They're trying to "rebrand" it, you know.

Right then, sunshine permitting, let's get back to this whole moving image case study thing. I’ve been doing a bit more thinking overnight, and I'm still convinced there's a real gap in the market. Schools are desperate for engaging, affordable resources, especially ones that demonstrate practical application. I agree entirely. The spark of an idea really came from seeing the lackluster visuals Ms. Davies used for her history lessons – just endless still images of dusty portraits. The kids were visibly zoning out. But it’s the ‘affordable’ part that’s going to be tricky, isn’t it? Producing quality video, even short case studies, has overheads. Absolutely. That’s where my entrepreneurial brain kicks in. We don’t need Hollywood production values. Think accessible – mobile phone footage, clever editing, maybe even incorporating existing public domain footage where appropriate. We focus on the  story  – showing real-world examples of how these concepts are used, rather than just lecturing. I like the emphasis on the story. And I think tapping into current social media trends could be brilliant. Short, digestible content designed to be shared – TikTok snippets, Instagram Reels versions… we could even build a little community around it, with teachers sharing their own adaptations. Exactly! We’re not just selling case studies; we’re selling a  system . A library of adaptable resources, a platform for sharing, and maybe even workshops to show teachers how to best integrate them. What about the actual case studies themselves? We started throwing around ideas yesterday – sustainability in farming, architectural design, even leveraging local storytelling for language arts... I think focusing on subjects that have a lot of visual potential to start would be smart. Architecture is a good one - showing the thought process behind a design, maybe interviewing the architect… or perhaps a series on local indigenous art practices? That could be really powerful, especially given we’re house-sitting in Australia. Indigenous Australian art, definitely. Done respectfully, of course. We’d need to consult and collaborate with local communities – absolutely crucial. That's a mindset shift from my previous ventures, frankly, focusing on ethical sourcing and genuine partnerships. It’s…well, it feels more  meaningful . It  is  meaningful. It aligns with so much of what I try to teach my students – critical thinking, cross-cultural understanding, appreciating different perspectives. We’d need to be very clear about our educational objectives for each case study too.

Honestly, I still can’t quite believe how calm the sea is today. It’s practically…glassy. I was expecting a proper bluster after that rain yesterday. It is lovely, isn't it? A bit deceptive, though. I reckon there’s still a bit of a swell just out of sight. Remember last summer? We thought it was calm like this, and then suddenly, metres of waves crashing over the promenade. Don’t remind me! Little Timmy practically swallowed half the Atlantic. Poor thing. It’s funny, isn't it? How quickly things can change. Speaking of people near the water, have you heard from Sarah and Mark lately? Sarah messaged me last week, actually. They’re down in Cornwall. Sailing lessons, apparently. Sailing lessons? Seriously? Mark? He gets seasick just looking at a paddling pool! I know! That's what she said. Apparently, he’s determined to conquer his fears. She said he’s been reading countless books on navigation and knots. He’s become quite the enthusiast. A very determined enthusiast, albeit a slightly green one, she admitted. Good for him, I suppose. Honestly, though, it sounds like Sarah's really driving it. She's always been the adventurer of the pair, hasn’t she? Remember when she backpacked through South America? Mark was practically in tears the entire time, terrified of spiders and dodgy tap water. Oh, absolutely. She's got that relentless optimism. And Mark, bless him, just goes along for the ride, even if he's silently panicking the whole way. It’s a brilliant dynamic, really. They balance each other perfectly. They do. Sometimes I envy them, you know? That kind of…unwavering commitment to try new things. I feel like I get stuck in a rut sometimes. Teaching, grading, endless paperwork... Don't be silly. You're incredibly adventurous. You just express it differently. Your research last year, trekking through Tibetan monasteries to record those chants? That's pretty adventurous. That was different. That was…work. It felt like a responsibility, more than a personal adventure. I was documenting, observing, analyzing. It didn't feel like I was truly  doing  anything. But you  were  doing something incredible! Bringing those ancient practices to light for so many people. You’re sharing something precious. Besides, you learned to cook yak butter tea, didn’t you? That has to qualify as an adventure! Alright, alright, you’ve got a point.

Honestly, this styling is  atrocious . Like, who greenlit this look for her? It’s just… beige. And shapeless. Aye, it isn't exactly setting the world alight, is it? Mind, I don’t reckon she's got much to work with, bless ‘er. That fabric looks like it’d swallow you whole. I actually don’t hate it entirely. It's minimalist, I suppose. But I agree, it needs  something . A bold necklace, maybe? Or a pop of colour in the shoes. She looks like a librarian who’s lost her glasses. A librarian who's accidentally wandered onto a red carpet! It's the proportions. Everything is just… off. See how the sleeves are too long, and the skirt doesn't cinch at the waist at all? Creates this horrifying, floaty silhouette. You're right, petal. Proportion's reet important. My nan used to say, “If it ain’t got a proper waist, it ain’t got no sense.” She’d have had words with the designer, she would. I’ve been trying to get a bit more shape myself, you know? Buying stuff that fits properly, rather than squeezing into things I used to wear. Good for you! It makes such a difference. I was stuck in a skinny jeans and oversized jumper phase for  months . I think my flatmate was starting to worry. I've recently found a tailor, actually. Little independent place near my work. It’s amazing what a few tweaks can do. A tailor? That’s a brilliant idea! I’ve been meaning to do that for ages. I always feel like things are just… almost right, but not quite. I’d love a bespoke blazer. Something tailored to actually  fit  my shoulders. Smart. That sounds reet classy. Though, I'm on a bit of a budget, to be honest. Conference budgets are tight enough as it is! I've been browsing Depop and Vinted. Found a couple of cracker jackets. Got a floral bomber jacket the other day, proper retro. Depop and Vinted are goldmines! I’ve scored some incredible designer pieces for a fraction of the price. You just have to be patient and hunt. Anything you’re specifically looking for at the moment? I’ve been on the lookout for a decent trench coat. Proper London weather requires a decent trench. Ooh, a trench! Yes! I've been thinking about that too.

Honestly, Mum, Mr. Davies just doesn’t  get  it. He marked down my photo of the pier for being "too moody." Moody! It was capturing the atmosphere, the… the loneliness of a grey day in Hastings! Oh, bless him. Mr. Davies always was a bit… predictable, wasn't he? What was the lighting like? Did you try a different filter? I did. I did loads! I tried a warmer tone, I tried black and white, I even played with the contrast. Nothing felt right. It needed that grey, that almost cold feeling to really convey it. He just said it didn’t “celebrate the beauty of Hastings.” As if everything has to be sunshine and seagulls! He’s missing the point then. Photography isn't always about pretty pictures, is it? It's about telling a story. Like that exhibition we saw last year at the De La Warr. Remember the stark black and white portraits? Those weren't smiling, happy people, but they were powerful. Yeah! Exactly! I was trying to do something like that. I was thinking about that comedian, Stewart Lee. He’s so good at finding the humour in bleakness, you know? Like, making you laugh at the sadness. Stewart Lee, yes! He’s brilliant, isn't he? A bit… niche, perhaps, but brilliant. It takes a special kind of talent to turn melancholy into comedy. What are you reading at the moment? Anything good? I know you’re always buried in a book. I’m reading "Mexican Gothic" by Silvia Moreno-Garcia. It's properly spooky! And the atmosphere is incredible. It's got this crumbling mansion and this unsettling family… it’s really tapping into that feeling of isolation I was trying for with the photo. Oh, I’ve heard good things about that! You know, my job at the reception desk can sometimes feel like living in a slightly unsettling novel. Endless parade of people, all with their own little secrets… plus, Mrs. Hawthorne keeps leaving me cryptic notes about the filing system. Mrs. Hawthorne sounds terrifying. Is she still convinced the answering machine is listening to her? Absolutely! She whispers into it when she thinks no one's around. It's quite entertaining, actually. Though it does make me wonder what I'm going to do when they finally update the system. I’m dreading learning all that new software. You'll be fine.

Blimey, that's a bit of a sit, that is. Lovely cuppa, mind you. Proper brew. Thanks, love. You're very welcome, Arthur. You look a bit knackered, dear. Didn't sleep well, did you? I’ve noticed you rubbing your eyes a lot lately. Not a wink, Betty. Not a blessed wink. Keeps hearing things, I do. Can’t rightly say what it is, though. Could be the neighbours, could be… well, could be anything, really. They’ve got that dreadful cockerel, you know. Absolutely raucous thing! Wakes me up at sparrow’s fart, it does. Morning, both! Arthur, you sound like my dad when he complains about the foxes in the garden. Betty, lovely to see you. Brought a bit of a housewarming gift, actually – some filament for your 3D printer. Thought you might like it. Oh, David, you shouldn't have! That's ever so kind. What colour is it? Let me see... Ooh, metallic silver! Perfect for the little birdhouses I’ve been designing. Birdhouses, are we? Speaking of birds, I've got a nest in the ivy on the side of the house. Little robins, they are. Just hatched, I reckon. Saw the parents flitting about earlier. Lovely little things. Got a proper soft heart for the wildlife, I do. They are. I used to have a bird table when I was a kid. Remember watching the blue tits fight over the sunflower seeds? Right little scoundrels. You mention houses, Arthur - how's that application form progressing? You were going on about needing a hand with it last week. That blooming thing! It’s a nightmare, David, it really is. All these questions… “Household income”, “assets”, “future intentions”… Seems like they’re trying to pry into me soul! I can barely fill out me shopping list, let alone a form like that. Don’t you fret, Arthur. We’ll do it together. I’ve got a bit more of a head for paperwork, as you know. David, you’re good with computers, aren't you? Perhaps you could give his laptop a quick look-over to make sure everything's working alright? Absolutely. I can certainly take a gander at it. It's usually simple stuff, just clearing out unnecessary files. You wouldn’t believe the amount of junk builds up over time. It’s like the problem children I used to teach – needing constant decluttering!

...and honestly, Moira, I still can’t quite believe it’s happening. After all these years, Elara is actually moving here. To Brighton. It feels…surreal. Well, it’s wonderful news, isn't it, Margaret? You’ve been talking about it for years, ever since she went off to Australia. A bit sudden, coming after all this time, but wonderfully wonderful nonetheless. Are you nervous? Nervous is putting it mildly! I’m a whirlwind of emotions, really. Excited, of course. Overjoyed to have her near. But also…terribly anxious. It’s been so long. She's a grown woman now, with her own life, her own experiences. Will we even…connect properly? Will she like living here? Brighton’s changed so much since I last visited. Brighton always changes. That’s part of its charm, isn’t it? And Elara’s not a stranger. She’s your daughter. You've built a bond that distance hasn't completely eroded. And she’s coming to  you , Margaret. That says a lot about how much she values your presence. Think about the stories she’ll bring! And you’ll finally get to see her settle down, build a life… That's what I desperately want, isn’t it? To see her happy. But the thought of the responsibility… I feel so…unprepared. I haven't tackled having a young adult in the house for decades. Everything's geared towards a quiet, solitary life now. Responsibility? Margaret, you’re her  mother . You don’t need a manual! Just be you. Be the warm, supportive woman she’s always known. And don’t try to force anything. Let her find her feet, her own way of doing things. She's not a child needing constant supervision, remember? I know, I know. It's just… I worry. I worry about her finding a job, about her making friends, about whether this decision was the right one for her. I’ve spent so many years worrying about hypotheticals, it's a habit. You always were a worrier, my dear sister. Remember when you used to fret over whether I packed enough sandwiches for school trips? This is a bit bigger than a soggy cheese and pickle, admittedly. But the same principle applies. Worrying achieves nothing but heightened anxiety. Focus on the positives. Focus on welcoming her, on creating a comfortable space for her. You’re right, of course.

This is lovely, David. Really cozy. Much better than staring at a screen grading essays, that’s for sure. Thanks for having me over. My pleasure, James. Glad you could make it. It's a bit of a whirlwind lately, isn't it? Everything feels like it's moving a mile a minute. Did you catch any of the debates around the Scottish referendum? A bit, yeah. It's... complicated. Honestly. I can see both sides, but the potential implications for the whole UK are pretty significant, aren’t they? Difficult to see a clear outcome, that's for sure. What’s your take? I'm leaning towards staying together, to be frank. Too much history, too much intertwined. Though I understand the desire for autonomy, you know? It’s a difficult thing to balance. Reminds me a bit of the arguments we used to have back at school debating club – always passionate, rarely conclusive. I can imagine! Going back to school days… speaking of which, how did that interview go for Mark? You were pushing him pretty hard for that Head of Department role at Crestwood. Well, that’s where things get a bit tricky. He didn’t get it. Apparently, the new Head wants someone with more… ‘cutting-edge experience’ in online learning. Which ironically, Mark spearheaded a lot of that at our school! The irony isn't lost on me. That’s rotten luck. Mark’s brilliant, really. I always thought he’d be perfect for something like that. A bit disheartening to see talent overlooked like that. Did he seem alright about it? He’s taking it gracefully, putting on a brave face. But you could see the disappointment. He’s been a bit quieter than usual, actually. I’m trying to be a good friend and remind him of all his accomplishments. Trying to bolster him a bit. You're doing the right thing. Sometimes a bit of perspective is all someone needs. My daughter, Sophie, had a similar setback with her university application last year. Devastating at the time, but she ended up at a smaller college that’s actually a much better fit for her. It's funny how life throws curveballs, isn't it? They’re often blessings in disguise. Speaking of daughters, yours is studying archaeology, right? Still fascinated by ancient pottery shards? Absolutely! Just got back from a dig in Greece, apparently.

Right, so this is the base, yeah? Like a really wonky castle. It looks more like something a badger built. Are you sure this is going to catch a mouse, let alone entertain anyone? It's a mousetrap game! It's supposed to be ridiculous! I’m using the actual mousetraps, just with cardboard and string to make it look like something out of a cartoon. It’s got hazards and stuff. Well, it’s certainly… ambitious, darling. Reminds me a bit of that disastrous attempt at a Christmas tree we had when you were little, Edward. Remember those tinsel spiders all over the ceiling? Oh, don't remind me! I spent a week getting rid of those. Though I must say, Edward, your enthusiasm is commendable. Mousetrap themed fun? That’s a bit different. You know, it’s funny you're building a mousetrap game. We had a housekeeper in Maryland, Agnes, who was convinced her house was overrun. She set out these absurdly sophisticated traps, with little bait dishes and everything. Looked like miniature restaurants for mice. Seriously? Like, proper high-end mouse dining? Exactly. She swore they were stealing her gingersnaps. It was a whole saga. You might want to level up your bait presentation, then. Forget the cheese, think petit fours. Right. Mouse Michelin stars. I like it. It’s a charming thought, all this talk of America. My time in Boston was so vibrant. The children were… well, they were something else. So loud, so boisterous! Everything was bigger, brighter, louder. It was quite overwhelming at first. I remember you saying that. You were so used to the quiet politeness of Stratford. Exactly!
