And their school systems… so different. Very focused on sports, it seemed. My friend's daughter, Bethany, was obsessed with cheerleading. Bless her heart, she'd spend hours perfecting routines. Cheerleading seems intense! Do they take it really seriously over there? Very seriously. It’s a huge deal for many kids. And the competitive element is fierce. It’s almost like a minor professional sport. I was reading a fascinating article the other day about the business side of it. Is it like, billionaires funding cheerleading squads? Don't exaggerate, Edward. But there  is  a lot of investment involved. My cousin, Sarah, worked as a coach for a while. She said the pressure from the parents was… substantial. They certainly expect a lot.

Honestly, darling, you will  not  believe what I managed to find today! Let me guess...another silk scarf? You've got enough to wrap a small village, you know. Don't be silly! Although, I did see a rather lovely cashmere one... no, this is different. It's a dress. A dress? What kind of dress? Something for the conference next month? No, not really. It’s… well, it’s quite bold, actually. I never thought I’d go for something like it, to be honest, but it was just  perfect . The colours, the cut… everything. Bold, you say? My interest is officially piqued. Details, please! China can inspire some intriguing fashion choices. Did you find it in that little boutique near the park? They have some good stuff. Actually, I went to that new department store, the 'Golden Phoenix'. Remember I mentioned wanting to check it out? It’s huge! And this dress… it’s emerald green – a really rich, deep emerald – and it has this incredible, slightly flared skirt. And sleeves! Proper, dramatic, bishop sleeves. Emerald green and bishop sleeves? Gosh, that  is  bold. Are you sure it suits you? You usually favour more subdued palettes. Exactly! And that’s why I wouldn’t normally have even considered it. But the sales assistant, bless her, she said it would bring out my eyes. And… she was right. I tried it on, looked in the mirror, and I just felt...confident. Confident is a good look. It’s not about the clothes themselves, is it? It’s about how they make you feel. But emerald green... it's a commitment! Are you planning on turning into a Bond villain? Not quite! Though, maybe I should start practicing my evil laugh. No, I thought I might wear it to that gallery opening next week. It’s the one for the modern Chinese artists, right? Yes, the Zhao exhibition. That’s a good choice. It's quite a glamorous affair. Will you need occasion shoes? That might change the whole aesthetic. Already thought of that! I found a pair of silver heels to go with it. They're not too flashy, but they pull the whole look together. It was a complete lucky dip, really. I wasn't even looking for shoes, but they were on sale and just… clicked. "Clicked," eh? You’re on a roll today. So, the dress, the shoes… are you going to tell me about any accompanying accessories?

Well, that was… something, wasn’t it? A proper ding-dong battle. I nearly lost my voice shouting at the telly! Yeah! It was brilliant, Dad! That try in the second half, from Murphy, was amazing! I reckon he's going to be a star. Did you see his sidestep? It  was  exciting. I wasn’t quite as invested as you two. I mostly just enjoyed watching you two get so worked up about it. It’s a bit… loud sometimes! Hmph. Rugby, you say? In my day, we played proper games. Real team sports. Rugby’s all just a scrum of pushing and shoving now, isn't it? Though I did appreciate the strategy. A good hooker is worth his weight in gold. Now, now, Nan, don't go turning your nose up at it. It takes skill and fitness, you know. Oisin, are you finished with your nuggets? So you can help me with the cards? Nearly, Dad. Can we look at the stars later? Mr. Davies said in science we could see Jupiter if the clouds clear. Proper visible, he said. Oisin, sweetheart, finish up and then straight to bed, okay? You've had a long day. We’ll have a look at the stars tomorrow night, love. It's a bit late tonight. Jupiter, you say? Used to teach my class about the planets. Little darlings, all so fascinated. Do you know how many moons Jupiter has these days? Keeps adding them, they do! Nan, you're brilliant. Always something new. Oisin, seriously, eat your dinner. We need to get those birthday cards signed. Auntie Maureen's wants them for Friday. Okay, okay. But promise we'll look tomorrow? I even learned a constellation – Ursa Major, the Big Dipper! We promise, love. Right now, though, action stations! We need to get you brushed and into your pyjamas. You're getting a bit fidgety. Right, birthday carnage commences. Maureen’s always expecting a whole poem and a drawing, doesn't she? They're all pretty standard, luckily. Nan, you take this one for Geoff. He always loved your stories about teaching. Geoff was a good lad. Always asking questions. "Mrs. MacIntyre, why is the sky blue?" "Mrs. MacIntyre, how do caterpillars turn into butterflies?" Never stopped. He sounds lovely. I miss Geoff, you know? It’s been a long time since we spoke. I should give his daughter a ring.

Honestly, it’s absolutely mad, isn't it? Aunt Carol is already suggesting names for the baby. Like, we haven’t even told anyone we’re  definitely  trying! Carol’s always been ahead of the curve when it comes to family milestones. Remember when she started knitting tiny hats for Noah before my sister even confirmed she was having a boy? Exactly! Though tiny hats are rather adorable, aren’t they? I did feel a bit sorry for Mum though. She kept saying, "Honestly, let them enjoy being pregnant first!" Mum’s right. You’d think people would let you savour those moments. Are you feeling okay, by the way? You seem a bit… tired? It's just the house hunt, really. It’s exhausting. I mean, Cambridge property is notoriously bonkers. We’ve put in three offers already, and been rejected each time. It's like everyone's got a hidden savings pot just for bidding wars! We're thinking of looking further out, but the commute would become a nightmare. Oh, I can imagine. Lincoln’s similar, though not quite as insane. Finding somewhere with enough space for both of you, and eventually, a little one... it’s tricky. Are you still thinking about the Victorian terrace near the river? We were, but it has ironically wonky floors! Apparently, that's a common issue with that era of build. Honestly, the surveyor practically laughed when he pointed it out. It’s the light though, that's what drew us in. It feels so warm. Right. Location, light, and potentially wonky foundations! Sounds about right for Cambridge living. Listen, if you're struggling to find things, do remember I've started clearing out my wardrobe. Loads of stuff I just don’t wear anymore. Baby-related things too - I've got a huge box of nearly-new baby clothes. You're welcome to anything! Seriously? That's so lovely of you! I’d take you up on that. I'm already dreading the thought of buying  everything . It’s such a waste, really. And it’s not like we're exactly rolling in it, are we? Definitely not! The cost of everything is ridiculous. Actually, on the topic of wasted money... have you made any progress with your Catalan? You were so keen to start lessons. Don't even remind me! Life got completely in the way. The house hunt, the baby planning… it’s been a whirlwind.

Right, so, Alex was going on about this 'received pronunciation' thing again, wasn't he? Proper lecturing us all on vowels. As if anyone cares. He does go on a bit, doesn't he? It’s almost… academic. I mean, I’m all for good grammar and stuff, but coming down on people for having a bit of Eastern accent? Bit harsh, innit? I mean, I’m probably full of it, really. Loads of southernisms are creeping in, thanks to uni in London. He's trying to sound learned, that's all. Thinks knowing the IPA chart makes him superior. Honestly, the irony of a guy teaching English being so pedantic about it…it's magnificent. Though, you're right, Liam. It’s a bit much. He was just saying my Bedford accent was 'convoluted'. Convoluted! Like I'm speaking in ancient Sumerian. Convoluted! I love that. Want a biscuit? Mum made shortbread. Yeah, please. Shortbread’s always good. So, Alex, convoluted. That reminds me... remember that time he tried to explain mixed martial arts? He was using these massive, complicated terms. Like, “leveraged rotational displacement resulting in kinetic energy redirection.” I nearly choked on my pint. Oh god, yes! Trying to sound like a sports analyst instead of explaining a simple takedown. I think I told him he sounded like he was describing rocket science. He needs to relax. Martial arts is supposed to be freeing, not… mathematically precise. I've been doing a bit of kickboxing myself, you know. Keeps you sharp. No way! Really? You? You, the guy who spends his days wrestling weeds? It’s good exercise. And you learn a bit about protecting yourself, which is always useful, especially if you're bringing back rare orchids from the Continent. Orchids? That’s a sudden turn of conversation. You're expanding your horticultural horizons, I see. Anything specific you're after? My student, Elena, is Cypriot; her grandfather’s got this incredible nursery. Might be worth a chat. Seriously? That'd be brilliant! I’m trying to get some  Paphiopedilum rothschildianum  – Rothschild’s slipper orchid. Bit of a holy grail for gardeners, that one. Apparently, the flowers are  stunning . It’s just… ridiculously expensive. Rothschild’s… wow. You’re going for the big leagues, then. I’m just trying to keep my succulents alive. Speaking of expensive… anyone ever tried selling stuff online? I'm thinking about clearing out some old computer bits.

Honestly, I don't know why I bother making shepherd’s pie. It’s a logistical nightmare getting everything timed right, and then there's the mashed potato mountain to deal with. Sounds dramatic! It's comfort food, Elara, and you make a really good one, even if it is a  bit  involved. Besides, you’ve been having a rough week with the office renovations. You deserve a proper, home-cooked meal. Rough is an understatement. They’ve basically turned the whole floor into a construction zone. I've been dodging builders and dust all week. And the commute… don’t even get me started. Yeah, I saw that picture you posted. Looks like a scene from a demolition derby. Did you end up having to take the bus a couple of times? Twice. And the bus was jam-packed, smelling faintly of damp dog and disappointment. It made me seriously reconsider my whole life choices, you know? Like, why am I saving for a car when I could just… move to the countryside and raise alpacas? Alpacas? That's a serious change of pace. You’d need land, though. And you’d still need to get around. Still, a car would definitely be easier. What about that little Mini we looked at last month? The one with the surprisingly good mileage? I keep going back and forth on that. It’s adorable, definitely, but is it practical? I mean, think of grocery runs. Think of the camping trips we were planning. A Mini is not exactly built for hauling tents and sleeping bags. True, but we could get a roof rack. And honestly, the price point is appealing. We're putting a decent chunk of money away each month. We’re almost halfway to the down payment on something bigger, but the Mini would get us mobile  now . Less relying on public transport, less stress. You're right. The stress is the killer. The constant planning around bus schedules… it’s exhausting. And I miss having my own music instead of listening to whatever dreadful announcements are being blasted over the speakers. Exactly. It's about freedom, really. You feel trapped without a car. Remember when my mum's car broke down and she was stranded at the supermarket? It was a total fiasco. Oh God, yes! She called me in a panic, convinced she was going to be living in the car park forever.

Right then, let’s just sort this out. Grandparents are due any minute, aren't they? Arthur’s promised to get the fire going, bless him. He means well, but sometimes… well, you know. Aye, they should be here soon. Mum said they rang, said they're just leaving the bus stop. Did you move the Lego out of the way like I said? I did, love, but I’m not sure it’s all gone. There’s still a suspicious-looking red brick lurking under the armchair. Honestly, that boy has a talent for hiding the things. Is that all your homework done, by the way? Don't want you slacking off just 'cause Gran and Grandpa are visiting. Hello dears! Come in, come in! Don’t just stand there like a pair of scarecrows! That's right, pet. Don't be shy! A bit chilly out there, though. Needs a good bit of sun, this weather. Gran! Grandpa! Wonderful to see you. Arthur, put your game down and give your grandad a proper hello! And give your grandma a hug, for goodness’ sake. Hi, Gran! Hi, Grandpa! How were the buses? Awful! Packed tighter than sardines, love. Arthur used to complain about the buses when he were a lad, didn't he? Remember, Arthur, complaining about the number 10? Every single day! Said it always smelled of fish and chips. Silly boy. Come on in, sit yourselves down. Arthur's just got the fire lit, so it should be nice and warm in here. I’ve made a pot of tea, and I’ve got some biscuits. Chocolate digestives, your favourites, Gran. Oh, lovely! That’s just what I needed. My knees are playing up something awful today. I swear, this damp weather... Want me to get you a cushion, Gran? That would be grand, love. Thank you. You've grown into a fine young man, you have. Aye, he’s a credit to you, lass. Not like that cousin of ours, always mucking about. Remember young Derek? Now, now, Grandpa. Let's not start comparing Derek to Arthur. He’s doing alright, isn’t he? Sixth form, hard work… I’m trying, Grandpa. Maths is a killer though, honestly. Well, that’s why you’ve got me, love! I’m a GCSE Maths Examiner, remember? I can help you with anything. Though I have to admit, some of this new stuff is a bit beyond me too!

Right, pirates! Leo, did you know that real pirates used to bury treasure? Not just in stories, apparently. Real treasure? Like gold doubloons and jewels? Did they have parrots? Squawk! Parrot! Yes, Leo, they  sometimes  had parrots. The stories exaggerate a bit, of course. It was usually more practical things – navigation tools, spices, even gunpowder! And not everyone buried it, sometimes they just...took it. But why bury it? If they were going to take it, why not just keep it? Good question! Well, sometimes they'd be escaping ships, or hiding from authorities. Burying it was a way to keep it safe until they could come back for it. Though most of the time, they probably didn't. It’s much easier to just spend the money! Can we be pirates? I want an eye patch! We absolutely can be pirates, darling! We’re practicing being pirates right now! And yes, we can get you an eye patch. We already have one, don't we? Remember when we bought it for the dressing-up box? Yes! Can we make a pirate ship out of cardboard boxes? A really big one? We could! That’s a wonderful idea. We’ll add it to the list. Speaking of lists… Shakespeare week is next week at school, isn’t it? Are you both ready to delve into the world of iambic pentameter? Is that…hard? It  can  be a little tricky at first, but we’ll make it fun! We’re going to Stratford-upon-Avon, remember? To see a play! That should help. It’ll be like stepping back in time! Will there be swords? And costumes? Definitely costumes! And probably some swords, although hopefully action figures rather than real ones. More importantly, we'll get to see how Shakespeare's words come to life. We’re even doing a little workshop while we’re there, about his language. What else are we doing? Well, remember the email I got about that circus workshop? The one  in  a real circus tent? A real circus! With clowns and a ringmaster and… ...and trapeze artists and acrobats and everything! They’re doing a stop motion animation workshop, which I thought you both would love. You're both so creative. We could even make a little pirate film! With me as the pirate captain! And Leo can be the parrot! And I can be the mermaid who helps the pirates find the treasure!

Honestly, ANON, this Merlot is rather good. Reminds me of something I had in Bordeaux, years ago. Though, nothing compares to the sheer audacity of Reginald’s story. Being arrested attempting to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus! Good heavens. Audacity is certainly the word, Edward. Though, I always felt it was more desperation than audacity. He was trying to escape Saudi Arabia with a bottle of scotch hidden in the hull, after all. Escape? Now  that’s  a story. Tell us, Margaret, how did Reginald even end up teaching in Saudi Arabia in the first place? It wasn't exactly a hotbed of English language enthusiasts back then, was it? No, it wasn't. It was during that brief period in the late 70s when there was a huge influx of expats to work on the oil projects. They needed teachers, desperately. Reginald, bless him, saw an opportunity. He’d always been a bit of a wanderer, you see. Ramsgate wasn't exactly holding his attention. I remember him mentioning something about having to conform to… certain cultural expectations. Living without a drop of alcohol must have been a trial for Reginald. He always did enjoy a good pint. Indeed. It was a trial for  everyone , I imagine. Though, the ingenuity some people displayed! I recall hearing stories of expats smuggling alcohol in fruit crates, tins of baked beans… even inside meticulously crafted wooden ducks. Wooden ducks! You’re pulling my leg, Edward. I assure you, I’m not. It’s a true story. A friend of mine, a pharmacist, swore he saw a whole consignment of whiskey concealed inside hollowed-out model ducks. Said the customs officials were baffled. Reginald tried a more direct approach, clearly. Hence, the boat and the scotch. He told me the police were remarkably polite, actually. Just utterly bewildered. They kept asking him, "Why? Why would you do this?" And did he get away with it? I mean, did they let him go after a bit of a grilling? No. He spent a rather uncomfortable night in a Jeddah jail. Thankfully, the school intervened. They managed to smooth things over, but he was deported. Quite a humiliating end to his Saudi adventure. Poor chap. Though, I've always admired his spirit. Not many people would attempt such a thing. I remember teaching in Athens, the access to decent wine was simply wonderful, a world away from Saudi.

Honestly, this bathroom renovation is pushing me to the edge. Another day, another delay! They were supposed to be fitting the tiles today, and what do I get? A phone call saying they're short on adhesive. Adhesive! Who gets short on adhesive? Oh, Brenda, you’re a marvel. You'd think they were building the pyramids, not a bathroom. It  is  a nightmare, isn't it? But at least it’ll be lovely when it’s done. I’m really hoping for a decent soak in that new tub. Can you guys keep it down a bit? I'm trying to message Liam. Liam, is it? Still messaging that Liam? Honestly, Daniel, you spend more time staring at that screen than you do breathing. Mum! He’s not  just  Liam. And it's none of your business. Now, now, Daniel. Let the boy have his space. Brenda, about Daniel – have you thought about having him do some babysitting for Mrs. Davies next door? She’s desperately looking for someone reliable, and he’s already shown he’s good with little Emily. Babysitting? He’s barely looked after himself! Remember when he left his school blazer at the park last week? That was  one  time! And it’s not exactly the same as babysitting. Little Emily is... well, she's a handful. True, but it would be good experience for him. A bit of responsibility. And it would earn him some pocket money. Thinking about it, he could use the money for that Explorer's Club thing he’s been talking about? The weekend camping trip to the Peak District? The Peak District? That’s right up my street! I used to go walking there all the time with my dad. Do you remember that time we got caught in that torrential downpour, Sarah? We were soaked to the bone! I do! We looked like drowned rats. Although, to be honest, those are some of my best memories. Speaking of trips, have you started looking at holidays yet? We need to book something for the summer. I've been browsing, but everything’s so expensive. Spain’s looking a bit pricey this year. Maybe we could do something a bit closer to home? Cornwall, perhaps? Cornwall’s boring. Can't we go somewhere with Wi-Fi? Like, actually decent Wi-Fi? Of course, darling. We’ll find somewhere with Wi-Fi.

Right then, who’s feeling peckish? Another hour or so until we reach Pula, and I'm already dreaming of some proper Istrian grub. Truffles, anyone? Truffles on  everything , Dad! Seriously, can we find a place that does truffle risotto, truffle pasta, truffle ice cream...the works? I've been reading up on them, apparently, the white truffles here are proper special. Aye, lass, you read your stuff, don’t ya? They  are  lovely. Remember that restaurant we went to in Livar, years ago, when your grandad was still with us? They had a truffle-infused olive oil… Oh, it were heaven. Can we just get pizza? Truffles are a bit... fancy. And expensive. I reckon I'd just eat the crusts anyway. Pizza's fine, son, but we’re in truffle country! A bit of culinary exploration doesn’t hurt. Besides, your Auntie Eleanor swore this trip was all about experiencing the local cuisine. Remember her lecture last week? "Immerse yourselves!" she kept saying. She does go on a bit, doesn't she? But she's right. I wanna try proper Istrian fuzi pasta, too. Heard that's a local speciality. What’s fuzi, Gran? It's a handmade pasta, love. Little ear-shaped things. They’re usually served with a wild game ragu. Proper hearty stuff. Reminds me of your Uncle Derek, he could demolish a plate of that in minutes. You remember Derek, don't you, lad? Vaguely. He always smelled like cigarettes and disappointment. Right. Well, moving on from that. You know, I was watching that cooking show,  Chef's Table , last week. They had an episode on a chef in America, doing some incredible stuff with molecular gastronomy. Wild, honestly. Almost like science. Ugh, molecular gastronomy. It looks like something a scientist would create, not a chef. Give me a good, honest cook any day. Like Marco Pierre White, now  he  knows his onions. Although, his temper's a bit fiery. You’ve got opinions, haven’t you? Just like your dad used to have about football. Always moaning about the ref. Remember the Manchester United game in '99? He near took the telly off the wall! That wasn’t near! It was a perfectly justifiable expression of frustration! Anyway, back to food. What do you reckon about stem cell research? They're using it to grow meat now. Imagine, lab-grown steak. No cows involved.

Honestly, I still can’t believe they chose  us  to assess the new font options. Me, a digital marketer, and… well, you, with your linguistics background. It feels a bit random, doesn't it? Random, perhaps, but also rather fascinating, actually. Fonts aren't just about aesthetics, are they? They subtly influence readability, comprehension, even the emotional impact of the text. It's all about the shapes, the spacing… it’s linguistic archaeology in a way. You two sound very serious about fonts. I was just thinking, “Please don’t let the colour palettes clash with the new cover designs.” My job’s mostly just ensuring spreadsheets don’t explode, so…fonts are a bit beyond my remit. Spreadsheets  never  explode, do they? They just… leak. Slowly. But yeah, I get your point, Alex. It’s visual impact for me. We’re trying to create something that'll grab attention online, not necessarily analyse its phonetic properties. There’s a synergy, though. Think about the rise of minimalist design. A clean, sans-serif font can feel modern and trustworthy, appealing to a younger audience. Whereas a more ornate serif might evoke a sense of tradition, suited for academic texts. It’s all about targeting the right perception. Right, right. It makes more sense when you put it like that. So, are we actually liking any of these options? They all look rather… beige to me. Beige is exactly the word. I was leaning towards ‘Nova Pro’ just because it feels cleaner than some of the others, but it's not exactly groundbreaking, is it? Marketing team’s going to want something a bit  more . I’m surprisingly drawn to 'Garamond Premier Pro’. It’s a serif, I know, but it’s surprisingly legible, and the slightly unusual curves give it a certain character. It wouldn't work for everything – a flashy children's book, perhaps not – but for a lot of academic content, I think it could be quite palatable. Garamond, huh? Feels a bit… stuffy? Like something my grandfather would read. No offense to grandfathers. None taken, Alex. And I think you’re onto something there. It's definitely aiming for academic seriousness. I’m just worried about engaging a broader readership. We need something that feels both sophisticated  and  approachable. That's the challenge, isn't it? Perhaps a blend? Could we suggest using ‘Nova Pro’ for headings and summaries, and ‘Garamond Premier Pro’ for the body text?

Right, according to this, we’re about fifteen minutes out of Tarnow. How are you feeling? Long journey yesterday, wasn't it? My back's aching something fierce. It was, love. Quite a trek. My knees aren’t particularly grateful either, you know. Fifty-odd years of not being massively active takes its toll. But I’m alright, mostly. A bit stiff. Are you sure you’re comfortable driving? You look a bit tense. Nah, I’m fine. Just concentrating really. These Polish roads… are an experience, aren’t they? A bit… enthusiastic, shall we say? And trying to decipher the signs! I’m glad I refreshed my Polish a bit before we left. Though I'm still not confident. Enthusiastic is a polite way to put it. I remember the first time I drove here, ages ago. Thought I was going to end up in a ditch. Have you spoken to Agnieszka recently? I haven’t heard from her since we messaged about the keys. Oh, yeah, I texted her about half an hour ago. She said everything's sorted. Keys are under the gnome in the garden, she remembered. A very Tarnow welcome, isn't it? I told her we were about fifteen minutes away. She said to just pull up and she'd be out. Said she’d made pierogi - my favourite! Pierogi! Oh, that’s lovely news. My goodness, I do miss those. I think I’ve developed a genuine addiction to them. I’m having three, minimum. I’ve not had proper Polish food in… well, far too long. Remember that awful hotel buffet in Krakow last year? How could I forget? Everything was beige. Absolutely everything. This'll be a vast improvement, I reckon. She’s a brilliant cook, Agnieszka. You know, it’s funny, I didn’t really connect with her properly until I started teaching. Turns out having to explain grammatical concepts highlights a surprising amount about someone’s personality! I’ve always liked her. A very warm, lovely girl. It’s remarkable, isn’t it, how working with people—in any capacity—can reveal something of their character. It's just... I wish I had something more fulfilling to focus on. All this free time... It's a bit much, to be honest. These TEFL lessons only fill a few hours a week. Don't say that, Auntie Eleanor. You're doing a great thing, helping people learn English.

Dead lively, innit? Absolutely buzzing. Proper spectacle, even if we can't hear a peep from the commentators. It is. Shame about the draw though, eh? Thought we had it there in the second half. Still, good entertainment. You reckon that new sponsorship deal with…what was it, 'Apex Tech'?…is a good move for them? Apex Tech, aye. I'm a bit on the fence, to be honest. The money's obviously brilliant - everyone knows that. But it feels a bit…sterile, doesn’t it? They’re all about AI and data analytics. Doesn’t quite have the same grit, the same…passion as the old sponsors, like. Remember when 'Brew & Bolt' did the shirts? Those were iconic. Brew & Bolt! Absolute classic. That red and yellow striped kit… Legendary. Apex Tech’s logo is just…grey. Very grey. It washes out the whole design, don't you think? This year's strip is alright, but the logo placement is off. Too high on the chest, feels a bit cramped. Dead right. It’s like they didn’t consider the kit at all, just slapped the logo on. And the font! It looks like something off a spreadsheet. Honestly, you could do better with Microsoft Word. Remember that horrible orange and black one they had in '08? That was bad, but this feels… bland. Oh God, the orange and black. Don't even mention it. That was a marketing disaster. Though, I do admire their willingness to experiment back then. Nowadays, everything is so risk-averse. They’re scared of upsetting anyone. Aye, it's true. Everything’s about focus groups and market research. Where's the heart gone? It's all about profit margins now, isn't it? Still, at least there's decent footie. Makes up for a lot. Fancy a burger after this and a rewatch? A burger? Now you’re talking! I'm starving. McDonalds? Aye, fancy a McDonald’s. I’m absolutely craving a Big Mac. Those onion rings, though…heavenly! You know, they should sponsor a team. Imagine – the McDonald’s Championship! Golden Arches emblazoned across the shirts. It’d be a bit ridiculous, but also… kind of brilliant. Oh, stop it! That’s pure madness! But imagine the advertising potential. They could have a different Happy Meal promotion every game, linked to a player. "Get your Ronaldo-themed McNuggets!" Exactly! And the stadium food would be all burgers and fries, obviously.

Honestly, Dad, I’m just… feeling a bit stressed. Uni's ramping up, deadlines are looming, and I feel like I’m running on fumes. Fumes, eh? Tell me about it. Been watchin' this documentary about… well, documentary about somethin’ boring. Makes you appreciate the simple things, you know? Like a spot of tea. Fancy another biscuit? Mum made those eccles cakes this mornin’. No, thanks, really. It’s… it's more than just uni, actually. I keep having this weird feeling I’m being watched. Like someone's recording me. Ridiculous, I know. Recording you? Who'd want to record you? You mostly just do essays and… well, you. What’s brought this on? I don't  know ! It started yesterday. I just feel… self-conscious. Like I’m being judged. It's making me paranoid. I was thinking about catching the train to London tomorrow, you know, for a bit of retail therapy, but now... London? With the kids? Right mess that place is. Full of pickpockets and strangers. Not good for little 'uns, not good at all. Remember that day trip we took to Southend? Little Liam kept runnin’ off and nearly got lost! Nearly gave Mum a heart attack. Dad, please. I’m not talking about the kids. I was thinking of going alone. Just to get out of Gillingham for a few hours. And it's not  just  about that. I also just got a package from eBay - a vintage record player. Should arrive tomorrow. Hoping it’s in good nick. eBay! Shoulda used me, love. I'm good at sniffin’ out a bargain. Although, most of what I find is just… junk. Like that ceramic frog I got for Mum last Christmas. Turns out one of its eyes was missing. Had a right confrontation with the seller about it, I did. Absolute cheek, tryin’ to fob me off! You and your eBay battles. I bet. It's just... people are so quick to judge nowadays. You see it everywhere. Like the other day, I was on the bus, and this fella… well, he clearly mistook someone for another person. Said something really inappropriate. Absolutely mortifying for both of them. People are daft, innit? No manners. No common sense. Reminds me of tryin' to get a meeting with the job centre. Endless forms, endless hoops to jump through. Job Seeker's Allowance… barely covers the gas bill these days, let alone a decent cup of tea.

Honestly, the traffic getting here was just appalling. Sat nav took me down this ridiculous little lane, barely wide enough for a bicycle! I swear, these apps are actively trying to make my life difficult. Aye, they do, don't they? I stick to what I know, I do. Use proper maps, still. You can't trust those things. Happened to my Harold once, led him right into a field full of cows! Cows, you say? Well, that’s a sight! Reminds me of when your father, bless his soul, tried to fix the shed roof. Ended up covered head-to-toe in soot and clinging to a guttering. A proper laugh that was. Oh, Dad was a character, wasn’t he? I remember. Though I'm not sure he'd appreciate you recounting that story to his daughter-in-law. He was fiercely protective of his DIY reputation - which was, let's be honest, questionable. He were a good man, though. Used to bring me a pasty from the shop every Saturday after football. Can’t get pasties like that anymore, mind you. Everything's gone all fancy, isn't it? Fancy? Everything's gone downhill, I tell you! Used to be a proper butcher's on the High Street. Now it's that…that SPAR. It wouldn't know a proper steak and kidney pie if it fell on it. You're preaching to the choir! I tried to get decent ingredients for a roast last week. The carrots were practically translucent. Honestly, you have to go to Waitrose now for anything vaguely resembling quality. It’s extortionate, of course. Waitrose? Oh, I wouldn't be caught dead in there. Bit too posh for my liking. I get everything I need from Tesco. Got a good deal on biscuits today. Chocolate Hobnobs – your cup of tea, aren't they? Absolutely! Although, I'm trying to be good. Doctor says I need to cut back on the sugar. Although… …one biscuit wouldn't hurt, would it? One biscuit never hurt anyone. Except maybe Harold’s dentist! Honestly, you two. Always talking about biscuits and roast dinners. Remember that dreadful plane crash they had on the news the other day? Makes you think, doesn’t it? It really does. Terrible, just awful. Although, with the way the traffic was…I’m almost glad I was on the ground. It makes you appreciate being here, doesn't it?

Honestly, this whole trainee teacher thing is just  weird , isn’t it? Like, Mrs. Davies is lovely, but having Mr. Peterson hovering around every lesson... it's a bit intense. Tell me about it! He keeps interrupting Mr. Jones. It’s so awkward. Last week, Mr. Jones was explaining photosynthesis, and Mr. Peterson was like, "Have you considered the potential impact of mycorrhizal fungi on the sugar transport pathways?" It was just… random! Oh my gosh, yes! Photosynthesis. I was struggling to keep a straight face. I mean, fungi are important, obviously, but not  during  a basic intro lesson! It totally derailed everything. Did you see Emily's face? She was completely lost. Emily's face was a masterpiece of confusion. Like, a silent, slowly-dawning realization of just how far beyond her current understanding we were. Speaking of which, are you stressing about the English lit test on Friday? Don't even  mention  it. I've read  Of Mice and Men  like fifty times, but I still feel like I'm going to forget everything the moment I open the paper. What if they ask me about Curley’s wife's motivations and I completely blank? I'm trying to memorize key quotes. I've got a whole sheet of them stuck to my mirror. It's a bit much, Mum keeps complaining. But honestly, I think I need it. What about you? Any good quotes ready to go? I’ve got a few, but I always worry I'll write them down wrong and then lose marks. It’s the worst! You know what  would  be good? If the test was about art instead. Remember that pottery class we did last term? I really enjoyed that. Oh yeah! I made that wonky vase. Mrs. Peterson said it had 'character.' I think she meant it was terrible, but I preferred to think it was ironically stylish. It was perfectly charmingly wonky. You're an amazing artist, you know. You should definitely apply for the art scholarship next year. You think so? It's just… feels a bit ambitious, doesn't it? Plus, science is surprisingly cool too. Did you see that documentary about deep-sea creatures last week? Absolutely bonkers! Some of those things look like they're from another planet. I did! The anglerfish were terrifying! But the bioluminescence was beautiful. See, science  can  be pretty amazing, if you ignore the fungi tangents.

Right then, dinner’s nearly ready. Liam, put your phone down, love. We're having a proper chat tonight. Do we  have  to? It's a bit… intense, isn't it? All this talking about… well,  everything . Intense? It’s family, Liam. And we’re all thinking about big things, aren’t we? Especially after that documentary Finn showed us last week. All that stuff about… Scientology. Frankly, it gave me the chills. Yeah, it was weird. But the Matrix was way more interesting. You ever think about it, like, what if  everything  we experience is just… a simulation? Like, a program? "Guh!" He’s trying to join the philosophical debate, I see. Little Finn wants to know about reality too. Darling, don't get too caught up in computer games. It’s easy to lose yourself. Remember what your gran always said about questioning everything but having a solid grounding in your own beliefs. But Gran was always talking about the Church and the nuns. It felt… old-fashioned. Like, what about people who don’t believe in that? Well, there’s plenty of ways to believe, isn’t there? And plenty of ways to  not  believe. Your Auntie Moira, she doesn’t go to church, but she’s got a strong spiritual side, she finds it in nature, in meditation. It’s not about ticking boxes in a building, is it? It’s about finding something that gives your life meaning. I guess. I just… I don't know. I had a chat with Jack at school today. He got really into this guy online who talks about ancient aliens. Says everything is evidence of alien intervention. Ancient aliens, eh? That  is  a rabbit hole. Same sort of feeling as that Scientology thing, really. People looking for answers somewhere that's... shiny and new. It's just… everyone seems to be searching for something, you know? Like, when I was watching the Matrix, it felt like everyone's searching for the truth. And when I watch videos about ancient aliens… It’s a human thing, isn’t it? To wonder about the big questions. Your grandfather used to spend hours poring over religious texts. He said it wasn’t about proving anything, but about exploring the possibilities. And asking yourself, "What does this mean  to me ?" So, it’s okay to be curious? Even if it’s… a bit out there?

Right, so, are we actually going to get lost again, or have you finally mastered the sat nav, Liam? Last time, we ended up in a field full of sheep! Relax, Liv. It's a direct route this time. And it wasn’t  my  fault last time; you were insisting we take the “scenic route” even though it was basically a track for tractors. And sheep appreciate being seen, you know. Aye, tractors and sheep. Sounds about right for a Saturday afternoon with you. Speaking of Saturdays, are you still going to those… line dancing lessons? I swear, every time I think of you doing the Electric Slide, I nearly choke on me tea. Hey, don't knock it 'til you've tried it! It’s surprisingly good exercise. And Gemma keeps saying I've got "natural rhythm.” You know she adores anything vaguely American. Besides, Fiona at work keeps teasing me about it, so I need something to laugh about. Fiona, eh? She's just jealous she can't pull off a cowboy hat without looking like a circus act. Speaking of things a bit out there, are you still obsessed with reading about Old English? I saw a stack of books about it on your bedside table last week. Honestly, what use is it these days? It’s fascinating! Understanding the roots of our language… it’s like unravelling a giant, amazing puzzle. It explains so much about modern English. Plus, my mate, Oliver, is doing a doctorate on it, and he keeps telling me about these incredible discoveries they’re making. It’s actually quite relevant to some computational linguistics work – a bit like what you do, right? Corpus Admin is  slightly  different from deciphering Beowulf, love. Though I can see the connections, I suppose. Sounds dreadfully dull though, to be honest. Did you finish that report for Uni? The one on… what was it, the effect of metric conversion on British engineering practices? Nearly. Just need to polish off the conclusion. It’s mind-numbing actually, all the arguments about which system is superior. Honestly, sometimes I think people are just being stubborn. You'd think we'd have embraced metric by now. Tell me about it! Try explaining to your nan why a yard is no longer a standard measurement. She'll give you the evils. Remember when we were kids and she’d always yell, "It’s six inches to the toe, girl, not some fancy decimal."

Right then, this Istrian countryside is proper stunning, isn’t it? Better than Surrey any day, I can tell you that. Though, I miss a decent pint sometimes. Aye, it's beautiful, Dad. Though, honestly, I'm already missing the lads. There's a Sons of Anarchy marathon on tonight. Aye, Elara, you and that show! Honestly, it’s all leather and growling. You’d think you were a biker chick yourself. At least the scenery is something to appreciate tonight, love. And put that phone away for a bit, will ya? Did you see that olive grove back there, Mum? It was massive! Can we stop at a market later and get some olive oil? The stuff we use at home's rubbish. We absolutely will, Liam. There’s a little market in Rovinj I heard’s brilliant. Fresh produce, local crafts… probably a bit pricey, mind you. Remind me to keep an eye on the pennies. Speaking of prices, did anyone see that vintage Fiat 500 back in Pula? Pristine condition. Must’ve cost a fortune. Always fancied one of those. Little bit of Italian style, you know. You and your cars, Dad. Honestly. It wouldn't fit all your spreadsheets and briefcases. Give me a campervan any day, something we can just pack up and go. Imagine, festivals, camping… proper freedom. Elara, you’re already planning our next adventure, aren’t you? Let’s just get through this week first! I'd rather a nice, clean hotel than a damp tent, thank you very much. My bones aren’t what they used to be. Center Parcs is better than camping, Mum. You get proper swimming pools and stuff. And those lodges are comfy. Center Parcs, eh? A bit sanitized for my liking. Give me a proper caravan holiday any day. Remember those, Margaret? When the kids were little? We'd spend weeks pottering around the countryside. Oh, don't remind me! Sand everywhere, leaky windows, and arguments about who was doing the washing up. It was lovely in its own chaotic way, I'll admit. But I'm glad we’ve moved onto slightly more luxurious holidays. So, where  are  we heading tonight? Rovinj, you said, Mum? Do you know any good restaurants there? I'm starving. All that driving has built up an appetite. Aye, Rovinj it is. Found a place online – Konoba al Mare, apparently does a mean seafood risotto.

“Right, so, like, I'm  still  not entirely convinced about this whole ‘recording our gaming sessions’ thing, are you? It just feels…a bit weird, dosn't it?” “Weird how? It’s literally just documenting what we already  do . Think of the potential! Funny moments, epic fails… we could cut it into a montage and put it on YouTube. It’d be brilliant!” “Aye, brilliant! Imagine 'em laughing their heads off at us messin' up in Mario Kart. Proper funny, that would be.” “Exactly! And it’s not like we're exposing anything too personal. It’s just gameplay. Think of it as, you know, a bit of creative fun. Besides, I reckon Finn would love it.” “Finn’s going to be mortified, I swear. He’s already got enough to worry about with his coding project. He won’t want everyone seeing him yellin’ at his screen over Apex Legends.” “He’ll get over it. He practically lives online anyway. And it'll show off his skills, honestly! He's a beast at Apex. We can even blur out his name tags if it’s a huge deal.” "Blur 'em out! And maybe add some funny captions, like, 'Finn's Rage Mode Activated!' Or, 'Feedin' the enemy team again!' " “You’re terrible, you two. But… okay, okay. The captions are a definite no-go though. Absolutely not. What about the  anal ysis? You were going on about doing proper analysis of our gameplay, weren't you, Chloe?" “Yes! That was the idea. Like, reviewing our strategies, pointing out what we could have done differently. It’d be more than just funny outtakes. We could actually get better at games. Think of the improvement! A proper breakdown of why we keep losing at Among Us.” “Exactly! Using the recordings, we can replay moments, see exactly what everyone was doing, and figure out where things went wrong. Much more effective than just arguing about it afterwards!” “Anal… like, on our backsides?” “No, love!  Analysis ! It’s a word! Don’t go thinking we’re doing anything… weird.” She wipes a tear from her eye. "She’s been watching too many true crime documentaries," she says with a chuckle. “Honestly, Beth. Restrain yourself. Anyway, so... who's got the headset? We should start testing the recording software. I’ve got a spare memory stick if anyone needs one.” "I've got a spare! And I’m ready to record.

Honestly, this afternoon’s Excel refresher course nearly killed me. Three hours of pivot tables... my brain feels like mush. Anyone else starving? Aye, you're tellin’ me, lass. Pivot tables are a right headache, aren’t they? I were practically nappin’ through some of it myself. Starving, definitely. I were thinkin' about nipping down to Greggs later for a sausage roll. Proper comfort food, that. Greggs? Respect. Classic. Though, I was thinking something a bit…healthier? I saw that new Thai place opened up on the High Street, “Spice Route,” I think it was. Apparently, their Pad Thai’s amazing. Thai sounds good! Anything's better than another sandwich from the campus cafe. They keep promising to update the menu, but it's still mostly beige. Thai… hmm. I'm not proper a fan of that strong stuff, to be honest. Too many chillies for this old Pelaw lad. Sausage roll’s safe, you know? Reliable. Can't go wrong with a sausage roll. Remember that bakery in Gateshead that did those massive, curly ones? Proper feasts they were. You and your sausage rolls, John. You're eternally loyal. I get it, though. There’s a certain comfort in knowing exactly what you’re getting. Spice Route does a green curry that's not ridiculously spicy, supposedly. They cater for different spice levels. I'm swaying towards the Thai. It'd be good to try somewhere new. Plus, I’m trying to be a bit better with healthy eating, you know? My mum keeps nagging me. Mothers, eh? Always somethin’. My mam used to make the best pasties, though. Big, meaty, proper hearty things. Not like these fancy, miniature versions you get these days. Used to fill you right up. Remember the smell of them bakin' in the oven? My grandma made incredible Lancashire hotpot. So rich and comforting. It’s a lost art, really. No one seems to bother with those traditional dishes anymore. Everything's either ready meals or overpriced restaurant food. Yeah, it is a shame. Though, I did have a brilliant Sunday roast at that pub down by the canal last weekend. Proper roast potatoes, crispy on the outside, fluffy on the inside... it was heavenly. Now you’re talkin'! Roast potatoes are essential. Mine's gotta be with dripping, not that olive oil stuff some people use. Ruins 'em, it does. Fancy some fish and chips later?

Right, so, Janice from IT was having a right go at me this morning. Apparently, I posted a picture of my lunch on LinkedIn. A cheese and pickle sandwich, mind you. A perfectly respectable cheese and pickle sandwich! She said it wasn't “professional.” Professional! I work in enquiries, not a law firm. A cheese and pickle sandwich? Janice needs to broaden her horizons. Honestly, the definitions of "professional" are getting tighter and tighter. I put a picture of a first edition of “Wuthering Heights” I was cataloguing on Twitter the other day. Got a few likes, that. Less outcry than your lunch, I imagine. Honestly, the obsession with portraying some perfect, polished image online is exhausting. Especially for us, in libraries. We’re supposed to be about accessibility and down-to-earth knowledge, not curated performances. I posted a picture of my cat, Bartholomew, asleep on a pile of periodicals yesterday. Got more engagement than anything about research databases in the last week. Bartholomew, you say? So, a feline stakeholder strategy, then? Clever. See, this is why I find the whole thing bewildering. LinkedIn feels...forced. Like everyone’s trying to be someone they’re not, just to impress their contacts. I tried to write a witty caption about the sandwich – "Fueling the enquiry engine!" – Janice nearly had a seizure. I get that. It's the performative aspect. Twitter's a bit better for genuine snippets, I find. Short, sweet, academic jokes. I had one the other day about Dewey Decimal and existential dread. Went down a treat. What about Instagram, though? Anyone brave enough to venture there? Instagram's a minefield. All perfectly lit avocado toast and picturesque bookshelves. I tried for a while, documenting rare book bindings. Felt instantly inauthentic. Ended up just using it to share photos of koalas I see when I visit my sister in Queensland. Far more honest. And significantly less pressure. Koalas are hard to argue with. Though my grandkids are obsessed with TikTok. Keep trying to get me to do a dance challenge. It's… not my forte. My dancing skills peaked somewhere around a 1998 office Christmas party. Oh, the horrors. I attempted a TikTok once. Demonstrating how to use a microfilm reader. Didn't quite resonate with the audience. Turns out, young people prefer cats and dances to historical documents. Go figure. Exactly! You know, I saw a presentation recently arguing that social media is actually  training  us to be more superficial, attention-seeking.

Right then, Eleanor, thanks for coming down. Tunbridge Wells is a bit of a trek from Stratford, I know. Coffee? Biscuits? Thank you, David. It’s lovely to be here, actually. A surprisingly pleasant drive. And no need to feel too guilty about the distance; I'm perfectly capable of navigating the M25 these days. So, the hospice… It's a weighty project, isn’t it? Weighty doesn't quite cover it. Transformational, I'd hope. But we've got a lot to iron out. I’ve been reviewing the initial business case, the numbers look sound, but I wanted your expert opinion on the rationale for Tunbridge Wells specifically. We've had some pushback – mainly from Rotherham, as you might imagine. I suspected as much. Yorkshire doesn't like relinquishing ground, does it? But I understand the thinking. The catchment area here is significantly underserved when it comes to specialist palliative care. The current services are stretched thin, and travelling to London – as many are currently forced to – is hardly ideal for patients or their families. Precisely. And the Council have indicated a willingness to work with us, allocate some land, and champion the project. But they want to see a robust consultation process. What are your thoughts on how we approach that? I was thinking a series of public forums, likely online as well, to reach as many people as possible. Forums are essential, definitely. But don't underestimate the value of smaller, more targeted groups. Focus groups with carers, discussions with healthcare professionals – GPs, district nurses, hospice nurses already working in the area. And crucially, Eleanor, engagement with the local hospices. We need to build bridges, not create competition. Their expertise and existing patient networks are invaluable. Good point. I’ve been trying to get in touch with St. Giles in Pembury, but their Director of Fundraising seems perpetually unavailable. I'm hoping our approach – emphasizing collaboration, rather than replacement – will ease that. We're not trying to poach patients, it’s about expanding capacity and offering a higher level of specialized care. Speaking of which, I've had preliminary conversations with a couple of estate agents about potential sites. One suggested an impressive plot just outside of town – a bit sprawling, perhaps, but with significant potential for future expansion. What are your thoughts on the architectural aesthetic? I don't want some sterile, institutional-looking building. Absolutely not.

Oh, look at this! Remember this, David? Ascot, must be…twenty years ago? Heavens, we were young! Blimey, you're right, Sarah. That was a good day. The weather was glorious, and I think we actually managed to make a bit of a profit on a couple of horses. Not much, mind, but enough for a decent dinner that night. Who’s that hiding behind you? That's Auntie Brenda's old friend, Penelope! Isn’t she a scream in these photos? The hat! Absolutely enormous. Penelope! Goodness, I'd completely forgotten about her. Used to flirt outrageously with your Uncle Barry, didn't she? Always a bit of a colourful character. She smelled permanently of lavender and gin. That's spot on, Sarah. Barry was always a bit flustered around her. Still, good memories. Say, Chloe, how’s the copywriting going? Any interesting projects on the go? Actually, yeah. I’m pitching for a big client, a luxury phone accessories company. Pretty cutthroat, loads of competition. I had the interview yesterday. Oh, darling, how did it go? You seemed a bit stressed about it. It was…fine. I think. The guy kept asking about my experience with social media campaigns, which is a bit of a stretch for me, mostly I just write website copy. I think I stammered a bit when he asked about ROI. Right. Return on investment. They always throw that one in to see if you’re thinking commercially. Don't beat yourself up about it. Did you mention your project for that local bakery? That showed initiative, didn't it? I did, but I don’t know if he seemed impressed. He was very…corporate. All sharp suits and intense eye contact. Intense eye contact doesn't always equal good, love. Sometimes it’s just a sign they're trying too hard. Honestly, I’ve seen more genuine smiles from patients with a broken leg. You've got to trust your instincts. Did you feel a connection? Not really. Which is worrying, isn't it? I thought I should be feeling some spark, you know? A spark's lovely, but don't rely on it. Being competent and showing you can deliver is more important. Did you follow up with a thank you email? Yeah, sent one this morning. Short and sweet, just a recap of what we discussed and reiterating my enthusiasm. Perfect. That's all you can do.

Right, alright. Ready for this then? I’ve got the popcorn, you’ve got the… enthusiasm, apparently. Enthusiasm is an understatement! I’ve been buzzing all day. You pick, though. You're the one who declared tonight "Scary Film Night." Though, just so you know, I have a  very  specific criteria. Oh, here we go. What’s your criteria this week then? No jump scares? No supernatural creatures? Only psychological horror with a slow burn and ambiguous ending? Because that sounds  thrilling . Okay, okay, you’re exaggerating. But I’m not a fan of the cheap stuff, you know? Like, predictable jump scares and ghosts that just go "boo." I want something that gets under your skin, something you'll be thinking about for days. Something with…atmosphere. Atmosphere, eh? Fancy. I just want to be scared witless for a couple of hours. Give me a good ol' demonic possession or a slasher any day. Something uncomplicated. Less thinking, more screaming. See, that's why we make such a good team. I can appreciate a good slasher, don't get me wrong, but I crave something deeper. Remember when we watched  The Babadook ? That stuck with us for weeks! Aye, that were a right proper unsettling one, that. Gave me nightmares for a good three nights. Too clever for its own good, mind. It were all about grief and… stuff. I just wanted a monster! That  was  a monster! Just a metaphorical one. See? You do appreciate a bit of depth. How about  Hereditary ? We've been meaning to watch that for ages.  Hereditary … I’ve heard things. Really bad things. Apparently, folk were genuinely distressed after watching that one. It’s…intense. But in a good way. It's beautifully shot, the acting is phenomenal, and the story is just… gut-wrenching. Gut-wrenching? Sounds a bit much for a Tuesday night, don't you think? I was hopin' for something a bit lighter. Like, maybe  The Conjuring ? We haven't watched that in ages. Classic.  The Conjuring ? Okay, that's a safe bet. It’s got the jump scares you want, and the haunted house vibe is always a winner. But... couldn't we  try  something a little different? At least look? Alright, alright. Fine. Let’s have a quick peek. But if it involves obscure symbolism and long, drawn-out silences, I’m switching to  The Conjuring , fair warning.

Right, Grandpa, feeling sleepy yet? It’s nearly ten o’clock. Nearly? It’s past ten, Eleanor! My bones feel it, you know. These old bones know the time, even if I don't always. And yes, I am feeling a bit drowsy. Though I'm still trying to fathom this newfangled Airbnb business. Airbnb? Still on that, are you? It’s just letting people rent out their homes while they're away, Grandpa. Think of it like a holiday let, but a bit more… modern. Aunt Carol is using it for the cottage in Cornwall next month. Says it’s much easier than dealing with a letting agency. Letting agency! That sounds more sensible. People traipsing through your house, strangers… I don't like the sound of it. Though, I must admit, your Aunt Carol did seem rather pleased with the money she's making. That’s tempting, I suppose. Is it like buying and selling on that… eBay thing? A bit, yes. But instead of selling a chipped teapot, you’re renting out a whole house. Speaking of which, remember you were saying you needed a new side table for the study? I found a lovely one online. Oak, really solid. £45 delivered. Delivered! Straight to my door? Good heavens. In my day, you'd go to the shop, haggle with the chap, and feel you’d had a proper deal. Now it's all done with a click. And what about these ipads everyone’s going on about? Do I  really  need one? You don’t  need  one, Grandpa, but it could make things easier. You could read your emails on it, see pictures of the family, even video call me when I’m at school. Remember how frustrated you were trying to enlarge the print on your emails? I do. The print's getting smaller every year, it seems. And these emails… my goodness, the sheer volume! I swear, I spend half my day deleting spam. It's all rather overwhelming. Still, I’d be completely lost without my laptop. You showed me those keyboard shortcuts, you know. Makes a world of difference. Glad to hear it! That’s what I'm here for. I was thinking, though, we could order a pizza tomorrow. Little treat. What toppings would you like? Pizza! Now  that's  a proper treat. Pepperoni, definitely. And a bit of mushroom, if they don’t mind.

"Aye, this is grand, isn’t it, Hamish? Proper peace and quiet. Beats battling the emails back in Edinburgh, that’s for sure.” "It really does, Alistair. Though, I confess, I’m finding it hard to fully switch off. Bulgakov's just got such a hold on me. Have ye read it? Truly remarkable.” “Bulgakov, eh? I’ve seen the name, of course, everyone’s seen the name. Never got round to it though. Been lost in a bit of Iain Banks recently. 'Transition' particularly. Dark, but brilliant. The way he handles the speculative, blending it with such grounded characters… superb, isn't it?” “Banks is always solid. ‘Transition’ is a beast, though. Quite relentless. But you're right about the characters. Bulgakov has that too, you know. This one, Woland, is just… unforgettable. A devil, naturally, but with a sly wit and a surprising amount of pathos. Reminds me a bit of certain politicians we know!” "Och, you’re not wrong there! Politics are a necessary evil, I suppose, but rarely bring a smile to your face. This trip's good for the soul. Reminds me of when we were kids, coming out here with the grandparents. Remember those summers? Endless days exploring the woods, building dens…" “I do! And the sheep! Always trying to chase the sheep. Grandfather used to shout at us, 'Leave the poor beasts alone, ye wee hooligans!' But we couldn't resist, could we? And remember that trip to Iceland we took, just after university? That was… transformative." "Transformative is the perfect word! I still think about the Northern Lights. Seeing them dance across the sky like that… otherworldly. I didn’t realise until then that the scale of the universe… well, it puts everything else into perspective, doesn’t it?" “Absolutely. It shrinks anxieties, expands your sense of possibility. Although, I could do with a bit of that right now. This Director of Studies role is relentless. Endless meetings, coursework marking… I’m feeling a need for some serious escapism. Perhaps a return to Iceland?" "I'd be up for that. Or… I was thinking about Patagonia recently. Heard it's spectacular. Vast landscapes, glaciers, mountains… Proper wild. It’s a bit further afield than Iceland, though, isn't it?" "It is. But think of the hiking! And the wildlife. Penguins! Alistair, we  have  to go. We could base ourselves in El Calafate, do some trekking in El Chalten, maybe even see Perito Moreno glacier.”

Honestly, Mum, I don’t know what to do with this application. It just feels… wrong. Wrong how, love? You’ve been pouring over it for hours. Is it the wording? The firm seemed really keen when you spoke to them. It’s not the firm, they seem lovely. It’s… the project. They want someone to lead the design for a luxury apartment complex, right on the river. All glass and steel and minimalist chic. It's exactly the kind of work I  should  be excited about, according to my degree and everything. But… But? Don’t leave me hanging, poppet. But it feels…soulless. All those expensive flats, for people who probably don’t even  need  the space. Meanwhile, there’s a desperate need for affordable housing in London. I feel like I should be designing something that actually benefits people, you know? Something practical, community-focused. Now you're talking. That's a really mature perspective, darling. I remember you sketching out plans for a community centre when you were little, with a rooftop garden and everything. You were worried about where elderly people could sit and enjoy the sun. I was, wasn’t I? It feels like I’ve lost that, a bit. Got caught up in everything the university wanted me to be – a ‘cutting-edge’ architect. Honey, universities try to shape you, but it’s  you  who defines yourself. This job doesn't have to change who you are. You can still do good work, even if it's for a company designing luxury properties. Think of the skills you'd gain, the connections you’d make. And honestly, the money would be…well, significantly better than what you’re earning now. I know, I know. Rent isn't exactly getting cheaper on its own. But it just feels…compromised. Like I’m selling out. Selling out is when you design something you  know  is shoddy or harmful. This doesn't sound like that. Maybe you can use this opportunity to push for sustainable materials, energy-efficient designs, even incorporate some green spaces? Little things. Building a reputation for responsible architecture, even in luxury settings. I hadn’t thought of it like that. I could suggest some changes to the brief, emphasise the importance of…well, not just aesthetics. Exactly. And even if they don't take all your suggestions, you're putting your voice out there.

Blimey, look at that drizzle, doesn’t it? Reminds me of a right downpour we had back in '78, flooding the river Wensum something awful. Remember that, Arthur? '78? Cor, that was before Brenda started her childminding, wasn’t it? Though I reckon I'd remember a flood like that. Costessey wasn’t immune to those, you know. Had a bit of a poke in the allotments that year. Nasty business. You’ve still got that old Ford Cortina, don’t you, David? Don't start reminiscing about cars, Arthur! David, dear, are you alright? You've been gazing at the rain like you're trying to decode it. And yes, I do still have the Cortina. A bit of a rusting relic, but she still gets me down to the shops. Though the hills are getting a bit much for her, I must admit. Still got the Cortina, eh? Good on you, Brenda. Bit of a dependable motor, those. Wouldn’t trust many of these newfangled electric things, not one bit. Too much technology. Give me a proper engine any day. They don’t make ‘em like they used to. Speaking of old times, do you recall the council houses they built round here in the sixties? All those neat rows of terraces? Oh, aye. Saw 'em going up. My cousin, Bernard, got one of the first ones. Said it was like winning the lottery, having a proper roof over your head that wasn't leaky and drafty. Though they didn’t last too well, did they? Started falling apart something shocking after a few years. Needed constant patching up. Well, it was a start, wasn’t it? Far better than some people were living in before. Though the quality did decline, I agree. You know, I was reading something the other day - dreadful article about the price of houses now. Absolutely ridiculous! Young people haven't a chance. Tell me about it! My granddaughter, Emily, lives up in Birmingham. She’s been trying to get on the property ladder for years. Saving every penny. Still, no luck. It's a different world from when I was her age. Buying a house was a realistic goal. Now… Absolutely. They're all working themselves to the bone, these youngsters. Never seem to have any leisure time. Mine's got a flat, mind you, but the rent’s nearly the same as a mortgage would be!

Right then, so the latest booking enquiry… they want the community hall for a birdwatching group. Seriously, birdwatching. In Brixton. Well, there  are  surprisingly lovely little pockets of greenery around, aren’t there? Mycroft Park's not far, and the community gardens are thriving. It’s a clever niche to fill, actually. We need to be thinking about diversifying our usage, Mark. Not just yoga and toddler groups. I know, I know. But a birdwatching group? It feels… specific. How much are they offering to pay? The last yoga instructor was leaving a decent chunk of cash each month. Let’s not be overly cynical. Every bit helps, doesn't it? Check their rates, confirm they have public liability insurance – standard procedure, of course – and if it’s a reasonable amount, let's try and accommodate them. It’s about building a reputation as a welcoming space for  everyone . Besides, it could be useful for generating some positive PR. Think about it – “Brix Supports Local Birdwatchers!” Catchy, isn’t it? Right you are. Catchy indeed. Speaking of PR, have you seen the state of the fire escapes? They're practically begging for a health and safety report. The rust on the third floor one is particularly worrying. Yes, I’ve noticed. I’ve emailed Maintenance again, but you know how slow they are. I'll chase them up directly. Perhaps we should look into getting a quote from a smaller, independent company? It might be quicker and more cost-effective. That’s probably a good shout. It’s just, with the community hall renovations dragging on, and now this… it's a lot to juggle. Have we put a halt on the new furniture order yet? That brighter, more modern stuff for the reception area? Not entirely. I paused it temporarily. We need to ensure we've got the budget breathing room after the contractor's invoice for the hall comes in. It’s essential we’re not overspending. I was thinking perhaps we could look at second-hand options, refurbished pieces. It's more sustainable, and kinder to the budget. Second-hand, eh? That’s a clever move. Keeps costs down. Reminds me of when I was a student, furnishing my flat with stuff from charity shops. Found a surprisingly swanky armchair for a fiver. See? There’s always a bargain to be had! We just need to be resourceful.

Honestly, this is phenomenal, Rhys. Absolutely phenomenal. You’ve outdone yourself. Thanks, Gareth. Just a bit of tweaking from my grandmother's recipe, you know? She was a whiz in the kitchen, my Nain. Used to say, a good Shepherd's Pie is a measure of a Welsh home. It really is. It reminds me of my gran’s cooking, actually. Though she was South African, so it was a little different – more curry spices, often. It felt like home when she made it. Curry in a Shepherd's Pie? Now  that’s  an interesting combo, Chloe! Never heard that one before. I'm always up for experimenting, though. Any chance you could share the recipe? Chloe: Maybe. It’s a bit of a family secret, honestly. But I could try to recreate it. It wasn’t precisely measured, you see. More… a pinch of this, a dash of that, a feeling in your heart. "A feeling in your heart," that's it, isn't it? My Mam used to say the same thing. Cooking isn't about following instructions; it's about putting love into it. And this, boyo , this has love all over it. That's a lovely compliment, Dai. I really wanted to make something everyone would enjoy, especially knowing we've all got different tastes. It’s lovely, truly. Reminds me of Sunday dinners at my parents'. We always had roast beef, of course, but always with a big bowl of mashed potatoes and gravy. Simple, but so comforting. Liam: See, that’s what’s missing from a lot of modern cooking. It’s all about fancy foams and deconstructed dishes. Sometimes, just a well-made, hearty pie is exactly what you need. I've been trying to get back to basics in the restaurant lately, actually. Less molecular gastronomy, more proper comfort food. Gareth: It's worked a treat, Liam. You look much happier. Remember that lavender infused pigeon dish you attempted last year? Nearly cleared the restaurant! Liam: Don't remind me! That was… a learning experience. I appreciate the honesty, Gareth. Thankfully, shepherds pie doesn’t involve anything quite so risky. Chloe: So, Rhys, how did you get into cooking with such a distinctly Welsh style? Did you learn from your Nain, as you mentioned? Absolutely. Nain was my biggest influence. She ran a little tea room in Cardiff for years, and I spent every summer holiday helping her.

Right, so, you're  serious  about this Florence trip then? Like, actually serious? 'Cos last time you got excited about Barcelona, we ended up in Skegness. That was different, El. I was… stressed about work. And Skegness needed rescuing, honestly. It was calling to me. Besides, it was a surprise! This is different. I’ve been looking at flights and accommodation for weeks. Genuine Florence. Renaissance art, gelato… the whole dreamy Italian package. Gelato, eh? Trying to bribe me? You know I'll find something to complain about, right? Probably the pigeons. They'll be massive, I bet. And aggressive. I’m prepared for your pigeon skepticism. I’ve factored in extra gelato to counteract any bird-related trauma. Look, I know you get flights to Cambridge for work all the time, but this is different. This is  us  time, proper time. We need a break. Me especially, with this new project. Aye, I get that. The Cambridge thing is just... functional. Pressing ‘send’ and hoping the data doesn’t spontaneously combust. Not exactly a holiday vibe. Still, Florence...blimey. Proper fancy, innit? More cobbled streets than I’ve ever seen in me life, I reckon. Exactly! Think about it – we could visit the Uffizi Gallery, climb to the top of Duomo…see David. You’d like David, I reckon. He’s a right handsome lad, even if he is made of marble. Don’t you start with the marble statues, love. I'll be more interested in where we can get a decent sausage roll. Seriously, food’s proper important. Is Italian sausage roll a thing? You and your sausage rolls. No, I don’t think Italian sausage roll is a thing. But they have amazing pizza. And pasta, obviously. And… other things. I’ll research the pastry situation specifically for you. You're a good lad, you are. It's just… posh holidays always make me nervous. Like, what if I spill something on me dress? Or say the wrong thing? Everyone'll be judging me. Honestly, El, no one’s judging you. It's Italy. They're used to tourists. Just be yourself. The slightly cynical, sausage-roll-obsessed, pigeon-fearing version of yourself. Aye. And what about Sarah and Liam? Fancy them coming? I was thinking that! I’ll drop them a message later. It’d be brilliant if they could make it. Imagine, four of us, scoffing gelato near the Ponte Vecchio… Right, right.

Honestly, Sarah, this whole thing with my dad… it’s just draining. The hospital appointments, the specialists… it’s relentless. They’re still saying it could be anything, you know? A nasty flu that just… didn’t want to leave. Aye, I know the feeling, love. Relentless is the word. My Harold had a spot on his lung they’re poking at now. Keeps him up at night, worrying. Says it feels “like a little bugger burrowing in.” Honestly, the things men say! They do, don't they? My dad’s all stoic, “Just a bit of a cough, nothing to worry about," but I can see the fear in his eyes. It’s just… I wish I could fix it. You know, magic wand, poof! All better. You can’t, love. Nobody can. That’s just how it is, isn't it? I lost me Nan last year, you remember. Quiet as a mouse, she was, right until the end. The funeral... it was something. All the cousins coming out of the woodwork. Oh, I remember. I'm so sorry, Sarah. Funerals are… well, they're a strange thing, aren’t they? Such a flurry of activity when all you really want to do is just… sit with the person who's gone. My Aunt Maggie won't stop crying. She's been like that for weeks. It's a bit overwhelming, to be honest. Maggie always was a sensitive one. My Brenda’s the same. Bawling her eyes out over Nan, even though they hadn't spoken properly in years - a silly argument about a wonky fence, can you imagine? Family's like that, innit? Holding onto all that baggage. Took me a while to realise you just have to let it go. What are you doing for the funeral arrangements? That's all a bit chaotic at the moment. My brother's taking the lead, but he's… well, he’s not exactly a natural organiser. He's trying to be, bless him, but he keeps getting bogged down in the details. He's insisted on a specific brand of roses, for crying out loud. Apparently, they’re Dad’s favourite. Typical. Men and their roses. My Harold’s the same way about lilies. Says they’re 'proper funeral flowers'. Silly things, really. Mine's been trying that new slimming club, you know. 'Slim Evolve' they call it.

Right then, full bellies and good company. So, anyone fancy talking about what they  actually  do all day? Besides, you know, being brilliant students, Liam and Finn. Oh, relax, Dad. We don’t  just  study. We… exist. And we play a lot of football. That’s undeniably true. Though I’m not sure 'existence' is quite a professional LinkedIn summary, Liam. Though, I suppose mine could do with some work too. Marketing and proofreading… it’s a bit of a mouthful, isn’t it? Most people just say “I work for myself.” "Freelancer" seems to be the default these days. I had a conversation with the CEO about that the other day, actually. He was asking about potential future recruitment strategies. Turns out, we’re looking at bringing in more freelancers, saving on overheads. It's a shift, but one I’m heading up. Interesting! So, your operations manager role is becoming… more strategic? Less about just making sure the trains run on time? Exactly. It’s more about anticipating needs and adapting. Thinking ‘What’s the best way to get things done, regardless of who’s doing them?’ Which is terrifying, frankly. Suddenly you're responsible for policies that impact people’s livelihoods. Sounds stressful, Dad. It has its moments. What about you, Sarah? Proofreading… is that all it is? Seems pretty solitary. It can be, yeah. But I love it, honestly. There’s a real satisfaction in spotting a tiny grammatical error that's slipped through. It’s detail-oriented, which I’m good at. And the variety keeps it interesting. I’ve proofread everything from marketing brochures for luxury hotels to academic papers on… well, something to do with theoretical physics, I think. I barely understood it! That sounds… boring. Boring to  you , maybe. It’s like being a detective, but with commas. You're selling it! Speaking of interesting, remember when I was working in Seoul? Honestly, the administrative hoops you had to jump through… it was ridiculous. Trying to get a simple document approved took weeks. Was it really that bad, Dad? Bad doesn't even cover it. It was like navigating a labyrinth designed by someone who specifically  didn't  want you to reach the end. And the paperwork! Mountains of it. At least the food was good. I remember you coming back with all those stories. It sounds like a completely different world. Did it make you appreciate the relative efficiency of British bureaucracy more?

Right then, look at this. Found this tucked away in the box of family paraphernalia. Remember this trip to Norfolk Broads? Must have been… what, ten years ago? Oh my goodness! Where did you find that? And yes, I absolutely remember! We rented that ridiculously tiny boat, didn’t we? The 'Seabreeze’ or something equally unimaginative. ‘Seafarer’s Dream,’ I think it was called. More like ‘Seafarer’s Nightmare’ given my navigational skills. See, that's you, attempting to steer while I’m trying to fish. And failing miserably at both, naturally. Failing gloriously! You spent more time accidentally steering into reeds than you did actually casting a line. I think we mainly just annoyed the local wildlife. Precisely! Although, speaking of wildlife... Here’s a good one. Badgers! Remember that evening, trying to spot them? Oh, yes! That was incredible. We sat out in the dark for hours, didn't we? Freezing cold, covered in midges, and finally,  finally , saw a whole family waddling about. They were far more graceful than I was attempting to be, crouching behind that ridiculous bush. I’m fairly certain I scared them off at least three times. I felt like a clumsy, oversized spy. You were a sight! We need to do that again, somewhere else. Somewhere with slightly fewer reeds and slightly less clumsy editors lurking about. Agreed. It reminds me, I was reading an article the other day about some amazing photographic opportunities in Hokkaido, Japan. Apparently, they have these incredible wildlife parks, specifically for badger photography. Hokkaido? Seriously? That sounds… incredible. I’d love to go to Japan. Always have. The culture, the food, the landscapes… it's just so different. Are you suggesting a trip? I am, actually. A rather ambitious suggestion, I admit. But it got me thinking. We've been talking about doing something big for a while now. And, you know, photography is a shared passion. Imagine the photos we could get! Oh my gosh, that  is  a big suggestion! But… Wow. Badger photography in Japan. That’s… amazing. What's the best time of year to go, do you think? And are the badgers particularly photogenic? Apparently Spring is best, for the cherry blossoms  and  badger activity. They say the Hokkaido badgers are a slightly different subspecies, too. Bigger, bolder. More photogenic, hopefully! I’ll do some proper research. Research sounds good! Do you think we’d need special equipment?

Right, so, skinny dipping in Ireland. Seriously, Liam? You didn’t tell us this earlier! Well, it wasn't exactly a highlight reel moment, you know? And I didn’t want to, like, bore everyone. Bore us?
