And the curriculum, as it stands, doesn't always encourage that. It's just a relentless march through timelines. I mean, my nephew's struggling with the Tudors, and it's because he's just memorising Henry VIII’s wives – he doesn't grasp the religious and political context. It's a problem, isn’t it? And it's not just history. The national curriculum feels so…rigid. Designed more for easy assessment than for fostering genuine curiosity. I worry about my Year 9s. They’re intelligent kids, but they’re being reduced to ticking boxes. Assessment. Always assessment. When I was at school…well, it was a different world. Exams were important, of course, but there was more room for...exploration. Less pressure. We weren't obsessed with league tables and Ofsted reports. That’s what we need to fix. Industry experience needs to be integrated from the very beginning. Higher Education Degrees need to map directly to the skills companies are looking for.

Lovely furniture you’ve got here, Margaret. Very…eclectic. Where did you get that sideboard? It looks like something out of a Victorian manor. Oh, that? Found it at an auction, dear. Years ago, mind you. Cost me a pittance, really. Needed a bit of TLC, of course, but a good polish brings it right back. Your Dave got right stuck in with the beeswax, didn’t you, love? 'E did, didn’t 'e? Spent a whole afternoon on it. Said 'e needed a project. Always did like fixin' things. Not much call for it when you’re, well, not working, you see. Though, come to think of it, fixin' things is what I mostly did in them days, wasn’t it? Fixin' the wireless, fixin' the telly... You know, the quality of craftsmanship back then was just astonishing. You don’t see things built like that anymore. The drawers slide perfectly, the wood is solid... modern stuff just falls apart. I remember when I was setting up the business, sourcing decent joiners was a nightmare. Everyone was cutting corners. Absolutely. They’ve got no respect for materials these days. They use chipboard and laminate like it’s gold dust. Speaking of the old days, Margaret, you were telling me about your dad being in the ARP during the Blitz, weren't you? Oh yes. My father. A good man, he was. Always worrying. The ARP, as you know, Air Raid Precautions. He used to patrol the streets with his little lamp, checking for blackout. Said it were terrifying sometimes, the noise. The bombs falling… You could smell the smoke for miles. Blimey, yeah. I weren’t born ‘til a bit after then, o’ course, but me mum used to tell tales. Said the whole village felt like it was holdin’ its breath. They all huddled in the Anderson shelter she did. Course, Costessey weren't directly targeted, but… the fear, eh? That’s what got to people. It’s hard to imagine now, isn’t it? The scale of it. Thinking about the disruption, the rationing... It shaped a generation, you know. Changed everything. We were so fortunate, weren't we, to have grown up in relative peace afterward. Though, of course, there’s been other conflicts since. Indeed. Russia’s stirring up trouble again, aren’t they? It’s a worrying state of affairs. It’s not like the old days, mind you.

Right, so, Northamptonshire. Feels… final, doesn't it? Like the last leg of a really long journey. Final is a bit dramatic, lad. You’re not emigrating to Mars, are you? Just moving a bit further out. Less Bedford, more… countryside. Good for you, really. More space. I know, I know. Just… saying goodbye to Mum’s. Feels strange. All those Christmases, birthdays… even the really awkward teenage years. Awkward teenage years are a universal constant, aren't they? Remind me of one of those sometime. Though, knowing you, it’ll probably involve a questionable haircut and a very intense interest in obscure indie bands. Very funny. And you were a saint through the whole Duran Duran phase, Dad. Really. Someone had to be. Your mother was convinced they were a menace to society. Still is, probably. So, you’ve sorted out the removal company then? They’re coming on Tuesday, right? Yeah, Tuesday's the day. They confirmed this morning. It’s a bit of a chunk of money, to be honest. More than I anticipated. Mortgages are the bane of everyone’s existence, aren’t they? Remember when I was trying to get on the ladder? Seems like a lifetime ago. The interest rates… they were ridiculous. At least yours are a bit lower now. Slightly. Still, it's tight. I'm hoping that bigger garden will be worth it. And the space for a study. Sarah’s been asking about having a dog too. A dog! You realize that means more walks, right? More early mornings, muddy paws... I know, I know. But she’s been wanting one for ages. Besides, a little fresh air would do us both good. How’s your knee feeling today? You were limping a bit last week. It’s… manageable. The doc says it’s just wear and tear. Nothing a bit of rest and some of those heat packs won't fix. These customer service shifts are hardly helping though, all that standing. Still, need to keep earning, don't I? Pension looming and all that. Don’t think about the pension just yet! You’ve still got plenty of useful years left. By the way, Aunt Carol called yesterday. She's sending her best wishes for the move. And she asked if you remembered that disastrous holiday to Cornwall when you were a kid? Oh, God. Don’t remind me!

Right, so we’ve got fifteen people confirmed for Sunday. Fifteen! That's a proper gathering. Are you absolutely sure Gran will be up for it, love? It's a lot for her. Yeah, she seems alright this week, actually. Bit forgetful, obviously, but she definitely perked up when I mentioned the cake. Said she was hoping for lemon drizzle, like her mum used to make. Lemon drizzle it is then. I can whip one up. Though, I was thinking maybe a couple of other desserts too? Something a little lighter? These southern portions are substantial, and some of the older crowd might not want to face a huge slice. Good shout. Maybe those little cheesecakes you made last Christmas? Everyone loved those. And some fruit salad? We could make it fancy with some mint and a drizzle of honey. Perfect. Okay, food sorted-ish. Table plan is proving trickier than I thought. Aunt Carol and Uncle Derek absolutely cannot sit next to each other - you remember the debacle at Christmas? Oh god, don't remind me! The passive-aggressive comments about Derek’s gardening...it was excruciating. We absolutely need to separate them. I’m thinking gran at the head of the table, naturally. Then Mum and Dad next to her. Yes, sensible. And we need to keep Sarah and Mark away from Uncle George; he’ll just interrogate them about having children again. Honestly, the man needs a hobby. I’m starting to think rearranging the cupboards at my office is more relaxing than dealing with family dynamics. Tell me about it! So, what about the fish? Are we doing that smoked salmon platter you always do? Gran loves that with the cream cheese and cucumber. Yes, definitely. I need to order it from that fishmonger on the high street – the one with the really fresh stuff. Remember last year when I got that dodgy cod from the supermarket? Disaster! Gran nearly sent it back. Oh yeah, that was awful. You had to sneak it into the bin when she wasn’t looking. Did you get any candles yet? We want it to feel nice and festive, you know? Not just a big, noisy dinner. I was thinking those scented ones, the vanilla and cinnamon ones. Quite subtle, not overpowering. I can grab them on the way home from work tomorrow. I also need to think about flowers.

Right, well, that’s been a right laugh, hasn't it? This whole wisdom teeth extraction thing. I feel like a blowfish. You do look a bit swollen, yeah. But seriously, are you okay? You kept trying to talk with your mouth full of gauze earlier. It was…a sight. Aye, I was. It's just… sore. Really sore. And I can’t feel anything on the left side of my face. It’s spooky, like. I keep reachin’ up to scratch me cheek and it’s just... numb. Not the best way to navigate the Louvre, let me tell you. I know, it's bizarre. But it  will  go down, promise. Remember when I had to have my tonsils out when I was like, eight? Felt like half my face was missing for days. This just feels like a slightly less dramatic version. Eight?! You were a tiny thing! I'm practically an adult here, and I feel like a right mess. Want a biscuit? They’ve got some reet good pain au chocolat here. Though I’m not sure how well I’ll manage it. Trying to eat with that face would be hilarious. No thanks, I’m good. So, on a completely different note, have you heard anything from your mum about the house? Are they finally sorting it out? Nah, not really. She says Dad's being "difficult" as usual. Apparently, he's gotten obsessed with getting the garden leveled before they even  think  about putting the house on the market. Honestly, the man’s got priorities seriously skewed. What about your folks? Are they moving? Everything’s a right upheaval, innit? They're trying, but Cambridge is so ridiculously expensive. My dad's been looking at places a bit further out, near Ely. Apparently, there’s a lovely little cottage they've seen, but it needs some serious work. Lots of holes, apparently. Literally. Structural ones. Holes?! Like, 'falling down' sort of holes or cosmetic holes? Because there’s a big difference, pet. Cosmetic holes can be patched up with some clever paintwork. The other kind is a nightmare. The serious kind, I think. My mum was saying something about needing to reinforce the foundations. It's a bit daunting, actually. It makes me think about all the things that need fixing, you know? Teeth, houses…life in general. Aye, I get that. It’s just… constant, isn’t it?

Right, I’ve nearly finished these lactose-free cookies. Honestly, finding decent recipes is a nightmare! Anyone want a taste test? Me! Me! Are they chocolatey? They should be, darling. I’ve added extra cocoa. Leo, you want one too? Can I use these for money? Use  chess pieces  for money? Leo, where did you get that idea? Benji at school said he swapped a rook for a packet of crisps. A  rook ! A rook! That's silly! It  is  silly, sweetie. Those are just toys. They're not real money. Though, thinking about it… Dad  does  have a lot of them. Maybe we could use them for a game, instead? A fancy game of shops? Can I be the banker? Of course, you can be the banker! Now, about those acts of kindness… remember we were talking about it? Chinese New Year’s coming up, it’s a good time to spread a bit of cheer. Like giving presents! Giving presents is lovely, but let's think of some little things we can do that don’t cost anything. Something extra special. Can I give Mrs. Higgins a drawing? She likes my dragons. That’s absolutely brilliant, Leo! She’d love that. What about you, sweetheart? Any ideas? Hmmm… I could help Mummy tidy up my toys! That would be wonderful, love! A huge help, actually. See, simple things can make a big difference. I was thinking, maybe we could bake some extra cookies and leave a plate on the doorstep of the elderly couple down the road. They live alone. Will they like my dragons too? They might! It’s a lovely thought, darling. And speaking of Chinese New Year, I was thinking of getting some temporary hair dye! Ooh! Can I have some? Purple! Purple hair! We'll see, sweetheart, we'll see. I was thinking maybe a bit of red or gold, to celebrate. It would be fun! Although, your dad might have something to say about it... Can we have fireworks? Well, not  real  fireworks, love. We can get some sparklers, maybe. Your dad needs to check it’s safe first. But we can definitely do something festive. And maybe… just maybe… Leo, if you’re very, very good at being the banker in our game, you can pick the colour of my temporary hair! Deal! I’ll be a super banker! Purple! Purple for Mummy!

Honestly, Mum, school's just… draining. Mrs. Davies is making us analyse  Alice in Wonderland  for English, and I just don't  get  it. Everything's so weird! It  is  a bit strange, isn’t it? But that’s the point, darling. It’s supposed to make you think. What’s bothering you specifically? The Mad Hatter's tea party? The Queen of Hearts? The whole thing really! All the riddles are nonsense and… and I keep thinking about that photo I saw online of a girl with a scar on her cheek. It just reminded me a bit of the Cheshire Cat vanishing, like… a missing piece. A scar can definitely feel like a missing piece sometimes. I have a few myself, you know. Remember when I fell out of the apple tree as a kid? Left a little one on my knee, mostly faded now. You’d probably barely notice it. Really? I didn’t even know! You never tell me these things. Do they hurt? Not anymore. Just a memory attached to it. It reminds me of warm summer days and being a reckless little thing. What about the girl online? Did you look into what happened to her? Not really. I got distracted. I was looking at costume designs for that theatre group in town. They're doing  A Midsummer Night’s Dream . I think I want to audition for a fairy. I was looking at these incredible winged costumes… and then I remembered the scar photo. It’s all sort of interlinked in my brain somehow. That’s quite a creative connection you're making. It's lovely to hear you're interested in theatre. Did you hear back about that music competition you entered? Yes! I got through to the next round! I have to perform in front of a proper panel of judges next week. I’m so nervous, but also really excited. I'm playing that Debussy piece, "Clair de Lune." "Clair de Lune!" Oh, darling, that's beautiful. You'll be wonderful. You've practiced so hard. It's just lovely to see you putting yourself out there. That’s more important than winning, though, isn’t it? Just enjoying the experience. I suppose so. It's just... I saw online that one of the judges used to be a famous concert pianist. Loads of people are saying he's really harsh.

Honestly, Bernard, that meeting with the Lower Bramble group last night left me quite drained. They’re so… earnest, you know? And utterly terrified of these solar farms swallowing up their fields. I felt rather like a seasoned general advising a fresh batch of recruits. I know the feeling, Eleanor. It’s incredibly frustrating seeing people so overwhelmed. It's not just about the aesthetics, is it? It’s the loss of landscape, the disruption to wildlife, and the creeping feeling of powerlessness. You were right to emphasise the need for detailed research, though. They need concrete arguments. Concrete arguments are the currency of these battles, aren’t they? Back in my day, dealing with boardroom mergers, it was all spreadsheets and projections. These lot, they need data points too, just… different ones. Did you mention the impact on property values, Eleanor? That usually gets people’s attention. I did, yes. Highlighted the potential depreciation, showed them some examples from similar cases. But it's more than that, isn't it, Arthur? It’s the principle. These developers promise the world – green energy, jobs for the community – but it rarely materialises. It’s all about maximizing profit, and the local community is collateral damage. Precisely. And the council… well, let’s just say the Development Control Committee has a rather cozy relationship with some of these companies, doesn't it? It wouldn't surprise me if there's some quiet lobbying going on. Councils are a complicated beast. You need to understand who's influencing whom. And don’t underestimate the role of local planners. They can be genuinely helpful, or completely beholden to their superiors. This reminds me - I remember a planning appeal in the Peak District decades ago... the local authority had been swayed by the promise of increased tourist revenue. It took a prolonged legal challenge to expose their flawed reasoning. A legal challenge! Goodness, I hope the Lower Bramble group hasn't reached that stage. It’s so costly and emotionally taxing. We need to focus on the evidence first. Arthur, you've got a background in company strategy; any thoughts on a more… proactive approach? Beyond just objecting to each application? Well, you need to disrupt the narrative. Show them that there are alternatives. Efficient energy storage, for example. Tidal power, geothermal… things that don't rely on sprawling, visually intrusive structures. But the problem is the research.

Right, so, Dad, we need to really nail down this driving situation. I've had my first lesson, and… well, it was  an experience . An experience, eh? Like what sort of experience, love? Don't tell me you stalled it three times in front of the instructor! That would be just like your Uncle Barry. He practically welded a clutch to the floor in his day. Not  quite  three times, but it wasn’t exactly graceful. Parallel parking was… a challenge. Think of trying to fit a hippo into a postage stamp. A hippo, really, Anna? You’re making it sound like a disaster. Remember when I first started driving? I reversed into a lamppost on my first drive! Everyone in the street saw. Mortifying. See, Mom! That’s precisely what I'm worried about! Although, a lamppost is slightly less traumatic than ending up in a ditch. So, about insurance… Clive from the driving school said it’s going to be eye-watering. It is, I’m afraid. Young drivers, practically bleed money these days. Have you looked at comparison websites, Anna? Being careful and doing a bit of shopping around can save you a pretty penny. I’ve had a quick look, but it's so confusing! There’s comprehensive, third party, black box… it's a minefield. And the excess! It's like they  want  you to crash. Black box insurance might be a good idea for you, love. It monitors your driving - how hard you brake, your speed, the times you drive. If you drive safely, you pay less. It’s a sensible thing to consider. Margaret’s right. It's a good way to prove you’re a responsible driver. I remember when your Gran got a black box… she was furious at first, thought it was spying on her! But it ended up saving her loads. Okay, I’ll look into it further. Right, changing tack completely – holiday plans! I finally booked flights to Rome! We're going for a week in September. Rome! Wonderful, dear! You’ve always wanted to go. Have you booked accommodation yet? Don't leave it too late, prices go up. Managed to snag a little apartment near the Pantheon. Apparently, it's got a gorgeous rooftop terrace. I'm so excited! It’s been ages since I’ve had a proper holiday. Rome, eh? All those ruins... you'll be walking miles!

Honestly, Dad, this parking in Brighton is just ridiculous. I circled for twenty minutes this morning just to find a space wide enough for my little Fiesta! And then it was double yellow lines! Twenty minutes, eh? Back in my day, in London, you could park anywhere, practically. Of course, there weren’t as many cars then. Remember the fifties? A Morris Minor was a luxury. You’d find a space on the street no problem. Things were… well, simpler. Simpler for you maybe! I'm trying to balance uni, lectures, my part-time job at the cafe, and finding somewhere affordable to live. Parking is the least of my worries, but it’s just another stressful thing. I'm thinking of just getting rid of the car, you know? Invest in a decent bike. A bike? Now, that's sensible. But Brighton's hilly, isn’t it? You’ll be fit as a fiddle though, lass. Still, a car’s handy. Reminds me of when I used to follow the races. Used to drive all over the place, chasing good tips. Remember that horse, "Lightning Flash”? Brilliant horse! Dad, please. Not the horse racing again. I appreciate the memories, but I'm trying to eat my sandwich. By the way, this is lovely. You’re getting better at this shepherd’s pie thing, you know. Used to be a bit… dry. It's all the clever recipes you showed me last Christmas. You're a good cook, you are. It’s important to learn, you know. Feeding children, feeding a family...it's a responsibility. Back then, you had to make do with what you had. Everything was about stretching meals. You wouldn't find all this fancy 'healthy eating' stuff. Well, times have changed, haven't they? I'm trying to eat more healthily, and it's tough when you're on a student budget. I saw a report the other day about the rise in people using food banks. It’s shocking, really. Awful, it is. Makes you think, doesn't it? Politicians all talking, but not doing enough. They didn't help me, not when I needed it most. Never understood why things had to be so difficult. Always chasing, always struggling. It's survival, innit? Exactly! And the system… it’s ridiculous. I know someone who’s been trying to get disability benefits for years, jumping through hoops.

...and then Mr. Davies, bless his cotton socks, actually  punched  his putter into the ground. Full-on, theatrical rage. He blamed the divot. Said the divot was conspiring against him. No way! Mr. Davies? The quiet accountant who wears beige? That’s incredible. You’re telling me he’s got a hidden golfing temper? Apparently. It only comes out under pressure. It was classic. We were all trying to keep a straight face. I think poor Emily nearly choked on her scone. Emily’s a legend though, isn't she? Remember when she tried to quote Shakespeare in response to someone asking her if she wanted sugar in her tea? "To sugar or not to sugar, that is the question!" Absolutely brilliant. She just delivered it deadpan too, which made it even better. She’s a natural at sarcasm. I swear, the woman could weaponize a raised eyebrow. She could. My grandma's got a similar skill. It's a Northern thing, I reckon. Bit of dry wit, a lot of unspoken judgment. She once told my cousin Mark he looked 'respectable' after he’d spent the entire day covered in paint trying to fix the shed roof. Oh, that’s ruthless! Reminds me of my uncle Bernard. He's always got a cutting remark ready. It’s part of his charm, really. Though, goodness knows why anyone bothers trying to teach him to play golf. It's rather painful to watch. It's the competitive spirit, I think. People get weird when they feel like they need to 'win'. I was thinking about that the other day, actually, about learning a new skill. Do you ever feel like you're just…flailing for a while? Like, I’ve been trying to learn basic coding, and it’s mostly just error messages and a creeping sense of inadequacy. Totally. I'm the same with Italian. I bought a Duolingo course, did it religiously for a week…and now I just know how to say "the cat is on the table." Useful for absolutely nothing. It’s humbling, isn't it? I think some people just have that innate talent, that ability to pick things up effortlessly. That’s what it feels like. Like some people are just born ‘winning’ at everything. Though, thinking about it, even Mr. Davies' exploding rage probably means he’s ‘winning’ at being outrageously dramatic. You've got a point.

Honestly, this production schedule is going to be the death of me. We’re chasing our own tails, and the client keeps changing their mind. It's a constant fire-fighting exercise. Sounds rough, Chloe. At least you've got a proper job, innit? Me, I'm still laying bricks. Beautiful, sturdy bricks, mind you. But bricks nonetheless. The weather's been awful too, rain every other day. My back’s killing me. Aye, laying bricks is honest work, Liam! Don't go knocking it. At least you're building somethin' proper. I spend my days organising spreadsheets and makin’ sure people have enough biscuits. It's glamorous, I tell you. Absolutely glamorous. This conference next month... I swear, if one more person asks for gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, sugar-free  everything , I'm going to lose it. Oh, I feel your pain, Maisie. Client demands are relentless. They want precision and perfection, but can’t articulate what either of those things even  mean . You’d think they’d be grateful for someone keeping things running. So, Maisie, what's this conference about then? Fancy stuff, like tech, or…? It’s a sustainable farming conference. Bunch of farmers, agriculturalists, policy people… Basically, a lot of serious people talking about very important things. And needing a mountain of vegan-friendly canapés. I’m having to source everything. It’s a nightmare findin’ decent Yorkshire cheeses that fit the bill, let me tell you! Sustainable farming! Seriously? That’s a niche market. Don’t they all just want proper bacon sandwiches though? You’d think so, wouldn’t ya? But no. Apparently, bacon is…problematic. Footprint-wise. The irony isn't lost on me. Right. Well, I'm problematic in a different way. My diet consists primarily of pasties and strong tea. Don't judge. It fuels the brick-laying. You're a case study, Liam. A perfect example of a hardworking man’s diet. Honestly, I've been trying to be good. This whole 'clean eating' thing. It's exhausting. Clean eating? I tried that for a week. Ended up eating a bowl of peas and crying. Give me a bag of chips any day. Do you ever actually  enjoy  your food, Chloe? Enjoyment is a luxury I can’t afford, Maisie. I'm trying to fit into my old jeans. They’re mocking me from the back of my wardrobe.

Right then, Doris, can you see this lot? Bit overgrown, I'm afraid. The bamboo's gone absolutely mad this year. It's takin’ over the whole back fence. Aye, looks it, Arthur! You've got a jungle back there. Costessey always did have a bit more greenery than Norwich, but that's somethin' else. You been neglectin’ it, 'ave you? Neglectin’? Now, don't start, Doris! I’ve been busy. Been tryin’ to get that owl box sorted, but the wood’s been a bit damp. And the neighbours… they’ve started puttin' up new fencing, haven't they? Right on the boundary. Hello, you two! Oh, Arthur, your garden is  gorgeous ! A little wild, perhaps, but gorgeous. And yes, I can see the fencing, Arthur. Sheila from next door was complaining about it earlier. Said it was higher than it should be. Honestly, people. Sheila complains about everything, doesn’t she? Always has. She’s probably got her binoculars trained on my bamboo. I said I'd look into it, but...well, you know. Things. Speaking of lookin'… did you see the eclipse yesterday? Truly remarkable. All those cosmic things… I did! Just a peek, mind you. My eyesight's not what it used to be. Still, quite clever, innit? All that star dust comin' together. Makes you think, doesn’t it? About the beginnin’s of space... It was breathtaking, Harold. To think of black holes, and the scale of the universe... it’s astonishing. I was watching that painting programme on telly last night, and the artist was talking about how he tries to capture the vastness of the cosmos on canvas. A rather ambitious project. Aye, ambitious is right. Though, I'd rather be lookin’ at somethin’ a bit more concrete than the cosmos. Like...should we be worried about this TV Licence thing? They're gettin' stricter, aren't they? Worried? Just gotta keep our noses clean, Arthur. Don’t go watchin’ anything you shouldn’t! Although, I did catch a bit of that cooking show… you know, the one with the posh bloke. Harold! You shouldn’t! You know we’re trying to be more… politically correct about these things. Anyway, it’s more important to be eating well. I made a lovely lentil soup today. You need to try it, Arthur. It's full of goodness. Lentil soup, eh? Not really my cup of tea, Doris.

Honestly, this roundabout is giving me the willies. Three lanes, and nobody knows what they're doing! It's like a chaotic ballet of stressed-out drivers. You always exaggerate, Liv. It's just a standard, if slightly complicated, roundabout. Happens everywhere. Relax. We’re getting closer to York. Relax? Easy for you to say, Mr. Consultant Engineer, master of efficiency and order! I'm a girl from Sunderland, love. Chaos is practically in my blood. Yorkshire and Sunderland ain't far removed from each other, mind you - a bit of grit and a healthy dose of frustration are common factors. Point taken. Still, you've managed to navigate some pretty dodgy roads in Sunderland, haven’t you? Remember that time we got lost trying to find that chip shop near Seaburn? Oh, don’t remind me! Ended up on a dirt track that smelled suspiciously of seaweed and regret. At least the chips were good when we finally found it. So, York... Where are we actually  going ? You’ve been awfully vague. I thought I mentioned it? We’re aiming for Skosh. Apparently, their tasting menu is incredible. Small plates, inventive flavours... Apparently booked solid weeks in advance, but I managed to snag a table. Skosh? Sounds fancy. Proper posh, even for you. I’m more of a curry and a pint kinda lass, to be honest. There's a brilliant Indian place back home, 'Bombay Breeze', best biryani you'll ever taste. Not that I'm saying York can't have good food, just... different priorities, you know? It’s not  that  posh, Liv. It’s just well-regarded. And I thought a change would be nice. Besides, I promised to take you somewhere special. Remember how you said you wanted to see York Minster? Aye, I did. That's a proper cathedral, that is. Bigger than Durham, I reckon? Definitely. It’s stunning. We could go tomorrow morning. It's practically unavoidable; it dominates the skyline. Though, finding parking near the Minster... now  that  will be a challenge. Almost as challenging as this roundabout! Honestly, you'd think they'd put a park-and-ride in, just for the tourists. They charge a fortune for parking anyway. Back in Sunderland, you could Park right outside the shops for a couple of quid. You know, when we were looking at houses last year, I almost applied for a job in York.

Honestly, Brenda, this Earl Grey’s a bit weak. Needs a good dunking of Yorkshire Gold, that’s what it needs! Still, better than nothing, eh? Lovely scrambled eggs though, Anon really does know how to start a Saturday. You and your Yorkshire Gold, Margaret! I’ve tried it, you know. Just…too strong for me at breakfast. Chester folk aren’t cut from the same cloth, I suppose. But yes, these are lovely. Did you hear that robin outside just now? Glorious. Aye, lovely bit o’ birdsong. I was trying to work out what it was. Not the usual chirpy chap, this one. Bit lower, more…melancholy, almost. Could be a blackbird, I reckon. You know more about these things than I do. Could be. Hard to tell without seeing them, isn't it? I’ve been trying to get better at identifying the different calls. It’s a little hobby, keeps the brain ticking over. Speaking of ticking…my alarm clock went off at 4:30 this morning. Absolutely dreadful! Woke me right up. I dreamed I was being chased by a giant cuckoo clock. Silly, really. A giant cuckoo clock! Now there’s a dream! Mine’s always either I’m late for a lecture – even though I retired five years ago! – or I'm trying to herd rogue sheep. Oh, you and your lectures. Still, I bet you miss it a bit. All those bright young minds… A wee bit, aye. But mostly I miss the free coffee. And not having to mark essays! Been trying to get the garden looking half decent this year, you know. Planted some sunflowers. Hoping to attract the birds. Got a new feeder for the finches, too. That’s lovely, Margaret. I’m trying to get a decent patch of lavender going. Apparently, the bees adore it. Though, you know, I'm a bit worried about the bees lately. Fewer and fewer about. Aye, it's a worry, that is. Speaking of worries… I had a bit of a squall at the dentist yesterday. Dreadful feeling. Oh, dear! What happened? Just a cleaning, but I had a nosebleed during it. Right in the middle of the hygienist's spiel about flossing. Mortifying! Made me feel like an old woman. Oh, Margaret, don’t say that! We  are  old women! There’s no shame in it. Nosebleeds happen, especially with dry air. My Elsie – you remember Elsie, from the language school?

Honestly, Sarah, it’s lovely to finally sit down with you. It feels like ages! Last time we properly chatted, I was still battling with Year 10s and you were… navigating mountains of paperwork, as usual. You’re not wrong! Paperwork is a constant. But yes, it  is  lovely to see you too, Eleanor. Cambridge is a treat, isn’t it? Much nicer than the council office, that's for sure. I needed this. Absolutely. So, tell me everything. I heard through the grapevine… things have changed quite a bit for you? They have. Quite dramatically, actually. Remember how I was always saying I wanted to do something completely different? Well, I finally did it. I left social work. No! Seriously? Wow. I can barely imagine. What made you finally take the plunge? It seemed like such a huge part of your life. It  was  a huge part of my life. And a rewarding one, don't get me wrong. But the burnout was real, Eleanor. So, so real. The constant exposure to trauma… it takes a toll. And I realised I needed something more… nurturing. I’m now running a small yoga studio just outside of town. That’s incredible! That suits you, though, doesn't it? You’ve always been so calm and centred. Did you do a full yoga teacher training? I did. Intensive, but brilliant. It's completely transformed my own mental health, and it's wonderful to be able to share that with others. It's early days, but it’s thriving. What about you? Still battling the teenagers? They're a force of nature, let me tell you. But yes, still teaching. I'm actually considering doing something different myself, actually. I've started writing. Writing? Really? What kind of writing? A children’s book, actually. It’s a bit silly, about a badger who learns to bake. I’ve finished a first draft, which is terrifying. That’s amazing, Eleanor! You always were creative. You should be proud of yourself. It must be wonderful to pursue something so personal. It’s just… daunting, isn’t it? Putting yourself out there like that? Absolutely. It's terrifying. Speaking of daunting, I heard about… well, I heard you had some news regarding… family expansion? Yes. It's… complicated. After years of trying naturally, and a couple of unsuccessful rounds of IVF, I decided to go it alone.

This is lovely, Anon. You’ve really made this place your own. Much nicer than that student flat I had in Bristol, believe me. Cramped doesn’t even begin to cover it. Aye, student flats. I remember my daughter lived in one down in Exeter. Said it was like living in a shoebox. Glad you approve though, love. Anon always had a good eye for decorating. It’s more than approved – it’s welcoming. Speaking of Bristol, I'm teaching a class there soon, going back for a weekend workshop. It’s on adapting language teaching for neurodivergent learners. Quite fascinating, really. Neurodivergent, eh? Sounds a bit… modern. When I was teaching, we just called them ‘challenging’ and hoped for the best! Didn’t have half the understanding we do now. Used to use a lot of repetition, that was my go-to. Did wonders for some of them, not so much for others, naturally. You a teacher yourself, then? I am! I teach modern languages – Spanish and French mostly. It’s rewarding, but the paperwork! Don't even get me started. How are you finding retirement, Anon’s Dad? I know you were a teacher too, weren’t you? Retirement's... a thing. Peaceful, definitely. But sometimes it feels like I'm just… existing. Teaching was my whole life for so long. Miss having those little faces looking up to you, eh? Miss the chaos, even. Though the marking… good riddance to that. I can imagine. It's strange, isn't it, how much you miss the routine sometimes? My mum always says I’ll miss the ‘buzz’ when I eventually retire. She’s a keen gardener, you know, always bustling around. Keeps her young. What do you do to keep busy these days? Gardening's a bit beyond me now, the knees aren’t what they used to be. I tinker about with old radios, mostly. Got a whole collection of them crammed in the shed. And I do a bit of volunteering at the local library, helping with the computers. Not quite the same as wrangling thirty teenagers, though! Have you heard about all the trouble they've had down on the High Street lately? Another robbery, apparently. Oh, really? That’s awful! I read something about it online. It's worrying, isn’t it? Seems like things are getting worse everywhere. The news is just non-stop bad.

Right, okay, so I'm officially baffled. Liam, you said you were attempting to make a Yorkshire pudding…with  marmalade ? Aye, well, it were a challenge, weren't it? Aunt Elsie sent me a recipe, said it were a family secret. Didn't say nowt about, like, proper gravy. Just… fruity. Liam, honestly! That’s…novel. I’m pretty sure Yorkshire puddings were  invented  to soak up gravy. I’m making a proper Sunday roast here, though. Chicken, roast potatoes, all the works. You lot hungry? Hungry doesn't even cover it. The week’s been brutal. That new bridge design is giving me grey hairs, I swear. Marmalade Yorkshire pudding sounds... adventurous. I'm intrigued, actually. Adventurous bordering on sacrilegious, Matthew! You're a civil engineer, you understand the importance of structural integrity and tradition. This is like building a bridge out of jelly. It weren’t  that  bad! It were a bit… sticky, mind. And the flavour was… unique. I think I'd stick to gravy next time, though. What sort are you doing, Anya? Proper gravy, Liam. Chicken stock, red wine, a bit of flour… the whole shebang. It’ll be good and rich. By the way, did you hear that The National are touring again? Seriously?! No way! When? Where? I’ve been waiting for them to announce something for ages. Oh, brilliant! I’d be up for that. Though, my ticket-buying skills are notoriously rubbish. Last time I tried for Radiohead, I ended up with seats three rows from the back. Don’t worry, I’ll take charge. I’m fairly ruthless when it comes to securing tickets. Are you both free next weekend? They've got a date in Manchester. Manchester's not too far. I could get a train. That’d be reet good, that. What about you, Matthew? Manchester works for me. Though, I might need to check if the structural integrity of my bridge project is holding up without my constant supervision. Always thinking about bridges, aren't you? Anya, should we put some music on? Something to drown out the potential marmalade-induced trauma Liam’s endured. Good idea. Let's put on some Phoebe Bridgers. It’s a bit melancholic, but it fits the Cambridge vibe, doesn’t it? And it’s a nice change from the... intensity of your construction updates, Matthew. Hey! It’s vital work! People need bridges!

Honestly, this Cambridge drizzle is relentless. I thought moving south meant sunshine! You've been here all of two weeks, Liv. Give it a chance. It’s not  always  like this. Remember that brief, glorious spell we had last month? A brief spell that felt like five minutes! I’m still clinging to the memory of picnics in Grantchester Meadows. Speaking of which, I’m thinking of dragging the kids to the gym this weekend. Little Leo is bouncing off the walls and needs to expend some energy. Gym? Seriously, El? They’re six and eight. They'll be climbing the monkey bars, not lifting weights. It’s not about weights, Dan. Just a bit of structured play, some trampolining. Anything to burn off the sugar rush from last night’s pizza party. They’re already obsessed with watching those fitness influencers online! Influencers? Oh, my god. So, are you finally joining one of those fancy studios then, Ellie? The ones with the dangling silks and the pulsing lights? Maybe! I was looking at that new one, "Flow State," near the market. It’s a bit pricey, but apparently the classes are amazing. Plus, it has a creche. Crucial, obviously. What about you, Tom? Still sticking to the university sports hall? Yep. It's functional, it's cheap, and it's close to work. Though I’m tempted to branch out. I keep hearing good things about "Ironclad" down by the river. The atmosphere seems pretty intense though. All grunts and protein shakes. Not exactly my vibe. Ironclad  is  intense. My mate goes there. He's practically living off creatine at this point. It’s all about optimization for him. Speaking of optimisation... I got a new build coming. The graphics card alone cost more than my entire last holiday. Don't even start with the tech, Dan! My brain hurts just listening. I’m dreaming of a holiday, actually. I’ve been looking at Portugal. Algarve maybe? Somewhere with sun, sand, and reliable Wi-Fi, naturally. Portugal sounds wonderful! We were thinking of Spain next year. Little Maya keeps asking about flamenco dancers. Though bearing in mind camp applications open next week, that might be a pipe dream. Kids' camp? Which one are you looking at? Camp Willowbrook. It’s a week of outdoor adventures – hiking, archery, pond dipping. Apparently, it's brilliant for building confidence. Leo’s been a bit… hesitant lately.

Oh, come  on ! That was a clear foul! Honestly, ref's having a blinder tonight, isn't he? Just a bit eager, love. They've both gone in for the ball. Happens all the time in games like this. Calm down, Maisie. It’s only the 68th minute. Easy for you to say, you're probably studying the physics of football tackles, aren't you? It's not  only  the ball, David. Look at the angle of his leg! He practically took him out! I swear, some refs think they're doing the players a favour allowing all this rough stuff. Always dramatic, aren't you? You know I’m working on particle collisions, not football tactics. Though, I suppose, trajectories and impact forces  are  somewhat related. Still, just let them play. They’re fighting for it, that’s what matters. Oh, you and your science. It’s brilliant, honestly. How can you be so detached about this? It’s the Tyne and Wear derby! My mum’s practically gnawing her nails to the quick, I can feel it. Your mum’s perpetually stressed, Maisie. It’s not just the match. Look, they’re pressing now. See, they’re responding. This is good! Good for  who ? The other team getting a free shot right on our goal? They've got a goal kick... Right. Well. At least the snacks are good. Did you remember to get those chocolate eggs? Of course. Chocolate eggs are a vital part of the Easter viewing experience. I got the ones with the caramel birds – your favourite. And I made that lemon drizzle cake you like. It’s cooling on the counter. You did? You're a legend, you know you are. Seriously, you're far too good to me. I’m gonna have a slice of that after this, guaranteed. Right, focus. Back to the game. You're distracted already. And have you seen that film yet?  Dune: Part Two ? Everyone’s raving about it. Don't even start. I keep meaning to, but honestly, research reports, grant proposals, and now this constant football anxiety… there aren’t enough hours in the day! You keep going on about the cinematography and how breathtaking the desert landscapes are. It sounds amazing. It  is  amazing. The scale of it all. You’d love it. It's visually stunning, the story is captivating... promise me you’ll watch it this weekend?

Oh, look at this one, Liam! He was just a tiny little thing then, covered head-to-toe in glitter from that funfair in Weston-Super-Mare. Remember that, Michael? Aye, I do. He absolutely  loved  the carousel. Kept shouting, "Again, Daddy! Again!" He was never going to leave that place. That was just after his fifth birthday, wasn’t it? It was. And you insisted on getting him that ridiculous inflatable hammer. He swung it at everyone! Caused a bit of a stir, that boy. He did have a bit of a spirit, alright. A right scamp. It's hard to believe he's almost sixteen now. Look at him, barely taller than your knee! Such a wee bairn! He's a handsome young man now, isn't he? Reminds me a bit of his father when he was that age. Strong jawline. Always a sign of good stock. He does. He's playing rugby now, too. Absolutely obsessed. Speaking of things he’s obsessed with, have you seen the pictures from Iceland? He and his mates went for a few days after his exams. Iceland? Honestly, wasn't that a bit…expensive? I thought you were saving for his birthday trip to London. We are still doing the London trip! This was just a quick getaway with his friends. They saved up. Apparently, they saw the Northern Lights! And he climbed a glacier. I’m rather proud of him. A glacier! That’s a bit extreme for a holiday, isn’t it? Still, good on him for being adventurous. Did he send you proper pictures? Not just those blurry ones he usually takes. He did actually! Look at this one. The colours are incredible. Makes you want to go yourself. Though, I'm not sure I'm cut out for glaciers. I'd prefer a nice cup of tea and a biscuit. Aye, me too. Glaciers are no’ for the faint of heart! I remember when I took a school trip to Scotland…the highlands were breathtaking, mind you, but the wind nearly blew us all away. You always did choose the most dramatic excursions, didn't you, Agnes? Remember that time you took the kids to Alton Towers and got stuck on the Nemesis for three hours? Don’t remind me! The children were beside themselves. It was a whole ordeal. But they were alright in the end, weren’t they?

That was absolutely lovely, Margaret. You really do make the best roast. Honestly, I try, but it never quite reaches this level of…comfort. Oh, you’re being kind, love. It’s just a bit of practice, innit? Forty-odd years of Sunday roasts will do that to a woman! And you always were a bit fussy about gravy, weren't you, Eleanor? Fussy! I just prefer a slightly richer flavour, that’s all. It reminds me of my grandparents’ Sunday dinners. They always had a little something extra in the gravy, a secret ingredient. Never could figure out what it was. Must have been something magical. It was a touch of marmite, dear. Always a touch of marmite. Your Grandma Elsie swore by it. Said it just gave it a proper depth. Marmite?! Grandma Elsie? I’m utterly shocked. I always thought she hated it. She'd always make a face when someone mentioned it. Elsie was a clever one, she was. Liked to keep things close to her chest. Remember that time she pretended the prize marrow at the village show was hers when it really belonged to old Mr. Peterson? You're kidding! Honestly, Grandma Elsie was a legend. I completely forgot about that. It feels like a lifetime ago, doesn't it? Playing hopscotch on the pavement outside Elsie's. Do you remember those little plastic jacks, Margaret? The ones with the tiny metal balls? Oh, goodness yes! We'd spend hours with those. Got so good at ‘kitty’ we could practically do it with our eyes closed. You were always better than me, Eleanor. Always had a knack for it. And remember skipping ropes? We used to have challenges, see who could skip the longest. You were always tumbling over, weren't you, Margaret? Bless your heart. I used to watch you two from the window, giggling. Had a little wooden dollhouse myself, you know. Painted it all myself, with little curtains and tiny rugs. A dollhouse! I completely forgot you had one, Elsie. That's wonderful. I was jealous, I really was! I got a Paddington Bear, remember? He was my absolute favourite. So well-loved, he practically fell apart. Paddington! He was a proper darling. You carried him  everywhere . You used to narrate his adventures. Remember when you told everyone he’d helped you find your missing slipper in the garden? Oh, stop it!

Honestly, Arthur, you wouldn’t believe the kerfuffle down at the community centre today. Mrs. Higgins got into a right tizzy about the flower arranging competition. Flower arranging, eh? Always a bit of a drama, that. People get awfully precious about their petunias, don’t they? Costessey never had much in the way o' competitions, you know. Just the annual village fete, and that was mostly about who could grow the biggest marrow. This was worse, really. Apparently, Mildred Periwinkle accused Gladys of using 'store-bought' roses. Can you imagine? Gladys grows her own roses, Arthur! She practically lives in her garden all summer. Store-bought roses? Good heavens. What was Gladys supposed to do, prove where she bought 'em? Seems a bit daft, don't it? Back in my day, if someone accused you of somethin', you'd just tell them to get on with it. No need for all this fussin'. We didn’t have time for fussin’, not when you were tryin’ to, well,  be . Exactly! And Mrs. Higgins, the organiser, tried to mediate, bless her soul, but she just ended up getting flustered and spilling tea all down her apron. It was quite a spectacle. Honestly, these little village dramas, they're better than television sometimes. They are, aren’t they? Reminds me of a right old row we had at the fete one year. Old Mr. Pringle, he'd entered his prize-winning gooseberries. Thought he was a shoo-in. But young Timothy Brown, bless his cotton socks, he'd snuck in a whole tin of tinned gooseberries he’d got from his mum. No! You're joking! I wish I were. Caused an uproar, it did. Mr. Pringle nearly had a fit. Called young Timothy every name under the sun. But the judges, they tasted 'em both and said Timothy's were sweeter. "Science, Arthur," they said. "Modern techniques." Utter nonsense, o' course. Oh, Arthur, you have the most wonderful stories! Why haven’t I heard this gooseberry saga before? Probably because I’ve been saving it for a rainy day, like this. It’s good for a chuckle, innit? Life was simpler then, you know. Less… complicated. Fewer flower arranging competitions and tinned gooseberries replacing the honest stuff. It was. But even then, there were always little dramas, weren’t there? People always find something to get worked up about. Remember when Mrs. Gable accused me of letting my cat dig up her prize-winning begonias?

Honestly, this algorithm is driving me bonkers. Trying to write compelling copy for a new dog food brand, and all the keywords are just… blah. ‘Nutritious,’ ‘delicious,’ ‘happy dog’ – where’s the sparkle? Sounds like my Year 3s trying to write poetry. Endlessly “good, nice, pretty.” You need to find the weirdness, don't you? The unexpected. You two are always so clever with words. I’m barely keeping my head above water with phonics this week. Little Leo is  determined  that ‘igh’ only makes the ‘i’ sound. We’ve been going back and forth for twenty minutes. Oh, bless him! You know, Leo’s name reminded me – did you ever get around to getting him a Christmas present? I found this adorable little knitted reindeer on Etsy… Oh, crikey, I completely forgot about Christmas presents! It was all SATs prep and parent-teacher meetings. I feel awful. A knitted reindeer sounds perfect though, actually. Does it have a little hat? Everything has a little hat these days, doesn't it? My mum’s bought a miniature Santa hat for Barnaby. He’s not best pleased. Barnaby’s a menace, isn’t he? Still shredding the sofa? Even more so. He's developed a particular aversion to throw cushions. I swear, he's plotting against them. Dad’s threatening to rehome him, but Mum will have a meltdown. Rehoming a cat? That's harsh! Though I can imagine the sofa cushions are a source of constant stress. My flatmate used to have a parrot, called Captain Squawk. He’d learned to mimic the microwave beep perfectly, and then scream it at 3 am. Nightmare. Oh my goodness, that  is  a nightmare. I'd rather deal with a thousand ‘nutritious’ dog food keywords. Speaking of stressful, how's the car situation? Still limping along? Don't even get me started. Turns out it’s not just the exhaust; it’s something with the catalytic converter. Expensive. Really, really expensive. I’m seriously considering selling it and joining the cycling revolution. Though Bristol hills are not exactly friendly. Oh, that’s awful! I remember you saying it was rattling a few months ago. Did you get a quote? Last time I had to get my car fixed – ridiculous! They practically laughed at me. Honestly, the prices these days... Have you seen anywhere good for a decent quote? I've got a little Fiat, so maybe they'd be more reasonable.

…So, I’m telling you, Janice, the council really needs to do something about that overgrown ivy on the corner of Granby Street. It’s a safety hazard, and honestly, it looks a right mess! Gives the whole are a bit of a neglected feel, don’t you think?      Aye, Klaus, you're right about that. It's been like that for months. You'd think they'd sort it. This area... it’s changed a lot, hasn't it? Not entirely for the better, mind. Used to be a real community feel, you know?      It’s okay, I think. It’s getting a bit… gentrified, maybe? A few new cafes popping up.      Gentrified means people with fancy money move in, right? Like the bloke down the road who bought two houses and turned them into a hotel.      That’s a good way to put it, Liam. Very astute observation! See, Sarah? This is why we need to have clever young people like you around to keep us on our toes. Though I must say, that figurine is rather impressive. Are you a fan of Harry Potter?      Yeah! Massive. I'm re-reading the whole series. Hermione’s the best. She’s really smart.      You read a lot, do ya, lad? That’s good. My granddaughter, Chloe, she's glued to that TikTok, bless her heart. Doesn’t read a book in sight.      Chloe's about my age, isn't she? It’s just… there’s so much entertainment competing for attention. It's hard to find the time, you know? I'm working those extra shifts at the school, covering for someone who's on maternity leave. It’s tiring.      I can imagine, Sarah. That extra work can really drain you. I'm lecturing on Victorian literature at the moment. Fascinating stuff, but grading those essays... it’s a beast! It's like trying to unpick a tangled ball of yarn. Do you ever get a chance to read for pleasure?      Not much. Mostly it’s keeping an eye on my grandkids. My daughter’s working shifts at the hospital, you know. Long hours, stressful. The news... it doesn’t help, does it? All that talk about ISIS and… it’s worrying, even for us.      It is. Sometimes I just switch off the news. It’s too much. Although, you hear things buzzing around the school, you can't completely avoid it.

Honestly, Nepal. It's quite ambitious, isn’t it, Brenda? I mean, at our age! Though, I always did fancy trekking somewhere… exotic. Ambitious, yes, but absolutely doable, Margaret! We're not ancient, you know. Remember that trip to the Lakes we did fifteen years ago? We were practically leaping over puddles! And it’s not just trekking, there's the culture, the mountains… I’ve been reading up on it. Do you recall? Speaking of leaping over puddles, did either of you see the Tour of Britain whizzing through yesterday? Absolutely astonishing, those cyclists! Such power. And so close to home. These sausages are homemade, by the way, proper pork. Want one? Oh, goodness, yes please, Doreen. They smell divine. And the Tour! I watched a bit from the window; blurry, of course. My eyesight isn't what it used to be. Brenda, about Nepal... are you seriously aiming for some high altitude trek? My knees aren't exactly thrilled at the prospect. Well, not  high  altitude, Margaret. There are lower altitude treks, guided ones. And plenty of tea houses along the way. I'm thinking something manageable, a few days. I've been doing a bit of training, you know. Gentle walks mostly. My daughter, Sarah, finally tackled an Iron Man last year - that gives you some perspective on endurance! An Iron Man! My goodness! My daughter, Emily, is doing one next year. Training is relentless. She's often out on the bike before dawn. You wouldn't believe the dedication. Speaking of dedication, remember trying to get gluten-free bread at the Village Shop? It was a nightmare! Oh, don’t remind me! They brought one in eventually, after I and half the village complained. But it tasted like cardboard. The Farm Shop’s much better, although it does cost an arm and a leg. I’ve started making my own bread, actually. It's no bother. I completely agree about the Farm Shop. Worth every penny for decent ingredients. Although, getting good sausages there is a challenge too; it’s all about finding someone who knows what they’re doing. Back to Nepal… Doreen, remember when your mother-in-law used to tell that incredible story about escaping Siberia during the war and ending up in Africa? Oh, don’t. It was harrowing, even listening to it. Imagine the hardship! She lost everything. Food was… well, it wasn’t exactly a feast, was it?

Right, so, tell me everything! How was the production run this week, Liv? You looked a bit frazzled when you arrived. Oh, Elsie, don’t even  start  me. It was chaos. Absolute, utter chaos. We were short on a vital component for half of Tuesday, and Mr. Harding was breathing down my neck the whole time. You know he gets like that when deadlines loom. Honestly, I felt like I was herding cats. Mr. Harding? Sounds charming. What component was it? Sounds exciting! Not exciting at all! It was a microchip. Relatively small thing, but crucial for the entire assembly line. And getting it shipped here from Germany in time… well, let's just say I spent a lot of time on the phone, sweet-talking customs officials. You’re a miracle worker, lass. Honestly, I admire your patience. My boss, Mr. Featherstonehaugh, is bad enough, but he’s nothing compared to a man stressed about microchips, I reckon. How's the new intern getting on? Last time you mentioned her, she seemed a bit...lost. Chloe? She's improved. Still a bit slow, needs a lot of hand-holding, but she’s actually started to grasp some of the processes. She accidentally deleted a whole spreadsheet last week though. Nearly gave me a heart attack. I had to rebuild it from backups at, like, eleven o'clock at night. Oh dear! That's terrifying. At least it was recoverable. Sarah, how’s the conference planning going? Big one next month, isn't it? Aye, the Annual Tech Symposium. It’s keeping me busy, that's for sure. We’ve got speakers from all over the world, caterers, AV technicians… it's a logistical nightmare sometimes. But it’s also really rewarding when everything comes together. We've got a really interesting keynote from a woman who's developing sustainable energy solutions. I’m dead chuffed about that. Sustainable energy? That’s cool. You always manage to snag the most interesting speakers. I mostly deal with making sure the machines don’t break down and the parts actually arrive! It’s vastly different careers, isn't it? I'm still basically being a glorified filing system for Mr. Davies. He keeps asking me for documents I swear he had on his desk five minutes before. I'm starting to feel like a human post-it note. It’s the same in every job, isn’t it?

Honestly, David, I’m still fuming about this library thing. Demolition? For a shiny new block of flats? It's absolutely ridiculous. Have you seen the council plans? They’re calling it “urban renewal.” Sounds so…sterile. Urban cleansing, more like. I saw them too, Sarah. It’s appalling. I mean, it’s a vital community resource. Where are the kids supposed to go after school? Not everyone has access to decent internet at home, you know. Exactly! And the history! That library has been there since the 1930s. Generations have used it. And Mrs. Peterson, the librarian, practically runs a life-support system for the elderly. She brings tea and biscuits, helps them with their pensions... It's far more than just books. Absolutely. So, the petition... how's that going? Have you managed to gather a decent number of signatures? I volunteered to circulate it at the office, but people are so busy these days. It’s slow. I’ve got about eighty online, and I've been going around the local shops, getting paper ones. But we need a lot more to make any difference, especially with this Council. They rarely listen to anything unless it's a massive outcry. Right. We need to tap into the local Facebook groups, too. There’s a surprisingly active Plumstead Residents’ forum. I'll have a look tonight and see what I can do. By the way, how are things at work? Still juggling those ridiculous shifts? Don't even ask. They've changed the rota again. I’m on 6am to 2pm next week! How am I supposed to function on that? It’s brutal. My brain feels like mush by lunchtime. It's genuinely impacting my transcription accuracy, you know? I keep misspelling things. That’s outrageous. They can’t keep doing that to you. Have you spoken to your supervisor? I did, but she just shrugged and said “it's operational needs.” Honestly, sometimes I wish I’d invested in that brain training app everyone’s talking about. Something to sharpen the focus. Do you remember that mnemonic I was telling you about, the one for remembering the order of planets? Vaguely. Mercury, Venus, Earth… something about a ‘My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles’? Exactly! It actually works! I was thinking, maybe we need a mnemonic for arguing with the council. Something like, 'Remember, Local Voices, Evidence, Persuasion, Petition, Action’!

Cor, this is lovely, Marjorie. Proper cuppa. You've really done well with this spread too, haven’t you? Sausage rolls, egg salad sandwiches… reminds me of picnics we used to have down by the River Wensum when I were a lad. Oh, Ronald, you always make me feel so old reminiscing! But yes, it's nice to have a proper lunch together. Cyril’s being a bit quiet today, isn’t he? He usually has a comment about everything. Just savouring the peace, Marjorie. Peace and a good sausage roll. These are a bit dry, though, aren't they? A touch more mustard would’ve done the trick. Cyril, you're always finding fault with something! They're perfectly acceptable. Though I do agree, a touch more mustard wouldn't hurt. Speaking of fault, did you hear about Old Mrs. Higgins and her parking at Cromer? No! What happened? Don’t tell me she got another ticket. That woman has a terrible time with parking. She did! Right in a disabled bay, mind you! But she claimed she didn’t see the sign. Said it was obscured by a seagull. A seagull! A seagull, eh? Always an excuse. These coastal towns, they should just widen the roads, that's what they should do. It's a nightmare trying to park anywhere. Speaking of things that are a nightmare, I read something the other day about the council tax going up again. Oh, don't even start with the council tax, Cyril! It’s ridiculous. Where does all that money  go ? You’d think with Mattishall being so… well, Mattishall, they wouldn’t need to fleece us like this. Exactly! And what about voting? Do you all still bother? I try to, but honestly, it feels like nothing ever changes. Politicians promise the world, and then… nothing. I voted once. Back in '79. Labour. Never again. Waste of time. They all want your money no matter what. I always do. You have to, Ronald. Even if you don't think it makes a difference. It’s a civic duty, isn't it? And I always ponder the Jehovah's Witnesses. They were at my door again last week. Such lovely young people, but I just… I don’t. Aye, they're persistent, aren't they? We get them too. We mostly just don’t answer, though. Wouldn't want to get into a lengthy debate.

"Honestly, Mum, Dad, you haven't touched your tea. Please, have a piece of this fudge. It's a new recipe, salted caramel, I thought you'd enjoy it." "Very kind, dear. It  is  rather lovely, actually. Salted caramel, you say? A modern invention, isn't it? Not like the butterscotch we used to have." "Modern inventions, eh? Back in my day, fudge was fudge. Simple, honest… and sticky!" "Right. So, the log burner's behaving itself tonight, thankfully. I was worried about the new batch we got; they seemed a bit damp. Touch wood." "They are! Though I did have a bit of a panic earlier when I realised I'd completely forgotten to order more logs. Luckily, Mr. Henderson next door offered to share some of his - bless him, he's always so helpful. Though his cat, Bartholomew, nearly tripped me on the way back!" “Henderson, you say? Such a peculiar man. All those gnomes in his garden. Quite… striking.” "Striking indeed. Reminds me of a chap I taught Latin to, used to collect miniature porcelain frogs. Highly eccentric, but a brilliant mind." "Speaking of brilliant minds, did I tell you about the outsourcing proposal at work? They’re suggesting we shift some of the administrative tasks to India…" "Oh, no. Not again. That's terrible, David. People’s jobs…" "Outsourcing? Honestly! In my day, we trained our own staff. A proper apprenticeship. These modern methods... no loyalty, no sense of commitment." "Exactly! When I was at the school, we fostered a real sense of community. Everyone knew everyone. Now… academies, targets, KPIs... it’s all become so impersonal." "I know, it’s frustrating. But the budget’s tight. I’m trying to fight it, but…" "Did you see that new restaurant that’s opened on Elm Street? 'The Golden Spoon,' it's called. Apparently, the mashed potato is divine." "Mashed potato? A staple, of course. Though a good mashed potato requires proper butter and a dash of cream. None of this margarine nonsense.” "Indeed. My cook, Mrs. Higgins, made a mashed potato that could bring a tear to your eye. She used Jersey cream. Absolute perfection." "We should go sometime! It'd be nice to get out. Remember that antique shop we visited in Rye last year? I've been thinking about getting that old armchair reupholstered. The fabric is falling apart." "Reupholstering? That’ll cost a fortune, won’t it?

Right then, that’s a bit of sugar added. Still can’t quite get me head around this new property tax, can ya? Seems steeper than it used to. Steep? Arthur, it's highway robbery, that’s what it is! Used to be, you paid yer rates, kept yer garden tidy, and that was that. Now, they're finding new ways to get their hands on yer pennies, ain't they? Even if you  don’t  ‘ave any pennies! It’s all so complicated, isn't it? I tried to ring the council about it, the automated system just kept looping me around. Eventually, I gave up. Honestly, sometimes I feel like shouting at the television. Tell me about it, Margaret. I had a go at the website – dreadful thing, that. Buried in jargon. They expect people to understand all this just like that! I spent a good hour just trying to find out if they’d finally stopped charging for bins. Oh, the bins! Don't get me started. Remember when we used to just put ‘em out and they took ‘em? Now we’ve got these colour-coded monstrosities and they only collect certain things on certain days. Trying to keep up with the recycling is like doing a university degree! I’ve gotten quite good at it, actually. I even buy those little compostable bags for the food waste. Though, honestly, having everything so separated is a bit of a faff. At least it's better for the environment, I suppose. Environment's all well and good, Margaret, but at what cost? My pension barely covers the heating, let alone all these extra bins and taxes! Pension, eh? Don’t mention pensions! Got a letter from them the other day, saying they’re fiddling with the rates again. They tell you it's going up, but you look at the figures and it's barely enough to buy a box of biscuits these days. It’s the same with everything, isn’t it? House prices, food costs… It’s all gone mad. Still, I’m glad ANON bought this place. It's lovely, and so much bigger than my flat. Though getting the Sat Nav to actually  find  it was a nightmare. Honestly, it kept sending me down fields! Sat Navs, hmm. Give me a good old-fashioned map any day. At least you could orient yourself with a map.

Right, so, about Liam's tablet… it's still doing that funny thing, isn't it? Keeps freezing right in the middle of games. Yeah, it’s rubbish. I was about to beat that level, honest! Just when I was getting the hang of it,  freeze . Completely ruins it. Is it covered on warranty still, do you reckon? Warranty? Let me see… I think you mentioned something about Argos, didn’t you, love? It must be ages ago you bought it though. Little one was barely walking then. It was nearly two years ago, Sarah. Argos... definitely. I think the warranty was a year, maybe? I’d have to check the paperwork. It's somewhere in the abyss of the study. You know how it is. Oh, Finn! You’re a little terror. Honestly, saving the world, one potato at a time. Liam, don’t stare at your brother like that, you’ll encourage him. He’s just having fun. Anyway, the tablet? Is it worth trying to fix it yourself, Dad? Or are we just going to have to bite the bullet and buy a new one? Well, that’s what I was thinking about. It’s just a bit of software likely, a dodgy update or something. I’m fairly handy with that sort of thing. I could have a poke around, see if I can sort it. No harm in trying, surely? I’ve got that toolkit I got for Christmas, the one Sarah thought I’d never use. And you’ll be careful, won’t you? Don’t want you taking it apart and ending up needing to buy a new one  anyway ! I wouldn’t dream of it. It’s just a matter of opening it up, flashing the firmware or something. Shouldn't take more than an hour or two. Though, finding the blasted screwdriver bit that fits… that’s the real challenge. An hour or two? Seriously? I could use that time to practice my rugby tackling. The team's doing drills on Saturday. Rugby is important, son, but so is a functioning tablet. Keeps you occupied. And, let's be honest, keeps  me  occupied. Speaking of Saturday, are we still on for the match? I swear, everytime I think about standing in the rain… Absolutely. I’ve already sorted tickets. It’s supposed to be dry-ish. And I got that waterproof jacket you like.

Right, that was  delicious . Absolutely demolished that pizza. You two look like you enjoyed it too! It was the bestest pizza ever! Especially the pepperoni! More, please! No more, sweetheart. You’ll burst! We need to save some energy for Operation Fairy Garden later. Are you excited about that? Super excited! Can we use the sparkly rocks? The really, really sparkly ones? Absolutely. Though we might need to be careful with those. Remember what happened last time you got hold of the glitter glue? I made a very shiny dog! A very shiny dog, indeed. It took ages to hoover up! Anyway, speaking of sparkly things… have you two been behaving for Grandma and Grandpa? They seemed a bit… quiet on the phone earlier. We were very good! We just… talked about the Loch Ness Monster. A lot. Oh really? And what interesting things did you discover about Nessie? She breathes fire! And she has a party dress! A pink one! A pink party dress? That’s brilliant! See, that's why I love talking to you two. Where did you get that idea from? We were watching that documentary. The one with the blurry pictures. She just  looked  like she was hiding a pink dress. A blurry dress-hiding monster. I like it. It’s much more exciting than the usual theory. So, have you two figured out how many sparkly rocks we have left? I think we used quite a lot for the gnome's beard. Let me see… We have five… and then three… and then two… That’s… seven! Excellent! Seven sparkly rocks should be plenty. Right, let's try a trickier one. If I have four slices of pizza left and you each want one, how many will  I  have left? He gets one! And then you have… three! You're both brilliant! Honestly. Though, sometimes, it feels like communicating with you two is like learning a whole new language. You come up with these amazing stories and ideas. Because we’re clever! You certainly are! But sometimes explaining things to grown-ups… It's hard. Like, trying to explain to grown-ups why we  need  to build a tiny tea set for the fairies. They just don’t understand the importance. It’s very important! Fairies need tea! And biscuits! Absolutely right. You're preaching to the choir. Now, let's talk about this party we’re going to next weekend.

Speaker_1 :   “Right, I am  stuffed . Honestly, that truffle pasta... I never knew I could eat so much. It was unreal though, wasn’t it? Best thing I’ve had this whole trip, easily.”   Speaker_2 :   “Aye, it was lovely, Elara. Hearty though, definitely hearty. I’m just glad we found a spot with a view. Look at that sea, sparkling like diamonds. Reminds me of that holiday we had in Cornwall years ago with Liam – remember?”   Speaker_3 :   "Yeah, but this is way better than Cornwall, Mum. Cornwall was just... rocks. This is proper blue. I’m gonna try and get some good photos later. My phone camera's not the best, but I can still manage a few decent ones, I reckon."   Speaker_4 :   "It  is  rather spectacular, isn’t it? Though, I must say, the service here is a bit... relaxed. Took a rather long time to get the bill. Efficiency isn’t always a priority everywhere, is it? Back in London, everything’s calibrated to the second."      "Relaxed is good, Julian! Let's embrace it, eh? And anyway, compared to the airport getting here...that was a mission and a half. Remember that immigration officer searching every single bag? He looked proper suspicious, like we were smuggling something."      “Oh, don’t remind me! I was convinced he was going to pull me aside and ask me about my handbag. Honestly, the way he was eyeing up Finn’s rucksack… I thought he suspected him of carrying… well, something illegal, I don't know!”      "It was so random! He just kept staring. He probably thought I was carrying a drone or something. I want action shots of the pool later, you know? Gotta get some cool stuff for Instagram.”      “Instagram… right. The relentless pursuit of likes. Honestly, it’s fascinating – this whole evolution of photography. Remember when we had to develop film? The anticipation… the darkroom… it felt more… considered, somehow. And the skill required!"      “Yeah, but it's instant gratification now, isn’t it? Plus, you can edit everything! I was learning about food technology at school - weirdly enough, they were showing us how they use digital imaging to make food look more appealing in adverts. Pretty scary, actually!”      “Food technology… Goodness. When I was training, we were just grateful if it  looked  edible! In this day and age, they're even thinking about 3D-printed meat. Makes you think, doesn't it?

Honestly, this article. It's dreadful. Saying PPI claims are practically closed? Absolute rubbish. There are still valid cases out there, you know. I saw something about that on the news, David. They were saying the deadline's passed, but… it all feels a bit underhand, doesn’t it? Like they're trying to discourage people. Discourage 'em, they were! I got a letter the other day, right proper threatening language. Said they were sending someone round to ‘discuss outstanding debt.’ Outstanding debt! From a company that mis-sold me insurance in the first place! Cheek of it. Well, that's the problem with these debt collection agencies. They operate on volume, not necessarily justice. They send out these letters hoping a few people will panic and pay just to get them to stop. Precisely, Michael! It's a predatory system. I've been advising my colleagues – you need to check  everything . Don’t sign anything without reading the small print. And if they’re being aggressive, report them. Reporting them... where do you report them, David? The Financial Ombudsman Service, primarily. They're the ones who adjudicate on these things. I've dealt with them before, you know, through work. It's a slow process, but it's worth it. Too much bother for an old fella like me. I just want it gone. It’s giving me the jitters, honestly. Don’t let them get to you, Arthur. Fight it if you can. It’s the principle of the thing. Remember that article I mentioned last week, about the community garden? They were talking about seed swaps. Oh, lovely! I brought some spare sweet pea seeds. They're climbing varieties, excellent for trellises. I always get a good show with them. Sweet peas… reminds me of my mother’s garden. She could grow anything, she could. Always singing whilst she was at it. Speaking of singing, are you all definitely coming to the Church concert next Saturday? They’re doing a few pieces from the Abbey. Should be quite something. Absolutely! I've already RSVP'd. Though, goodness, parking’s always a nightmare around there. I’ll drive. Fewer headaches that way. Besides, I can always navigate the one-way systems. It  is  good to get out though, isn't it? A bit of fresh air… escaping all this… paperwork. Escaping the paperwork is a universal desire, Michael. Though, honestly, I’m still trying to get my head around this new computer software the council’s rolled out.

Honestly, what a day. Year 9s arguing about verb conjugations… it’s enough to drain anyone! How was your day, Margaret? Anything particularly… interesting in court? Oh, dear. Year 9s, eh? You have my sympathy, love. Mine wasn’t exactly  exciting , but it certainly was busy. A few minor theft cases, mostly teenagers, you know the drill. And a rather heated dispute about a parking ticket. People get so worked up about those! I’ve seen more anger over a £30 fine than some serious crimes, I swear. I can imagine! It's strange, isn't it, how seemingly small things can cause such immense frustration. It's almost… symptomatic of something bigger. You know, the cost of living crisis, the feeling of being squeezed everywhere. Exactly! It is, isn't it? You read the news, and you just feel the pinch everywhere. Travel’s gone up, food's gone up… and the petrol! Don't even get me started on the petrol prices. I drove in from Sutton Coldfield today – used to be a breeze, now it takes nearly an hour. Do you drive, dear? I do, yes. Though I'm seriously considering getting an electric car. The government grants aren’t massive, but it feels like the sensible thing to do, for the environment and, eventually, the wallet. Though that's another big outlay upfront, of course. A sensible thing, indeed. Though I worry about the infrastructure, I do. Where are all these people going to charge their cars, when the grid can barely keep up as it is? And what about folks who live in flats? No driveways, you see. It’s a whole pile of complications. Though, anything’s better than what’s happening with the climate, isn't it? I read something awful about the Arctic ice melting even faster than predicted. It's terrifying, isn't it? Makes you feel quite powerless, sometimes. I try to teach my students about it, about sustainability, but it's hard to get them engaged when they're struggling to understand present continuous. Well, you’re doing your bit. Every little helps. I tell my grandson the same thing. He’s at university now, studying Environmental Science at Birmingham. Bright lad, he is. Makes me proud. What about your family, dear? Still living near Hitchin? Yes, still there. My parents are getting on a bit, so it’s nice to be relatively close.

Right then, you two. Mummy’s had a lovely day, haven’t I? Absolutely smashing. And you both looked so happy at school today – Miss Davies sent a little note, said you were both being brilliant. I drew a sparkly rainbow, Mummy! And it had unicorns! I built a really tall tower with the blocks. It almost touched the ceiling! Oh, well done, darling. See? That's what makes me happy - knowing you are both having fun and learning. It’s a good feeling, isn't it? Like sunshine inside. Sunshine inside! That’s a good rhyme! Rainbow, sunshine… Ooh, a budding poet, are we? That’s brilliant, love! Tell me, what else makes you happy? Besides rainbows and unicorn drawings. Playing with my diggers. Diggers! Absolutely! Diggers are wonderful. And you, my little sunshine? ... Ice cream! And snuggles! And when you read me stories about princesses! Those are all very good things to be happy about. You know, sometimes people think being happy means having lots and lots of money. Like, mountains of it! Enough to buy a giant bouncy castle and all the ice cream in the world. A bouncy castle? Really? Well, that  would  be fun, wouldn't it? But you see, money can buy some nice things, and it can make things a bit easier. But it doesn't always buy happiness.
