Giving people jobs to do, apparently discovering things! Aye, well, ‘dynamic’ is one word for it. Mostly it's spreadsheets and chasing people down for data. But I did get to commission a study on the impact of regional identity on consumer choice recently. It was brilliant, actually. We found such a strong correlation between someone’s accent and the brands they buy. Seriously? Give me an example. Well, for instance, a strong North East accent, particularly a Sunderland one, seems to correlate with a preference for brands seen as "authentic" and "honest" – things like local breweries, even certain supermarket own-brands. Whereas a more Southern accent tends to gravitate towards bigger, flashier brands. It's fascinating stuff, really. Makes you think about how much our identity shapes what we buy. That’s brilliant! I'd love to see the full report. You know, it kind of links back to my own work, in a way. Bias isn't just in algorithms; it's in all sorts of societal preferences, shaped by these subtle things like accent and… fashion, I suppose. Oh, you’re going there, are you? Fashion. Don't even get me started on the clothes people wear here. Everything’s so… beige. Beige? You think so? I thought you'd appreciate the understated elegance. Understated elegance is a polite way of saying depressing uniformity. Back home, even going to the supermarket is an explosion of colour. Bold patterns, clashing textures... It’s like a walking art exhibition. Here, everyone looks like they's raided a charity shop for a selection of neutral tones.

Right, Grandma, so, this Sunak fella… everyone at school’s goin’ on about him, but I’m not sure why. They’re sayin' he's brewin' somethin’ with taxes again. It's all a bit much, innit? Oh, Rishi, is it? Fancy name for a politician. Taxes, eh? Aye, they’re always at it, aren’t they? Tinkering about with our pockets. It’s been that way since I was a lass. Remember when Harold Wilson was Prime Minister? That was a different kettle of fish altogether. Harold who-now? No one mentions him at school. It's all Brexit and inflation and... and stuff I barely understand. Is he, like, really old even for  you ? Oh, he was! Though, not as old as me, of course. A different era, love. Labour man, he was. Tried to do right by the working folk, he did. Used to listen to his speeches on the wireless. Proper serious they were. Not like this lot now, just shouting at each other. That's how it seems, doesn’t it? Like they’re more bothered about arguing than actually, you know,  doing  something. My mum says Sunak's supposed to be good with money, but it doesn't feel like it, does it? everything’s goin' up. Good with money often means good  for  money, not good for the rest of us. Don’t you let them fool you, lad. They all promise the world before an election, don’t they? And then… well, then you get more of the same. Remember Thatcher? Ah, that's a story for another day, that is. Brings back a lot of grim memories. Thatcher? Like… the Iron Lady? I got a bit about her in history, but it was all pretty dry. Was she that bad then? Everyone seems so divided about her now. Bad? She broke a lot of hearts, she did. Closed the mines, you know? My cousin, Peter, he worked down the pit. Lost his job when they shut it. Never really recovered, poor lad. Had to move south, away from his home, away from everyone he knew. That was the human cost of all that supposed "economic progress." Wow. That's… that’s a lot more than just numbers in a textbook. So, you reckon no politician’s ever really been… decent? Now, that’s a harsh thing to say, isn’t it? There's been a few with a bit of backbone, a bit of common sense.

Honestly, this is lovely, Liam. Absolutely lovely. Though, a bit heavy on the gravy, wouldn’t you say? My digestion isn’t what it used to be. Sorry, Mum. Just a bit enthusiastic with the gravy boat, I suppose. Daniel, stop poking your nose in your mashed potato, will ya? It's not a construction site. I'm  making  a volcano, Dad! It's science! Daniel, darling, volcanoes go  in  volcanoes, not all over your plate. Granny’s right, it’s a lovely meal, Liam. You’ve really outdone yourself. Your daughter's got a good head on her, Sarah. Reminds me a bit of myself, actually. Always poking about, wanting to know how things worked. Though, my volcanoes were a bit more... theoretical, in my day. We didn't have the internet to show us realistic eruptions. Well, he’ll be showing me realistic eruptions in the living room if he’s not careful. Speaking of which, did you see that article about the blood moon, Mum? They say it’s a particularly spectacular one tonight. A blood moon, you say? Och, I remember those! Used to frighten the living daylights out of us as children. My grandmother, God rest her soul, used to say it was a sign of bad luck, a warning from the wee folk. Bad luck? Does that mean I can’t go out and look at it then? I want to take some pictures for my science project. Daniel, Granny's just telling you an old story. It’s just an optical illusion – sunlight filtering through the Earth’s atmosphere. Nothing to worry about. It  is  quite beautiful though. Perhaps we can go for a walk in Fitzgeralds Park after dinner and see if we can spot it? That's a grand idea, Sarah. Fresh air would do us all good. Mum, you in? Fitzgeralds Park… That’s a lovely idea. Reminds me of when I used to take the children there. It's changed a bit since then, hasn't it? More… modern. Still, a good place for a stroll. Though, I’ll need to take it slow. My knees aren’t exactly cooperating these days. We’ll take it nice and easy, Granny. Daniel will keep you company, won't you, darling? Yeah, yeah. As long as it doesn’t clash with my stargazing. You and your stargazing! It’s good to have a hobby, son.

Honestly, Bernard, I’m still reeling from the whole Scottish referendum thing. Did you catch that piece on the BBC last night about the renewed calls for another vote? Aye, saw a bit of it. Makes you wonder, doesn't it? All that fuss a few years back, and now here we are again. Seems like the pot never really boils down, does it? The country's always simmering. Exactly! And the arguments… they’re so complex. The economic implications alone are enough to give you a headache. My daughter, Emily, she’s quite passionate about it, you know. Fiercely pro-remain, naturally. Emily, eh? Always a bright one, that girl. Remember when she was little and insisted on reciting Shakespeare in the supermarket? Gave the poor checkout lady quite a fright! I do! A precocious little thing. Anyway, she was going on about the oil revenues and the currency… I just tried to listen and nod. Sometimes I feel like I understand half of what she says! Understandable. Politics these days… it’s all numbers and projections. Not much room for common sense. Speaking of numbers, I had a bit of a kerfuffle myself this week. Another interview for the apprentice position down at the workshop. Oh, really? How did it go? Was there anyone particularly promising? Well, there was this lad, Daniel. Seemed keen enough, good looking, clever, but… I don't know. He kept using all these fancy terms, buzzwords mostly. ‘Synergistic approaches’ and ‘optimising workflow’. Honestly, it was a bit much. I’m looking for someone who can actually  weld  a frame, not write a business plan about it! Sounds like he’d be better suited for an office job then. You need someone practical, with a good pair of hands and a willingness to learn. A bit like old Mr. Henderson, your previous apprentice. Exactly! Henderson was gold. Solid as a rock. This Daniel… I’m not sure he'd last a week. Reminded me a bit of that new colleague of yours, isn't his name... Timothy? Timothy Finch. Yes! He's… an experience. Keeps suggesting “innovative pedagogical strategies” to teach Year 7 grammar. They just want to know when they can play football at break time, Bernard! Sounds like a right one, that. Some people just like to complicate things, don't they? I had a customer in today, trying to argue about the price of a set of bolts.

Right then, are we all comfy back there? Bit of a squeeze, innit? Just hoping the traffic holds up. This move is proving to be more of a logistical nightmare than I anticipated. Yeah, it’s a bit cramped, Dad. But alright, I've got a good view of the fields though. Rolling along nicely so far. Smell’s pretty good in here too, mum made that sausage roll thing, right? Sausage rolls, yes! I made loads. Thought you'd both be peckish on the journey. You are starving, aren't you, Aaron? You always are. Absolutely starving! They are brilliant, Mum. Seriously, you need to open a bakery. Seriously! My students always ask where I get my energy from. This is it, isn't it? Ann's legendary sausage rolls. Legendary, eh? You’re laying it on a bit thick, Liam. Though, I will admit, they’re pretty good. Better than anything I can manage, that’s for sure. Speaking of energy, this driving is draining. All this stop-start traffic. You’re doing brilliantly, love. Just concentrate. And check your mirrors, dear. Right, right. Mirrors. Always the mirrors. So, Liam, how’s the teaching going? Still wrestling with the pronunciation of ‘world record’ with those Japanese students? You have no idea. One of them was trying to say 'world record' as 'word recreation'! It was a whole thing. They get tripped up by those vowel sounds. It’s fascinating, actually, how different languages process information. It makes you think about how  we  hear things, you know? Different accents sound bizarre to different ears. Like how I sound, I bet to anyone from further north. My vowels are apparently all over the place. Don't be daft, Aaron. Your accent's lovely. Just… cheerful. It’s a good thing. Although, I did hear you arguing with that bloke at Tesco’s last week about where the sweetcorn was. Sounded like you were having a full-blown debate. He put it in the wrong aisle! It was a matter of principle, Mum! Besides, have you seen how much they’re charging for sweetcorn these days? It's daylight robbery. Speaking of supermarkets, I dread to think how much this move is going to cost us. All the cardboard boxes, the bubble wrap… and the petrol! Have you thought about pensions, Ann? With all this upheaval... Don’t start that now, David.

Honestly, this is a slice of heaven, isn’t it? The countryside just… breathes differently. Aye, it’s bonny, alright. Much better than bein’ stuck intae Sunderland city centre, that's for sure. Though, I’m still gettin’ used to drivin’ on these lanes. Feels narrower than back home. Narrow? Narrow! You haven’t seen narrow, lass. Back in my day, when I was learnin’ to drive, there were tracks barely wide enough for a donkey cart! And no power steering, mind you. Just pure muscle. A donkey cart, Arthur? Really? Absolutely! Timperley was a lot more rural when I was a lad. Farms everywhere. You wouldn’t recognise it now. Full of houses and… and what do they call 'em? Commuter towns! Going and spoiling a perfectly good bit of farmland. Reminds me a bit o’ Sheepwash Lane back home, this does. Full o’ blind corners and tractors. Gotta be on yer toes. Did you ever see many sheep, Arthur? Sheep? Of course, I did! My Uncle George had a small flock. Used to help him with ‘em, you know. Shearin’ ‘em in the spring, drenchin’ ‘em against the flies... Hard work, it was, but good honest days. You learnt to respect those animals. Not like these city folk who think a pet rabbit is hard labour. You’re rather hard on city folk, Arthur. Not all of us are unfamiliar with nature. Though, I admit, I’ve mostly seen wildlife through a screen these days. Engineering projects tend to keep you confined to concrete and steel. Concrete and steel! Sounds like a grim life, that. I'd rather be elbow-deep in data, to be honest. Less… cold. Data? What's 'data'? Sounds like somethin' to do with machines. Not much room for sheep in data, is there? It's… well, it's information, Arthur. Organized information. Like, numbers and words, used to understand patterns and make predictions. I use it to design bridges and buildings. Ensuring they’re safe and efficient. She's basically gatherin’ all the facts and figurin’ things oot, Arthur. Like figurin’ oot the best way to herd sheep, but with computers. Hmph. Computers. Used to be you just looked at the sheep and  felt  what they were gonna do. Weather, the way they grazed… that's how you knew. Couldn’t put that into a computer, could ya? Maybe not directly, but we can analyze weather patterns, soil conditions... build models to predict how they'll interact.

Right then, so, dinner's almost ready. Honestly, this Cumbrian lamb is just incredible, isn't it? Mum, you’ve really outdone yourself. It's a local farm, dear. Best lamb I've tasted in years. Much better than anything we ever got back in Dublin, I must say. Though, I do miss a good Irish stew… Aye, nothing beats a proper Irish stew. Though, I’m quite partial to this lamb myself. Reminds me of a spit roast we had at a company barbecue back in the day. Utter chaos, though. Someone tried to set the shed on fire… Dad! Must you always bring up near-disasters? It was just a spark, remember? Anyway, I was thinking about that choir we talked about. The Hunsonby Harmony Singers. Oh, the choir! I was wondering about that. Have you looked at their repertoire? I’d hate to join and they’re all doing opera. My voice isn't exactly suited for dramatic soprano, you know. I had a quick look online, Mum. They do a mix. A lot of folk songs, some gospel, and apparently, they’re putting on a Christmas concert with some carols. It seems pretty welcoming. Think you’d enjoy it, honestly. It'd be good for you to get out, do something different. It’d be good for all of us, wouldn’t it? Agnes has been a bit withdrawn lately. A bit of singing and socialising would do her the world of good. Well, I don't know. I’m still getting used to… everything. Retirement, being here in Hunsonby… it’s a big change. Remember Mrs. O’Malley, my maths teacher? Strict as could be, but brilliant. She always said a change of scenery was good for the soul. Exactly! And speaking of changes, have you both confirmed you're coming to Sarah’s graduation in York next month? She’s really stressed about it. Sarah’s graduation? Of course. Wouldn't miss it for the world. Need to book the train tickets, though. She called asking if I could pick up some of the catering. Said they’re having mini Yorkshire puddings. Honestly, Sarah, always going over the top. Yorkshire puddings! Lovely. I'll bring a little something too. Perhaps a fruit cake. I used to make a wonderful one for the school bake sales. Do you remember the parents, back then? It felt like a whole village gather every week.

Right, so, parent's evening. Bit of a mixed bag, wasn’t it? Mmmph! Was Mr. Grumbles cross about my sums? Cross? He looked like he was going to explode, Lily! Like a volcano! Well, not explode, Finn. Ms. Davies said you both are struggling a little with the long division. Lily, you were getting distracted, fidgeting a lot. And Finn, you just… shut down. Said it was too hard. It  is  too hard! Numbers go all wiggly when I try to do it! It’s like… like trying to catch smoke! You can’t! I know, love, I know. But we need to find a way to tackle it. Maybe some extra practice at home? I can try to make it more fun, less… volcanic. Can we have a circus instead? With clowns and lions! And acrobats! And popcorn! Ooh, can we see the ones that fly through the air? We can  talk  about a circus. Maybe for the weekend. But first, let’s focus on conquering those numbers. Did Ms. Davies mention anything else? Like, about World Book Day? She said I need to dress up as a character! But I don’t know who! I'm going as a scary pirate! With a hook and an eye patch! That's brilliant, Finn. You’ll look amazing. Lily, have you been thinking about it? Anything you’re drawn to? We read  Alice in Wonderland  last week, perhaps the Queen of Hearts? But she’s mean! She shouts at everyone! Well, lots of characters are. That's what makes them interesting. Speaking of interesting… Ms. Davies also said you've been asking some rather… unusual questions in class. I asked what cooked human flesh smells like! You… you did, did you? And what did she say? She said it was a very silly question and I shouldn’t ask it again! But I still want to know! It probably smells yucky! Like old socks! Right. Let's just stick to pirates and queens for now, shall we? And perhaps leave the culinary curiosities to the professionals, eh? After school, Finn, I’m going to work with you on those division problems. Lily, you can read with me for a bit, just fifteen minutes, okay? Then we can talk more about characters. Okay. Can I read about princesses? Can I have another helping of pasta? I need energy for pirate adventures!

Right then, so, little Oisin’s birthday is next week. Are we still thinking the bounce house in the garden, or should we look at something else? The weather's been a bit changeable, hasn’t it? A bounce house sounds lovely, honestly. He’d adore it. But, yeah, the weather. Remember last year’s barbecue? Torrential rain. We ended up crammed into the kitchen. Boing! Boing! Boing, indeed! A bounce house is a grand idea, lass. Just make sure you’ve got a backup plan in case it rains. A hall, perhaps? Or even a good old-fashioned indoor games party. A hall would be pricey, Moira. And we’ve got Maggie’s cousin, Liam, working at Fitzgerald’s curtain shop now, haven't we? Maybe he could get us a deal on some bunting and decorations? It’d be a bit different than last year's streamers. That’s a fantastic idea, Declan! I’ll give him a ring tomorrow. He seemed to be enjoying the work, last time we spoke. Said it was a bit of a change from… well, everything else he's been doing. It's good to see young people finding their feet, isn't it? Especially these days. My wee grandson, Thomas, is obsessed with rugby. Is Oisin still playing mini-rugby? He is. He’s mad for it, the wee scamp. We’re going to the Munster match next Saturday. Tickets are sold out, of course, but I managed to wrangle a couple through work. Oh, that's wonderful, Declan! He’ll love that. He always asks about rugby. Speaking of things he loves… the way he talks! It’s just the sweetest thing. He’s picked up so many funny phrases. Aye, he has. He called the cat "a big, fluffy sausage" the other day. Nearly choked me with laughter. You wouldn’t believe some of the things he comes out with. Gets it from somewhere, I swear! Children are a constant source of amusement, aren't they? I used to have a boy who insisted on referring to the school bell as the "ding-dong monster." See? It’s universal! Although, with him being here now, a wee bit away from his own family, I do worry sometimes if he’s missing them. He talks about them all the time, love. And they send pictures and videos all the time. He’s settling in well, genuinely.

Right, so, you’re  sure  this isn't just a posh game, then? Like, a ridiculously complicated version of Scrabble for trust fund kids? Because honestly, "Lexicon Leapfrog" sounds a bit… much. Relax, Liv. It’s not about money, it's about language. Think of it as a linguistic workout. My aunt invented it, actually. She’s a retired classics professor, obsessed with etymology. It’s surprisingly clever. Clever and potentially humiliating, from what I've heard. I’m still recovering from the last time we played. Remember when I couldn’t think of a word for “serendipity”? Oh, aye! You were fair stuck, weren’t ya? Guffawing fit to burst. Serendipity! It's not that hard, is it? It's a tricky word, Liv. It has a specific root and prefix. That's often the challenge. The rules are simple, though. We each get a theme – let's say, "Travel" this time – and we have to connect words, one to the next, based on shared etymological roots, or surprising connections in meaning. And you get points for the cleverness, the unexpected links, and the obscure words you manage to pull out of the linguistic ether. Obscure words? That’s where I’m gonna struggle. I’m good with everyday speak, you know? Like, I can tell ya all about the subtleties of Geordie slang, but asking me about Anglo-Saxon verb conjugations? Forget about it. That’s part of the fun! It’s about expanding your vocabulary, seeing how words have evolved. It's less about knowing obscure words and more about making interesting connections between them. For example, you could start with ‘journey’ – common enough – and then link it to ‘peregrination’ because both relate to travelling, and 'peregrination' actually comes from the Latin 'peregrinus,’ meaning 'foreign' or 'wandering'. Exactly. You’re building a chain. And the longer the chain, and the more surprising the link, the better. We can set a point limit, or just play until someone gets completely flustered. Flustered's my middle name. Reckon I should just stick to counting my tea leaves then, eh? Come on, Liv. Give it a go. It's genuinely a good way to think about language. I'll be gentle to start. I'll even let you have 'Transport' instead of 'Travel', if it feels easier. I'm going to go with 'Exploration'. Seemed fitting for a Cambridge afternoon.

Look at this! Remember this? It's us at Ellie’s 16th, covered in glitter and looking like we'd just wrestled a unicorn. Oh, bloody hell! That’s brutal, isn't it? You've got, like, a full-on sequin beard. And my hair… what IS that hair? It looks like a badger tried to nest in it. You were going for the "rock star" look, weren't you? Clearly failed spectacularly. Ellie’s Mum nearly had a heart attack when you started air-guitaring during her speech. She was a fair shout. I was feeling it! Anyway, you look like a Christmas elf exploded on you. Remember how we spent ages trying to get that glitter off? It was everywhere for weeks. Tell me about it. Mum was fuming. She scrubbed the bathroom tiles 'til they were practically translucent. Right proper state, that night. Say, you been sleeping alright? You look knackered. Nah, not really. Been struggling to get any decent shut-eye. I keep nodding off in lectures. Professor Davies nearly caught me yesterday. I was practically slumped on the desk, drooling. He gave me a right look. Oh, that’s awful. You need to sort that out. Lack of sleep makes you proper grumpy, you know. And you’re already a grumpy git when you're rested. Hey! I am not! And it's not just lectures. It's everywhere. I even nearly fell asleep on the sofa watching telly last night. I swear, I could nap standing up at this point. Right, well, what's going on? Stress? Studying? Any lurid love life drama I need to hear about? It's probably just the workload, to be honest. Got that history essay looming, and the stats one's a nightmare. Speaking of music, have you heard anything new decent lately? I've been listening to that new Wet Leg album on repeat. Absolutely brilliant. Actually, yeah. Found this band called 'The Northern Lights' – proper indie sound, a bit like early Arctic Monkeys. Check them out. You’d probably like 'em. They're playing a gig in Manchester next month. Ooh, Manchester? We should go! Get a proper day out of it.

Right, so, let’s tackle this. The application needs to be watertight, doesn’t it? Especially considering Mrs. Higgins’ objections. Honestly, you’d think she personally built the allotments herself. Absolutely. She's a force of nature, isn’t she? But I think we’ve addressed most of her concerns in the revised plans. The buffer zone is significantly increased, and we’ve added the hedgerow detail. Did you manage to get those photos of the existing green space to include? Yes, I did. I focused on the wildlife - the nesting birds, the slow worms... things that tug at the heartstrings, you know? The committee's always a bit swayed by environmental arguments. Though, getting that ecologist’s report was a nightmare. He kept wanting to add even  more  detail about the fungal ecosystem. He’s thorough. But we just needed the highlights, didn’t we? Look, about the overall structure… I was thinking we hit them with the community benefit first. The increased access to fresh produce, the social aspect for the elderly – really lean into the "improving wellbeing" angle. That’s good. And then address the concerns directly after, demonstrating we’ve taken them seriously. Before they even get to the traffic impact assessment, they'll have hopefully bought into the positive side of it. I'm still worried about the traffic, though. The modelling was…optimistic, wasn't it? It was based on the best data we had. We can’t make it up. And we’ve agreed that the staggered entry and exit times for deliveries should mitigate the worst of it. Plus, the foot traffic will increase, which will hopefully discourage car use around the allotments. Fingers crossed. Are you confident about your presentation? You always get a bit flustered when you’re speaking in front of them. I'm better now, honestly. I’ve rehearsed it. It's just... they can be intimidating. Those planning officers have seen it all, you know? They're looking for any chink in the armour. But I think we've prepped well. What about you? You're presenting the visual impact assessment, right? Yeah. It's less stressful than presenting the whole thing, to be honest. Just need to confidently explain the design rationale and how it blends into the existing landscape. I've got those drone shots which hopefully will showcase that really effectively. I was thinking of highlighting the solar panels on the community hall too – shows we're thinking about sustainability.

Honestly, this Earl Grey tastes like dishwater today. Did you change brands, Liv? Nope, haven't touched the tea. Maybe you're just extra grumpy this morning. Rough day at the office? You have  no  idea. Mr. Henderson decided to micromanage the entire social media rollout. Like, every single emoji had to be pre-approved. Emojis, Liv! Can you believe that? It's soul-crushing. Oh, bless. Sounds like classic Henderson. Remember when he tried to ban glitter during Christmas decorations? Don't remind me! The rebellion was glorious. Speaking of rebellions, have you heard anything from Chloe lately? I saw on Insta she's actually  enjoying  her law internship. No way! Last I heard she was seriously contemplating dropping out and becoming a florist. People change, I guess. Mental health nursing is certainly teaching me that. It has its moments. Last week I had a patient who swore he was Elvis. Trying to convince him he wasn’t was…a challenge. But there are small victories. Seeing someone take that first step towards recovery is unbelievable. Wow. See? That's a proper superpower. I just managed to convince Brenda from marketing that beige isn't a personality trait. "Luigi's," apparently they do a killer tiramisu. Ooh, tempting. I was meaning to go to that vintage market in Brighton, but it’s a bit of a trek. Though... pasta  does  sound good. And I'm desperately needing a day out. This Henderson-induced gloom is starting to cling to me. We could go on Saturday? I finished my shift early that day. We can grab lunch in Brighton and wander around the market. Plus, we can finally have a look at that antique shop you were talking about. Yes! Definitely. That sounds absolutely perfect. What about Mrs. Higginbottom next door? She's been putting her Christmas decorations up... in August. It’s borderline disturbing. I know! I saw a Santa on her front lawn yesterday. It’s baffling. I think she lives in a different dimension where Christmas is a year-round event. It's the sheer commitment, isn’t it?

Blimey, this advert’s a right load of rubbish, innit? Like, who buys a vacuum cleaner based on someone jumping around in a sparkly dress? Honestly, you'd think they'd appeal to, you know,  logic  for once. It's just manufactured aspiration. It's the same with all those ‘clean your house with ease!’ claims. Total nonsense. Remember last Sunday when I asked you to hoover and it ended up looking like a small furry animal had exploded in the living room? That was a windy day, love. Dust bunnies everywhere! Besides, you know I'm not the best at housework. You're the tidy one, that’s why we're still together. Flattery will get you everywhere. Speaking of things we should be doing, have you sorted out your mum's car boot sale stuff yet? She's proper stressing about it. Nah, not yet. Been a bit busy marking those essays, you know? They’re full of grammar horrors. Want to go Saturday? We could grab some chippy after. Saturday sounds good. I could even have a look at some of the things - see if any of them lend themselves to some NLP techniques. You know, framing them in a more appealing way for potential buyers. NLP at a car boot sale? You're kidding, right? Not really. It's about the presentation, the storytelling. "This beautiful teapot has seen many a family tea party over the years" is better than "old teapot - 50p". It's all about influencing perception, same as in psychology, just…on a smaller scale. You're mental, you are. Using your fancy psychology degrees to flog a chipped mug. Still, might work. What are you watching anyway? This show's rubbish. It's a documentary about investigative journalism. It's actually quite fascinating. They're following this reporter who’s looking into a string of burglaries in a nearby town. Apparently, the police are struggling to connect them. Burglary, eh? Proper grim. You thinking of using your therapist skills to get into the burglar’s head? Don’t be ridiculous. Though, crime's always interesting from a psychological standpoint. The motivations…the patterns… It’s way more compelling than any of those reality shows. Yeah, well, I'd rather watch someone eat a mountain of doughnuts than listen to some bloke ramble on about the inner workings of a burglar’s mind. Speaking of eating, fancy ordering a takeaway?

Honestly, this Pinot Grigio is exactly what I needed after battling through a particularly dreadful press conference today. Politicians, honestly! Never a dull moment, but rarely a  good  one. Sounds familiar. Teaching teenagers French is only slightly less infuriating. They all seem to think ‘je suis’ applies to everything. It’s exhausting. But at least they’re not actively trying to deceive the public. Aye, you’re lucky. I’ve been wrestling with a documentary series about the history of Britpop. Hours of archive footage and interviews. Turns out, a lot of the ‘rebels’ were just incredibly well-behaved middle-class lads from the suburbs. Massively undermines the whole narrative, doesn't it? Blimey, sounds a right palaver, that does. At least it's music, though. I'm grappling with a local council report on traffic flow. Riveting, I tell you. Absolutely rivetting. My ears are still ringing from the consultation meetings. Anyone else got anything exciting going on? Actually, yes. I’ve finally started seriously looking at buying a place. Found a couple of potential spots near the canal, surprisingly affordable. But the mortgages... ugh. The paperwork is enough to give you a headache. Oh, really? That’s amazing, Ben! Whereabouts? Near Brindleyplace? I know a brilliant solicitor, she’s ridiculously good with mortgages. Give me her details if you want. That'd be brilliant, Chloe. Seriously, I'm drowning in forms. It’s terrifying, the amount of money involved. I keep having these nightmares about interest rates shooting up. Tell me about it. I’m looking at remortgaging myself. The rates are just insane. Have you looked into fixed-rate deals? Might offer some peace of mind, even if they are a bit pricier initially. Speaking of stressful… I just spent an hour trying to figure out why my podcast app keeps crashing. It’s infuriating! It's supposed to be making my  life  easier, not harder. Anyone else struggling with technology lately? You and me, mate. My phone's decided it no longer recognises my fingerprint. It’s just me, entering a passcode like a relic from the past. Then it drains the battery in five minutes flat. These things are designed to make you buy a new one every year, aren’t they? Absolutely. Planned obsolescence, it's the bane of my existence. I still have a phone from, like, 2015 that works perfectly well. But no, I have to keep up with the latest shiny object.

This is lovely, ANON. Really lovely. Thank you for having us. It’s a pleasure to be here. It’s funny, isn't it, how quickly time flies? Seems like only yesterday we were all young and… ambitious. Absolutely, David. Though I suspect “ambitious” might be stretching it a bit, looking back at some of our early attempts at adulthood! It's wonderful to see you all. It feels a bit like stepping back in time, doesn’t it? All of us here, sharing memories of the sixties. Indeed, Margaret. The sixties… quite the decade. I remember arriving here for the interview – a young, eager teacher, fresh out of Cambridge. The whole area felt so… different then. Much quieter, certainly. And renting a place! Goodness, it was an adventure just  finding  something. Renting! You’re telling me, Brian! I practically lived in temporary accommodation for six months before I found a decent flat near the University. Landlords back then were a different breed altogether, let me tell you. Wanting a deposit equivalent to the house’s value! Speaking of interviews, did you ever have any particularly memorable ones, David? Memorable is one word for it. I remember coming for the interview at the practice here. The senior dentist - a rather gruff gentleman – spent the entire time quizzing me on obscure dental procedures. At one point, he asked me about the proper way to extract a wisdom tooth from an Egyptian mummy! I honestly thought I’d failed. I stammered something about preserving historical artifacts and he just grunted. Apparently, I was employed! Oh, goodness! How utterly bizarre. It sounds like something out of a film. Finding somewhere to live afterwards, though, was a puzzle, wasn’t it? I ended up in a tiny cottage, all damp and drafty. Took me nearly two years to sort out the plumbing. The estate agent swore it was "full of character." It was full of mould, more like! I can relate to that! My first flat was in a converted stable. Mice were regular visitors, and the heating only worked sporadically. But it was cheap, and I was young. It didn't matter so much then. Margaret, did you buy or rent when you first came? I rented to start with, as you know. Then I tried buying, but the banks weren’t exactly throwing mortgages at unemployed EFL teachers! Eventually, I found a small terraced house that needed a  lot  of work.

"Honestly, dear, this Earl Grey is just  perfect . Thank you, Marion. It's lovely to finally sit down and chat properly. I feel like we've been rushing past each other at the gallery for ages.”      "You're very welcome, Penelope. It  is  lovely to have you. All those gallery openings, they’re a whirlwind, aren’t they? And you’re usually darting about, rearranging a porcelain shepherdess or something. Tell me, did you always know you’d end up surrounded by antiques?"      "Goodness, no. Not at all! It rather blossomed, you see. My father, he was a landscape painter, a bit of a bohemian sort. I dabbled, of course. Somerset countryside, you know – utterly inspiring. But I just… I wasn’t as gifted as he was. Still, I loved the visual, the history of things. Started collecting bits and bobs, mostly bits and bobs my aunt would send me from her attic. Then, one thing led to another, a little shop in a village nearby, and then this gallery. It’s been a surprising adventure, really. What about you, darling? Speech and Language Therapy – that sounds utterly fascinating.”      "It was, Penelope. I loved it. Started in the NHS, then moved to private practice a bit later. Mostly children, you know. Helping them find their voice, literally and figuratively. I was born in Sydney, actually. Quite a different landscape to Somerset! Sunshine and eucalyptus rather than rolling hills and cider orchards."      "Sydney! Imagine! Was your family… holidaying over? Or…?"      "My father was a diplomat, stationed there for a few years. It was wonderful, though I barely remember it, to be honest. Came back to England when I was six. Mum always said it was the best cocoa I’d ever tasted, apparently – that’s one of my earliest memories!” “Did your father ever exhibit much? I'm a bit of a patron of the arts, you see, although with running the gallery it’s often a case of admiring rather than acquiring.”      "Oh, he did. A few local shows, a couple in London, but he was never one for the hustle and bustle of the art world. Preferred his little studio overlooking the Levels. A peculiar man, really. Never did well with money, stubbornly insisted on using the best paints, naturally. We were always a bit…  comfortable , shall we say, but not lavish. My mother managed the finances very well, bless her.

Right, so, I’m thinking butternut squash risotto for tonight. Fancy that? Bit autumnal, yeah? Sounds lovely, Liam. Much better than last week’s attempt at paella. Remember that? The rice was… crunchy. Don't remind me! That was a disaster. A culinary tragedy. I blame the saffron. Definitely the saffron. Did you manage to get those gingerbread men cutters I asked for? Yep! Found a set in that little vintage shop down the road. They're adorable, proper old-fashioned ones. Gonna decorate ‘em later tonight, once we’ve got the risotto sorted. Thinking loads of icing and maybe some little candy canes. Candy canes already? Bit early for that isn't it? Nope. Christmas starts now! Besides, I like to be prepared. My aunt Maureen would have a conniption if I wasn't at least halfway through the Christmas prep by mid-November. You know her. Oh, I know her alright. A force of nature. Speaking of which… any word from Chloe? Should she be here soon? She texted. Said she's just finishing up at the cafe, a rush on pumpkin spice lattes. She’ll be here in about half an hour, wants to help with the decorations. Perfect! I was thinking we could get the fairy lights up in the living room tonight. Last year’s plastic one was looking a bit sad, even covered in tinsel. Good thinking. Though finding a decent one that isn't shedding needles everywhere is always a mission. Maybe we should order one online? Chloe's got experience with that, right? She's constantly getting things shipped to the cafe. Yeah, she's a pro. We'll ask her. Oh, and I saw a really cute little candy reindeer decoration at the market last week. Should I grab it? Go for it! You’re getting me properly excited for Christmas now. I was feeling a bit... resistant, to be honest. All the commercialism and everything. Honestly, it's just an excuse to eat loads of chocolate and hang out with people you like. Can't complain about that. Speaking of people we like… that'll be Chloe. Right, risotto's nearly ready. Let's go say hi! Hey guys! Sorry I’m a bit late, it was absolutely manic at the cafe.

It’s… a lot of fields, isn’t it? Between here and London. Feels like we’ve been driving for hours already. It is a bit monotonous, yes. But think, all that land used to be woodlands, before the enclosure acts, you know. History’s layered under everything, even boring fields. Almost like my editing desk - layers of text needing careful sifting. You and your metaphors, Mum. So, about the desk… any progress on finding someone to take over your role at the publishing house? You’ve mentioned you're hoping to slow down. A little. There's a young woman, fresh out of Oxford, applying. Seems bright, enthusiastic. Reads well, which is half the battle, honestly. Though, she lacks a certain… grit. Something you have in abundance, even when grumbling about fields. Grit? Thanks, I think? It’s a consequence of fighting with professors about Foucault for three years. Speaking of which… how's the thesis coming along? You haven’t asked, have you? Don’t want to trigger the existential dread. I’m a mother, darling. Existential dread is a practically required skill. And yes, I have asked. Vaguely. A few times. Need a little update. Feeling a bit overprotective about your future, even though you're practically a grown-up. It’s... slow. Honestly. Chapter three is proving particularly stubborn. I'm questioning everything about the initial premise. I’m starting to think maybe I should have just focused on Derrida. Much cleaner, less messy. Derrida’s brilliant, naturally, but you’re clearly drawn to this post-structuralist exploration of mythology. Don’t abandon it just because it's difficult. Remember what Professor Davies said? About wrestling with complexity being the entire point? He also said I needed to “tighten the argument,” which is basically academic code for “rewrite the whole thing.” And… it’s the thinking about  after  the thesis that’s getting to me. What then? Well, that's the big question, isn't it? You've always said you wanted to work with literature, but in a more… dynamic way. Not just academia. Exactly. I've been looking at those digital humanities projects, the interactive narratives… but that feels like a complete career shift. And the job market is… well, it's not exactly booming. No, it isn’t. But you’re smart, resourceful. And you’re not entirely tied to London, are you? Remember discussing looking at houses in Bristol?

"Honestly, this event is a whirlwind, isn’t it? So many people, so much catching up…or, in my case, meeting for the first time. I'm Eleanor, by the way." "Hello, Eleanor. I’m Imogen. Yes, it  is  rather a lot. It’s my first Alumni Day too, actually. I work in language research, coordinating projects mostly. It seemed a good opportunity to network, and...well, soak up the atmosphere of Cambridge." She gestures vaguely around the bustling Law Faculty common room. “Atmosphere is one word for it. Mayhem might be another! Wonderful to see so many former students returning. I'm Arthur, a lecturer here, history and archaeology – a somewhat niche combination, I admit.” "Oh, archaeology! That's fascinating. I've always been drawn to it, though I’m firmly in the administrative side of things, sadly. I assist with research projects. What sort of history and archaeology do you specialise in, Arthur?" "Primarily, I focus on the Romano-British period, particularly settlement patterns. I’ve spent many years involved in excavations – quite a few of them uncovering whole villages, actually. Gruelling work, but incredibly rewarding to see a place come to life, even if it’s just reconstructing it in your mind." "That sounds incredible! Reconstructing lives from the ground up, that's amazing. It links interestingly with my work, actually. A lot of my current research is looking at language evolution – how communities adopt and adapt languages as they migrate and interact. It's amazing how much history is embedded in words themselves." "Absolutely! Languages are the ultimate living records, aren’t they?" "Precisely! When I was excavating a site near Lincoln – Eleanor, you're from Lincoln, aren't you? - we found some fascinating pottery shards with inscribed runes. It strongly suggested a significant Scandinavian presence earlier than previously documented. That single find reframed our understanding of the area’s history." "Yes, it’s true! Lincoln has such a rich history. I've no direct connection to the archaeology, but the past feels very present there. Do those runes relate to the Viking settlements?" "Indeed. It wasn’t just raiding, you see. They settled, integrated, and their language left its mark. Which brings me to a tangential point. I've become increasingly interested in the influence of Arabic on medieval European languages, particularly through trade routes and scholarship." “That’s such a fascinating connection! I’ve been researching loanwords in Southeast Asian languages, specifically how Chinese has been a conduit for various influences.

Right, so, another week done. Honestly, this shoot with the craft beer company was… exhausting. They wanted slow-motion shots of hops falling. Hops! For, like, an hour. Hops, yeah? Sounds peak. You’d think with all the funding they’ve got, they’d get some better visuals. Well, at least you’re employed, Liam. My sourdough starter is being a drama queen again. Refusing to rise. I swear, bread baking is just dealing with a temperamental alien. You’ll crack it, Maya. It’s just a phase. Remember when my flat white machine decided to self-destruct mid-rush hour? That was a fun morning. Almost threw the whole business out the window. Speaking of drama, did you guys see that video of the dog trying to steal a croissant? It’s viral, apparently. Especially when the world feels, you know…cracked. Plus, honestly, the dog  was  adorable. It reminded me of working a double shift and needing something sweet. True, true. It's easy to get bogged down in the negativity. People are just looking to laugh. But it does make you think, doesn't it? About perspectives. I mean, my café's doing alright, but it's a constant hustle. Supporting young baristas, trying to pay fair wages… it's tough. It’s all tough, isn't it? I'm seeing more and more grads struggling to find their footing. The pressure’s insane. My cousin, Ben, he’s still living with his parents a year after finishing uni. Can’t afford to move out of Bristol. That’s mental. I’m almost there. Got a place lined up, but the rent's eye-watering. Makes you wonder if all this education is even worth it sometimes. Don't say that, Liam! You’re clever, you’ll be fine. I dropped out of my Masters, remember? Couldn't justify the debt. But I'm happy with what I do. It’s tangible. You create something. And honestly, that degree isn’t everything. I left Sixth Form early, straight into opening the café.

Honestly, David, this whole NHS thing is just… exhausting. I spent half my lunch break today untangling a student's anxiety about getting a referral for physiotherapy. And the frustration falls on us, doesn’t it? We're constantly fielding these worries, trying to offer reassuring words that frankly, we don't entirely believe ourselves. Did you see that article in The Guardian about the private equity firms sniffing around GP practices? Don’t even mention it. It makes my blood boil. Turning healthcare into a commodity… it’s obscene, really. And thinking about our savings… even with that little nest egg we've been accumulating, the thought of needing significant private healthcare down the line is unsettling. It is. I’ve been crunching some numbers, actually. Considering that interest rate hike. We need to re-evaluate our investment strategy slightly. Maybe shift a bit more into bonds, reduce some of the riskier stuff? Just a small adjustment, to buffer against potential volatility. You and your spreadsheets! You always were the sensible one. But yes, probably a good idea. It does feel like we’re constantly bracing for the next economic downturn. Remember when we thought house prices couldn't possibly go any higher? Oh, indeed. That feels like a lifetime ago. Speaking of things that feel like a lifetime ago… did you manage to catch that new series of 'Detectorists' on BBC iPlayer? Oh, praise be! Yes! It was glorious. No bombastic plot twists, no dramatic confrontations, just… perfectly observed rural England.

Honestly, this sourdough is divine, Anne. You really outdid yourself this time. It's a far cry from that dreadful supermarket stuff we had last week. It  is  good! Much better. Thanks, Anne. So, Dad, how's your knee feeling today? Still protesting every time you try to walk to the shops? Just a bit grumpy, love. Nothing I can't handle.
